False identities, proxies, encryption and compromised machines frustrate attribution.

Portability and transferability

Data move instantly and are copied without loss, straining concepts such as theft.

Global, transboundary nature

Offender, victim, servers and evidence sit in different countries, raising jurisdiction and cooperation problems.

Notice how each feature breaks an assumption of ordinary criminal law. Theft assumes the owner loses the thing, yet a copied file leaves the original in place. Prosecution assumes the offender can be identified and reached, yet anonymity and borders get in the way.

Remember: "Scammers Are Anonymous, Portable and Global" = Scale, Accessibility, Anonymity, Portability and transferability, Global.

slides.title: R v Gold: why the old criminal law failed
slides.html:
In R v Gold the House of Lords refused to stretch forgery law to cover hacking, so computer misuse needed statutes of its own.

R v Gold [1988] AC 1063 (House of Lords, 1988)†

Facts
The defendants used another customer's identification number and password, obtained by a trick, to access British Telecom's Prestel service, including a royal mailbox.
Issue
No unauthorised access offence was then available. Could they be convicted of making a false instrument under section 1 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981?
Held
No. The House upheld their acquittal. Lord Brandon called the prosecution a "Procrustean attempt" to force the facts into an unsuitable statute: dishonestly gaining access to a data bank by a trick was not a crime, and making it one was for Parliament (class slide 3).
Key point
Offences built around tangible property and documents could not capture computer misuse.

Parliaments responded with laws aimed at computers themselves:

  1. United States: a computer fraud law in 1984, expanded in 1986 as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA).
  2. United Kingdom: the Computer Misuse Act, which class slide 3 dates to 1991 but which is usually cited as the Computer Misuse Act 1990.†
  3. India: the IT Act, 2000, primarily recognising electronic records and transactions; then the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008, in force from 27 October 2009, which added most offences in ss. 66A to 67C.

Law update. Class slide 3 gives 1991 for the UK Act; the usual citation is 1990.† The citation of R v Gold is also unverified.†

slides.title: Defining and classifying cybercrime
slides.html:
"Cybercrime" has no fixed definition, so classify it by the computer's role (target, tool or incidental), because the role tells you which law applies.

"Cybercrime" is undefined and is used interchangeably with computer, high tech, digital, electronic and technology enabled crime (class slide 4). A label with no legal meaning cannot decide a case, so lawyers sort cybercrime by the part the computer plays.

Role of the computerExamplesLegal consequence
As the targetHacking, malware, denial of serviceUsually needs cyber specific offences, such as ss. 43 and 66
As a tool for existing crimesChild abuse material, harassment, fraudOften also chargeable under general law
As incidental to a crime but holding evidence of itMessages on a murder victim's phoneRaises evidence rather than substantive questions

The logic follows R v Gold. When the computer is the target, older offences built for property and documents do not fit, so the IT Act's own provisions are needed. When it is only a tool, the crime already exists in the general law, and the question becomes overlap (Chapter 16). When it is merely incidental, the problem is proof, not liability.

slides.title: The Budapest Convention and the class statistics
slides.html:
The Budapest Convention, the first multilateral cybercrime treaty, sorts offences into four categories that map onto the IT Act; India is not a party.

The Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime, known as the Budapest Convention, is the first multilateral cybercrime treaty. It covers substantive law, procedure and international cooperation (class slide 5), which answers the global, transboundary feature of cybercrime.

Convention categoryIndian counterpart
Offences against the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and systems (illegal access, interception, data interference)IT Act ss. 43 and 66
Computer related forgery and fraudss. 66C and 66D
Content related offences (child pornography)ss. 67 to 67B
Copyright infringementThe Copyright Act

Law update. Class slide 5 records 64 parties; the figure changes, so check the current count. India is not a party.†

Trends shown in class. Class slide 6's NCRB 2017 infographic records a 77 per cent rise in cybercrime cases in 2017 over 2016, led by Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka, and a near 50 per cent rise in offences against the State between 2015 and 2017.

Law update. These figures are dated: cite the latest NCRB Crime in India. Recent digital arrest complaint data appear in Chapter 17.

slides.title: Two tracks: contraventions and offences
slides.html:
The IT Act runs two tracks: civil contraventions, needing no mental element and leading to compensation, and criminal offences, needing a guilty mind and leading to punishment.

Class slide 7 contrasts the two tracks. Contraventions cover unauthorised access and interference; offences add a mental element. Learn this table, because it frames every Module 7 problem.

FeatureContraventionsOffences
ProvisionsChapter IX: s. 43(a) to (j), ss. 43A, 44 and 45Chapter XI: ss. 65 to 74, with ss. 75 to 78
Mental elementNone (except s. 43(j))Intention, knowledge, dishonesty or fraud
NatureCivilCriminal
Decided byAn adjudicating officer or, above the pecuniary limit, a civil court (s. 46)Criminal courts, according to s. 77B
Investigated byThe Controller or an authorised officer (s. 28)An officer not below the rank of Inspector (s. 78)
OutcomeCompensation or penaltiesImprisonment, fine or both
CompoundingCompoundable (s. 63)Compoundable only within s. 77A

The tracks are not alternatives you choose between. The same act can sit on both: s. 66 punishes a s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulently (Chapter 16). So start on the civil track and then ask whether the mental element lifts the act onto the criminal one.

slides.title: Key definitions in s. 2(1)
slides.html:
Section 2(1) defines the building blocks of the Act; note especially that "access" is wide enough to include merely sending instructions to a computer.

Access (s. 2(1)(a))
Gaining entry into, instructing or communicating with the logical, arithmetical or memory function resources of a computer, system or network, so sending instructions counts.
Computer (s. 2(1)(i))
Any electronic, magnetic, optical or other high speed data processing device performing logical, arithmetic and memory functions.
Computer network (s. 2(1)(j))
The interconnection of computers or communication devices by any means.
Computer resource (s. 2(1)(k))
A computer, communication device, system, network, data, database or software: the umbrella term.
Computer system (s. 2(1)(l))
A device or devices with programs, instructions and data performing logic, storage, retrieval and communication functions.
Data (s. 2(1)(o))
Information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions in formalised form intended for computer processing.
Electronic record (s. 2(1)(t))
Data, a record, an image or sound stored, received or sent electronically, or microfilm or computer generated microfiche.
Information (s. 2(1)(v))
Includes data, messages, text, images, sound, voice, codes, programs, software and databases.

Why these matter: the width of "access" means a remote command, not only a login, can be access under s. 43(a). The width of "computer resource" explains why its addition to s. 43(a) in 2008 mattered.

Law update. The clause letters of s. 2(1) should be checked against India Code before you cite them.†

slides.title: A technical primer: attacks mapped to sections
slides.html:
Each common attack technique engages particular IT Act sections; learn what the technique does, then the clause it triggers.

TechniqueWhat it isSections engaged
HackingUnauthorised access by stolen or guessed credentials or exploited vulnerabilitiess. 43(a) and s. 66
MalwareViruses attaching to files, self spreading worms, ransomware encrypting data for payments. 43(c), (d) and (i), s. 66; s. 66F with terrorist intent
Denial of serviceFlooding a site with traffic; "distributed" when many machines are useds. 43(e) and (f) and s. 66
Phishing and vishingMessages or calls impersonating trusted bodiesss. 66C and 66D
SIM swappingMoving a number to a new SIM to capture one time passwordsss. 43, 66C and 66D
SkimmingCopying card data at ATMsss. 43(b) and 66C, and s. 66B for stolen devices
Image abuseCapturing or sharing private or explicit imagesss. 66E, 67 and 67A

Authentication

Confirms who a user is.

Authorisation

Decides what she may do.

Many "unauthorised access" disputes are really about authorisation: the user logged in properly but went beyond what she was allowed to do, as in Bignell and Allison (Chapter 15). Keep two more words apart: cybersecurity protects systems, while cybercrime punishes misuse.

slides.title: Exam guidance: the foundations
slides.html:
Cybercrime law exists because offences built around tangible property and documents could not capture computer misuse; the IT Act answers with civil contraventions and criminal offences.

A strong foundations answer follows the notes' own logic, in this order:

  1. The problem: the five features (class slide 2) and the failure of forgery law in R v Gold.
  2. The response: the CFAA, the UK Computer Misuse Act, and India's IT Act, 2000 with the 2008 amendment.
  3. Definition: "cybercrime" is undefined, so classify crimes by the computer's role (target, tool, incidental).
  4. The two tracks: compare contraventions and offences using class slide 7.
  5. The tools: s. 2(1) definitions and the technique to section map.

Exam focus. Three common mistakes: treating "cybercrime" as a defined term, confusing s. 43 with s. 66, and citing the 2017 statistics as current.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Section 43: the foundation of Module 7
slides.html:
Section 43 makes anyone who does one of ten acts without the owner's permission liable to pay uncapped compensation, with no mental element except under clause (j).

Section 43 underpins Module 7, because s. 66 makes its contraventions criminal when done dishonestly or fraudulently. Learn s. 43 well and you have already learnt the conduct element of s. 66. This chapter covers its clauses, unauthorised access, adjudication, s. 43A, the classroom problems and Aaron Swartz.

s. 43, IT Act, 2000. Where any person, "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge of a computer, computer system or computer network", does any of ten acts (clauses (a) to (j)), he is liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person affected.

ElementRule
TriggerNo permission of the owner or person in charge
ConductAny one of ten acts, clauses (a) to (j)
RemedyCompensation without any cap since 2008 (previously one crore rupees)
Mental elementNone, except under clause (j)
NatureCivil liability

Why no mental element? Section 43 compensates the person affected rather than punishing the actor, so doing the act without permission is enough. The guilty mind is what s. 66 adds.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: The ten acts of s. 43: clauses (a) to (e)
slides.html:
Clauses (a) to (e) cover getting in, taking data out, planting a contaminant, damaging and disrupting; each needs only lack of permission.

ClauseAct done without permissionPoint to remember
(a) (class slide 8)Accessing or securing access to a computer, system, network or, since 2008, computer resourceLack of authorisation is the key ingredient, which requires identifying the owner or person in charge
(b) (class slide 9)Downloading, copying or extracting data, databases or information, including from removable storageThe clause for data theft by employees
(c) (class slide 10)Introducing a computer contaminant or virusSee Explanations (i) and (iii)
(d)Damaging a computer, system, network, data, database or programDamage means to destroy, alter, delete, add, modify or rearrange (Explanation (iv))
(e) (class slide 11)Disrupting a systemAn unexpected deviation from normal operation

Class slide 10's example of clause (d)

A student changes a placement cell's email password, making the account unusable for days and costing candidates jobs. Changing the password "alters" the account, which falls within damage under Explanation (iv).

Notice how wide "damage" is: adding or rearranging counts, so nothing needs to be destroyed.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: The ten acts of s. 43: clauses (f) to (j)
slides.html:
Clauses (f) to (j) cover denying access, helping others in, charging services to someone else, destroying information and stealing source code; only (j) needs intent.

ClauseAct done without permissionPoint to remember
(f)Denying access to authorised personsAs in denial of service attacks
(g) (class slide 12)Assisting any person to gain access in contravention of the ActSuch as by sharing passwords; a clause of broad sweep
(h)Charging services used by one person to another's account by tamperingAimed at misuse of access codes, IDs and passwords
(i) (2008)Destroying, deleting or altering information or diminishing its value or utilityThe wording of the old s. 66 "hacking" offence
(j) (2008, class slide 13)Stealing, concealing, destroying or altering source code with intent to cause damageThe only "premeditated" contravention

Clause (j) is the exception to the rule of no mental element, which is why the notes call it "premeditated". Clause (i) shows the history: the pre 2009 hacking offence survives as a civil clause, and its criminal form now comes through s. 66.

Remember: each clause letter starts its own hook word. (a) Access; (b) Bring data out (copy); (c) Contaminant; (d) Damage; (e) Erratic system (disrupt); (f) Fence out users (deny); (g) Give a way in (assist); (h) Hand the bill to another (charge); (i) Information destroyed or diminished; (j) Jack the source code (with intent).

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: What makes access unauthorised
slides.html:
Access is unauthorised only if it goes beyond the particular data and kind of access the owner permitted, so the scope of "permission" defines s. 43 liability.

DPP v Bignell [1998] 1 Cr App R 1 (Divisional Court, 1997)†

Police officers who used the Police National Computer for private purposes did not commit unauthorised access, because they were authorised to access that data. It is the classic case of unauthorised use by authorised users.

R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex parte Government of the United States of America (the Allison case) [2000] 2 AC 216 (House of Lords, 1999)†

A credit card company employee accessed accounts outside her assignment. Access is unauthorised if the person is not entitled to control access of the kind in question and lacks consent from someone who is (class slide 8).

Read together, the cases say that authority is measured against particular data and kinds of access. A bad purpose alone did not make access unauthorised in Bignell; going outside the data assigned did in Allison. Under s. 43, the scope of the owner's "permission" defines liability.

Law update. Both cases are English and persuasive only in India.† Their reports were not checked for these notes.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Adjudication and appeals
slides.html:
Section 43 claims up to five crore rupees go to the adjudicating officer, then on appeal to the TDSAT and the High Court; larger claims go to civil courts.

  1. Forum. Claims up to five crore rupees go to the adjudicating officer appointed under s. 46 (typically senior State officers).† Larger claims go to civil courts.
  2. Powers and factors. The officer has civil court powers and must consider the gain or unfair advantage made, the loss caused and any repetition (s. 47).
  3. First appeal. To the Appellate Tribunal, now the TDSAT after the Finance Act, 2017 (s. 57).
  4. Second appeal. To the High Court on fact or law (s. 62).

Three supporting rules complete the scheme:

  • s. 61 bars civil courts from matters within the officer's competence, so a small claim cannot bypass the officer.
  • The Controller may investigate (s. 28).
  • Contraventions may be compounded (s. 63).

Law update. The Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 adjusted the wording of s. 46 from 30 November 2023 but did not change s. 43.

Remember: under s. 47 the officer weighs G-L-R: gain, loss, repetition. The appeal ladder runs officer (s. 46) → TDSAT (s. 57) → High Court (s. 62).

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Section 43A: compensation for failure to protect data
slides.html:
Section 43A makes a body corporate that negligently fails to secure sensitive personal data compensate those who suffer, until it is omitted on 13 May 2027.

Section 43 targets the intruder; s. 43A targets the custodian who fails to keep data safe. Its liability rests on negligence, not on any act of access.

IngredientWhat is required
WhoA body corporate: any company, firm, sole proprietorship or association in commercial or professional activity
DataPossesses, deals with or handles sensitive personal data or information in a computer resource it owns, controls or operates
FaultNegligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices and procedures (as agreed, as specified by law, or as prescribed)
ResultThereby causes wrongful loss or gain
RemedyMust compensate the person affected

The SPDI Rules 2011 define sensitive data (passwords, financial information, health conditions, sexual orientation, medical records, biometrics), require a privacy policy and consent, and treat IS/ISO/IEC 27001 or an approved code as reasonable practice.† Reported adjudication orders against banks for phishing losses (Tamil Nadu, 2010; Maharashtra, 2013) are illustrations only.†

Current law update. DPDP s. 44(2)(a) omits s. 43A from 13 May 2027. Until then, s. 43A and the SPDI Rules govern private sector data security; afterwards the Board penalises without compensating. Section 43 is unaffected.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Classroom Problem I: Ram and Sharpie
slides.html:
Sharing server credentials is assistance under s. 43(g); using them to alter a story is s. 43(a), (d) and (i); dishonesty adds s. 66 for both.

Problem I (slide 15 in class). Ram, a former SDTv web producer who left after a dispute in October 2019, shared a Tribune Co. server's credentials in an Anonymous chat room and encouraged their use, and "Sharpie" used them to alter a news story.

PersonCivil track (s. 43)Criminal track (s. 66)
RamHis disclosure is assistance to facilitate unauthorised access: s. 43(g)If aimed at causing his former employer wrongful loss, it is dishonest, so s. 66 also applies, with possible abetment liability
SharpieAccessed without permission (s. 43(a)) and altered information (s. 43(d) and (i))Dishonest given his purpose, so s. 66 applies to him too

Conclusion. Both owe compensation, and s. 66F does not arise without terrorist intent.

Use this as the model method for every problem: name the s. 43 clause for each person first, then ask whether dishonesty or fraud lifts it into s. 66, and only then consider any graver offence.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Classroom Problem II: Ajay
slides.html:
Copying code without permission is a s. 43(b) contravention whatever the intent, but s. 43(j) and s. 66 need intent to damage or dishonesty, which genuine inadvertence negates.

Problem II (slide 16 in class). Ajay, an IndiaBulls programmer, downloaded proprietary trading code before leaving and claimed he meant to copy only open source files.

  1. s. 43(b). Copying without permission is a contravention whatever his intent, so inadvertence is no answer to the civil claim.
  2. s. 43(j) and s. 66. These need intent to damage or dishonesty, which genuine inadvertence negates.
  3. s. 65. It needs code required by law to be kept, so it is unlikely to apply.
  4. Other remedies. Breach of confidence and copyright claims remain.

The problem shows the two tracks working apart. Ajay's excuse fails on the civil track, where no mental element is needed, but it can defeat the criminal track, where dishonesty must be proved.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: The case of Aaron Swartz
slides.html:
The Aaron Swartz prosecution asks whether breaking contractual terms makes access "without permission"; the better Indian view leaves such breaches on the civil track.

Class slide 17 recounts the CFAA prosecution of Aaron Swartz for downloading millions of JSTOR articles through MIT's network. Critics argued that the CFAA lets terms of service or codes of conduct define felonies. He died by suicide while facing up to 35 years.

The Indian question is the same: whether breach of contractual terms makes access "without permission" under ss. 43 and 66.

Authority

No settled Indian authority was located.

Better view

Reserve criminal liability for genuine dishonesty or fraud, leaving contractual breaches to the civil track.

The better view fits the structure of the Act. Section 66 exists to punish a guilty mind, so treating every breach of a website's terms as a crime would let private contracts decide what is criminal, which is exactly the criticism of the CFAA.

slides.part: Chapter 15: Civil Contraventions and Adjudication: Sections 43 and 43A
slides.title: Exam guidance: ss. 43 and 43A
slides.html:
Section 43 imposes uncapped civil liability for ten acts done without permission, needing no mental element except clause (j); claims up to five crore rupees go to the adjudicating officer.

From the adjudicating officer, appeals go to the TDSAT and then the High Court. Section 43A adds liability for negligent data security until 13 May 2027.

Exam focus. Four mistakes to avoid: requiring intent for every clause; citing the old one crore cap; forgetting that s. 43A lasts until 13 May 2027; and sending large claims to the officer.

Worked example

An employee who changes a server password before resigning and locks everyone out commits contraventions under s. 43(d), (f) and (i), and s. 66 if dishonest.

Why each clause: changing the password alters the system (damage, clause (d)); locking colleagues out denies access to authorised persons (clause (f)); and the information becomes useless, diminishing its value or utility (clause (i)).

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Section 65: tampering with computer source documents
slides.html:
Section 65 punishes knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying or altering source code that the law requires to be kept; that legal requirement is the ingredient most often missed.

This chapter covers ss. 65, 66 and 66B, and the overlap between the IT Act and the general criminal law.

s. 65, IT Act, 2000. Whoever knowingly or intentionally conceals, destroys or alters, or causes another to conceal, destroy or alter, computer source code used for a computer, programme, system or network, when the code is required to be kept or maintained by law, is punishable with up to three years, or a fine up to two lakh rupees, or both.

"Computer source code" means the listing of programmes, computer commands, design and layout, and programme analysis of a computer resource in any form.

IngredientWhat must be shown
1. Mental elementKnowledge or intention
2. ActConcealment, destruction or alteration
3. Subject matterSource code used for a computer resource
4. Legal dutyA legal requirement to keep that code: the ingredient most often missed

Without the fourth ingredient, s. 65 cannot apply, and tampering with ordinary code must be analysed under s. 43 (and s. 66 if dishonest), as Problem II showed.

Remember: "Keep Code Safe, Legally" = Knowledge or intention, Concealment, destruction or alteration, Source code, Legal requirement to keep it.

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Syed Asifuddin: device identifiers as source code
slides.html:
Syed Asifuddin read "source code" broadly: altering a handset's Electronic Serial Number attracts s. 65.

Syed Asifuddin v State of Andhra Pradesh, 2005 Cri LJ 4314; 2006 (1) ALD (Cri) 96 (Andhra Pradesh High Court, V.V.S. Rao J, 29 July 2005)

Facts
Tata Indicom employees allegedly reprogrammed the 32 bit Electronic Serial Numbers (ESNs) of Reliance's subsidised, network locked handsets so that they worked on Tata's network. The FIR invoked IPC ss. 409, 420 and 120B, IT Act s. 65 and Copyright Act s. 63, and quashing was sought under s. 482 CrPC.
Held
Prima facie, the ESN and the System Identification Code that each provider maintains and assigns to instruments are computer source code, so altering the ESN attracts s. 65. The proceedings under s. 65 and Copyright Act s. 63 continued, while the IPC charges were reportedly quashed.†
Significance
"Source code" is read broadly to include device identifiers.

Link it to the ingredients: the identifiers were codes that providers maintain, so later answers apply s. 65 on the Syed Asifuddin reasoning only if the codes must be maintained by law.

Law update. Class slide 18 dates the case to 2006. It was decided on 29 July 2005 and is reported at 2005 Cri LJ 4314 (also 2006 (1) ALD (Cri) 96).

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Section 66: a s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulently
slides.html:
Section 66 is s. 43 plus a guilty mind: the same act becomes a crime when done dishonestly or fraudulently.

s. 66, IT Act, 2000. If any person dishonestly or fraudulently does any act referred to in s. 43, he is punishable with up to three years, or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both.

Dishonestly
Intending wrongful gain or loss.
Fraudulently
Intending to defraud.

Both terms were defined in IPC ss. 24 and 25, now BNS ss. 2(7) and 2(9), and references to repealed provisions are ordinarily read as references to their re enactments under s. 8 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.†

Points. 43s. 66
ConductThe same conduct: the ten acts in s. 43
Mental elementNone (except clause (j))Dishonesty or fraud
NatureCivil contraventionCognizable, bailable offence
ResultCompensationImprisonment, fine or both

Class slide 14 shows that the two sections differ only in the mental element. Analysis therefore begins with the relevant s. 43 clause and asks whether dishonesty or fraud is proved. The pre 2009 s. 66 created a "hacking" offence close to today's s. 43(i).

Law update. Class slide 14 cites the IPC, which was repealed from 1 July 2024; read its references as the BNS equivalents above.†

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Section 66B: stolen computer resources and devices
slides.html:
Section 66B punishes dishonestly receiving or retaining a stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen.

s. 66B, IT Act, 2000. Whoever dishonestly receives or retains a stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen, is punishable with up to three years, or a fine up to one lakh rupees, or both.

Class slide 19 links it to IPC s. 411, now BNS s. 317.† The section is about holding the stolen thing; misusing the data or identity inside it is covered by other sections.

SituationProvisions
Buying a stolen iPhoneThe direct case of s. 66B
SIM swapping or cloningMainly ss. 66C, 66D and 43 with 66; s. 66B only where a stolen SIM or device is received
ATM skimmings. 43(b) for copying data and s. 66C for using it, with s. 66B where stolen cards or skimmers are received

Law update. IPC s. 411 on class slide 19 is repealed; the BNS equivalent, s. 317, is unverified.†

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Special law or general law?
slides.html:
Where the IT Act and the general criminal law reach the same conduct, compare ingredients: the general offence survives only if it has an ingredient the IT Act provision lacks.

The question matters in practice because the IPC charges were non bailable while the IT Act charges were bailable and compoundable. The law developed in three steps.

  1. Step one. In Sharat Babu Digumarti (2017) 2 SCC 18 (14 December 2016), the Supreme Court held that where electronic obscene material falls under s. 67, IPC s. 292 cannot be invoked for the same act, because the IT Act provisions with s. 81 form a special scheme (Chapter 19).
  2. Step two. In Gagan Harsh Sharma v State of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court, Ranjit More and Bharati Dangre JJ, 26 October 2018; 2018 SCC OnLine Bom 17705), employees accused of stealing healthcare software and data faced IPC ss. 408 and 420 (non bailable and not freely compoundable) and IT Act ss. 43, 65 and 66 (bailable and compoundable). The Court quashed the IPC charges because the IT Act covered the conduct, and a special leave petition was dismissed in limine.
  3. Step three. Another Division Bench disagreed and referred the question in Awadhesh Kumar Parasnath Pathak v State of Maharashtra (Criminal Application No. 2562 of 2019, Aurangabad Bench). The Full Bench held that the general law is not excluded where an ingredient of the general offence is missing from the special provision, such as deception in cheating, which s. 43 read with s. 66 does not require.

Current position. In the Bombay High Court, compare ingredients and allow the general offence alongside the IT Act where it has an additional ingredient; Sharat Babu still governs where both provisions cover the same conduct. The question is unsettled nationally and must now be answered against the BNS.

slides.part: Chapter 16: Source Code Tampering and Computer Related Offences: Sections 65, 66 and 66B
slides.title: Exam guidance: ss. 65, 66 and 66B
slides.html:
Section 65 needs knowing or intentional tampering with legally required source code; s. 66 is a s. 43 act plus dishonesty or fraud; s. 66B covers dishonestly held stolen devices.

SectionConductMental elementPunishment
s. 65Conceal, destroy or alter source code required by law to be keptKnowingly or intentionallyUp to 3 years, or fine up to ₹2 lakh, or both
s. 66Any s. 43 actDishonestly or fraudulentlyUp to 3 years, or fine up to ₹5 lakh, or both
s. 66BReceive or retain a stolen computer resource or communication deviceDishonestly; knowing or having reason to believe it stolenUp to 3 years, or fine up to ₹1 lakh, or both

Exam focus. Do not omit the legal requirement in s. 65, treat s. 66 as needing a separate act, or claim that the IT Act always excludes the general law.

Worked example

A repair shop that buys suspected stolen phones and changes their identifiers commits s. 66B (receiving), s. 65 (on the Syed Asifuddin reasoning, if the codes must be maintained by law) and ss. 43 and 66, with any BNS charge depending on a comparison of ingredients.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Identity in digital form
slides.html:
Online, whoever holds a person's credentials can act as that person, which is why credential misuse underlies most online fraud.

This chapter covers identity theft (s. 66C), cheating by personation (s. 66D), digital arrest scams and privacy violation (s. 66E).

Class slide 20 explains that identity now includes a virtual identity made of electronic signatures, passwords and biometric details. A password does not check who is typing it, so whoever holds the credentials can act as the person. That is why credential misuse underlies most online fraud, and why the law protects the credential itself.

s. 66C: identity theft

Using someone's credential.

s. 66D: cheating by personation

Pretending to be someone in order to cheat.

s. 66E: violation of privacy

Capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Sections 66C and 66D
slides.html:
Section 66C punishes using someone's credential; s. 66D punishes pretending to be someone, through a device or computer, in order to cheat.

Section 66C, IT Act, 2000 (identity theft). Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature is punishable with up to three years and a fine up to one lakh rupees.

Section 66D, IT Act, 2000 (cheating by personation). Whoever, by means of a communication device or computer resource, cheats by personation is punishable with up to three years and a fine up to one lakh rupees.

Points. 66Cs. 66D
Core ideaUsing someone's credentialPretending to be someone in order to cheat
Key ingredientThe credential must be used, not merely heldPersonation: pretending to be another, substituting persons or misrepresenting identity, with deception and dishonest inducement
Typical casesLogging in with a captured one time passwordPhishing, fake profiles and impersonation of officials by video call

Example from the notes

A fake bank caller who obtains a transfer commits s. 66D; if she then logs in with a captured one time password she also commits s. 66C.

Law update. Cheating by personation in the general law is now BNS s. 319.†

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Classroom illustrations: Hari, Bank NSP and NASSCOM
slides.html:
Three classroom illustrations show credential misuse (Hari), misuse of an employer's systems (Bank NSP) and phishing as personation (NASSCOM v Ajay Sood).

Hari (slide 20, hypothetical, shown in class)

A Bengaluru investment banker's unused credit card was misused after his records were stolen. Using his card credentials is s. 66C; charging purchases to his account by manipulating a system is s. 43(h), and s. 66 if dishonest.

The Bank NSP case (slide 21, 2013, shown in class)

A bank management trainee, after a broken engagement, created false email identities (one resembling a bar association's name) and used the bank's computers to email her former fiancé's foreign clients, costing his company business. The company sued the bank, raising misuse of an employer's systems and the employer's liability. No reported judgment was located.†

NASSCOM v Ajay Sood (Delhi High Court, 2005)†

A placement agency sent emails in NASSCOM's name to harvest personal data for headhunting. The case is usually cited as recognising phishing as passing off,† and although civil, it is the paradigm of the personation punished by s. 66D.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Digital arrest scams
slides.html:
In a "digital arrest" scam, fraudsters impersonate officials on video calls and threaten arrest to extort money; it is prosecuted as personation and cheating, not as a defined offence.

Class slide 22 describes fraudsters who impersonate police, enforcement agencies or judges on video calls, show forged orders, threaten arrest and seizure, and keep victims on calls for days.

The Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance after a senior citizen couple from Ambala lost 1.05 crore rupees between 3 and 16 September 2025 to impostors posing as CBI, Enforcement Directorate and Supreme Court officials.

Current law update: In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest Related to Forged Documents.

Cognisance was taken on 17 October 2025. On 1 December 2025, Surya Kant CJI and Joymalya Bagchi J directed the CBI to investigate digital arrest scams first, with other cybercrimes to follow, and sought the States' consent.

On 29 July 2026 the Court urged the Union to define "digital arrest" as a standalone offence, and on 4 August 2026 Surya Kant CJI, Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana JJ directed the RBI to frame a standard operating procedure on mule accounts and asked an inter departmental committee to examine shared liability and victim compensation.

Digital arrest complaints on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal fell from 1,23,672 (2024) to 58,249 (2025) and 16,377 (to 30 June 2026).

The proceedings continue; prosecutions use s. 66D (and s. 66C) with the BNS provisions on cheating, extortion, personation of public servants and forgery.†

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Section 66E: violation of privacy
slides.html:
Section 66E punishes intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of anyone's private area without consent, in circumstances violating privacy; it is gender neutral.

s. 66E, IT Act, 2000. Whoever intentionally or knowingly captures, publishes or transmits the image of a private area of any person without consent, under circumstances violating privacy, is punishable with up to three years, or a fine up to two lakh rupees, or both (class slide 23).

The Explanation defines five terms:

Transmit
Electronically sending an image intending it to be viewed.
Capture
Videotaping, photographing, filming or recording by any means.
Private area
Naked or undergarment clad genitals, pubic area, buttocks or female breast.
Publishes
Reproducing in print or electronic form and making available to the public.
Circumstances violating privacy
A reasonable expectation of being able to disrobe privately without being captured, or that the private area would not be publicly visible, in a public or private place.

The section is gender neutral: it protects "any person". Because the test is a reasonable expectation of privacy, it can apply even in a public place, such as a trial room in a shop.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Section 66E in the classroom events
slides.html:
The classroom events show s. 66E at work against hidden cameras and voyeurism, usually charged alongside the general criminal law.

Class slides 23 to 27 present these events:

  1. Delhi High Court restroom, 2013. Women advocates were reportedly filmed in a Delhi High Court restroom, which led to Binu Tamta v High Court of Delhi under Article 32 and the Supreme Court's Gender Sensitisation and Sexual Harassment of Women Regulations, 2013.†
  2. Filmed assaults. News reports of filmed and circulated assaults.
  3. Goa trial room, 2015. A camera aimed at a store trial room led to charge sheets under IPC ss. 354, 354C and 509 and IT Act s. 66E.
  4. Kerala, 2023. An IT professional was arrested for voyeurism while wearing a burqa, booked under IPC ss. 354C and 419 and s. 66E.

The pattern to notice: where charges were brought (Goa and Kerala), the s. 66E charge ran together with IPC charges, including voyeurism under s. 354C. The next slide explains how the two fit.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Voyeurism and stalking in the general criminal law
slides.html:
Voyeurism and stalking (IPC ss. 354C and 354D, now BNS ss. 77 and 78) protect women and overlap with s. 66E, so they are usually charged together.

Class slide 26 reproduces IPC ss. 354C and 354D, inserted by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013.

Points. 354C: voyeurisms. 354D: stalking
ConductA man who watches or captures a woman engaged in a private act where she expects not to be observed, or disseminates such an imageA man who repeatedly follows or contacts a woman despite clear disinterest, or monitors her internet, email or electronic communications
PunishmentOne to three years with fine; three to seven years on repetitionUp to three years with fine; five on repetition
Key detailA private act includes exposure of genitals, posterior, breasts or underwear, using a lavatory, or a sexual act not ordinarily done in public; consent to capture is not consent to disseminationExceptions: crime prevention by authorised persons, acts under law, and reasonable and justified conduct
Compared withs. 66EVoyeurism
ProtectsGender neutralWomen
CoversOnly images of private areasAlso watching private acts
Minimum sentenceNoneOne year

Section 66E is not compoundable when committed against a woman or child (s. 77A), and the two are usually charged together.

Law update. The IPC was repealed from 1 July 2024: these offences are now BNS ss. 77 and 78.† Do not cite IPC ss. 354C and 354D as current.

slides.part: Chapter 17: Identity Theft, Personation and Privacy Violation: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.title: Exam guidance: ss. 66C, 66D and 66E
slides.html:
Section 66C covers misuse of another's credentials, s. 66D cheating by personation through computers or devices, and s. 66E image based privacy violation.

In a problem, test each section by its core ingredient: was a credential used (66C), did someone pretend to be another to cheat (66D), or was an image of a private area captured, published or transmitted (66E)?

Exam focus. Do not use s. 66C where no credential was used, confine s. 66E to women, cite IPC ss. 354C and 354D as current, or call digital arrest a statutory offence.

Worked example

A fake CBI officer who keeps a retiree on a video call and extracts her savings commits s. 66D (and s. 66C if credentials were used), with BNS forgery and extortion.

The case is investigated by an officer not below Inspector (s. 78), possibly the CBI, and should be reported at once on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

slides.title: Section 66F at a glance
slides.html:
Section 66F creates two offences of cyber terrorism: Limb (A) needs terrorist intent and serious harm, while Limb (B) is in substance espionage. Both carry up to life.

Section 66F was the class focus of Module 7 (L3). This chapter covers, in order, the two limbs of s. 66F, critical information infrastructure, procedure, the classroom examples, the overlap with anti terrorism law and the main criticisms.

Hold the structure in your head before the detail. The section has two separate ways of committing cyber terrorism, followed by one punishment clause that covers both.

Limb (A): terrorism proper

A terrorist intent, one of three cyber acts, and serious harm that is caused or likely (class slide 28).

Limb (B): restricted information

Knowing unauthorised access that obtains restricted information, with reason to believe it may be misused. No terrorist intent (class slide 29).

Punishment (s. 66F(2))

Whoever commits or conspires to commit cyber terrorism: imprisonment which may extend to life.

Because the punishment can be life, s. 66F is the most serious offence in Module 7. That single fact explains its strict procedure, covered later in this chapter: it is non bailable and can never be compounded.

Exam focus. Answer a s. 66F problem limb by limb. First ask which limb is in play, then prove each element of that limb separately.

slides.title: Limb (A): intent, act and harm
slides.html:
Limb (A) needs three things together: a specific terrorist intent, one of three cyber acts, and serious harm that is caused or likely to be caused.

s. 66F(1)(A), IT Act (class slide 28). Whoever, with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India or to strike terror in the people or any section of them,

  1. denies access to authorised persons,
  2. attempts to penetrate or accesses a computer resource without authorisation or exceeding authorised access, or
  3. introduces a computer contaminant,

and thereby causes, or is likely to cause:

  1. death or injury;
  2. damage to or destruction of property;
  3. disruption of supplies or services essential to the life of the community (or knows such disruption to be likely); or
  4. adverse effects on critical information infrastructure specified under s. 70.
ElementWhat must be shownWhy it matters
IntentA specific terrorist intent: to threaten unity, integrity, security or sovereignty, or to strike terrorThis is what separates terrorism from ordinary hacking under s. 66
ActOne of the three cyber actsAn attempted penetration satisfies the conduct element
HarmSerious actual or likely harm"Likely to cause" catches attacks that fail

Remember: Limb (A) = Intent + D-A-C + Harm. The three acts are Deny access, Access (or attempt to penetrate) and Contaminant.

slides.title: Limb (B) and the punishment
slides.html:
Limb (B) punishes knowing unauthorised access to restricted information with reason to believe in its misuse. It needs no terrorist intent, so it is really espionage.

s. 66F(1)(B), IT Act (class slide 29). Whoever knowingly or intentionally penetrates or accesses a computer resource without or beyond authorisation, and thereby obtains information, data or databases restricted for State security or foreign relations, or any restricted information, with reason to believe that it may be used:

  1. to injure sovereignty and integrity, State security, friendly relations, public order, decency or morality;
  2. in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence; or
  3. to benefit a foreign nation or group.

No terrorist intent is required. The accused only has to know that the access is unauthorised and have reason to believe the information may be misused, so Limb (B) is in substance an espionage offence.

Punishment (s. 66F(2)). Whoever commits or conspires to commit cyber terrorism is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to life.

Note the word "conspires". Conspiracy is expressly covered, so conspiring to commit cyber terrorism is itself punishable with up to life, even if the attack is never launched.

Limb (A)Limb (B)
Mental elementSpecific terrorist intentKnowledge or intention, plus reason to believe in misuse
ConductDeny access, penetrate or access, or introduce a contaminantPenetrate or access without or beyond authorisation and obtain restricted information
ResultDeath, injury, property damage, disrupted essential services or harm to CII, actual or likelyNo harm element is stated
In substanceTerrorismEspionage
PunishmentUp to lifeUp to life

slides.title: Protected systems, CII and procedure
slides.html:
Section 70 lets the Government protect critical information infrastructure, and because s. 66F carries life it is cognizable, non bailable and never compoundable.

s. 70, IT Act. The appropriate Government may declare a computer resource affecting critical information infrastructure to be a protected system.

Critical information infrastructure
A computer resource whose incapacitation or destruction would have a debilitating impact on national security, the economy, public health or safety, such as power grids, telecommunications, banking and transport.
Protected system
A computer resource affecting critical information infrastructure that the appropriate Government has declared protected under s. 70. Unauthorised access to it carries up to ten years and a fine.†
Nodal agencies (background)
The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC, s. 70A) and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT In (s. 70B).

Procedure (18.4). Every procedural rule below follows from the possible life sentence:

QuestionAnswerProvision
Cognizable? Bailable?Cognizable and non bailables. 77B
Compoundable?Cannot be compoundeds. 77A
Who investigates?An officer not below the rank of Inspectors. 78
Conduct abroad?The Act extends to conduct abroad involving computers in Indias. 75

Reach is not the same as trial. Section 75 gives the Act reach over a foreign attacker, but actually trying him depends on extradition and international cooperation.

Unverified (†). The punishment under s. 70 (up to ten years and a fine) rests on secondary knowledge and was not checked against the primary text (Appendix G).

slides.title: The classroom examples
slides.html:
The leading classroom example is a press-reported trial court conviction: Anees Ansari, given life under s. 66F for researching a school attack on his employer's computer.

Anees Ansari conviction (Mumbai sessions court; Indian Express report updated 26 October 2022; class slide 30)

A Mumbai sessions court convicted Anees Ansari, a 32 year old computer engineer arrested in October 2014, who had used his employer's computer and internet to research a planned attack on an American school in the Bandra Kurla Complex.

He received life imprisonment under s. 66F and five years under IPC s. 115 read with s. 120B, and was ordered to pay ₹25,000 (25,000 rupees) under IT Act s. 43(a).

Why it matters: it shows that research and planning on a computer can amount to cyber terrorism. But treat it with care: it is a press reported trial court conviction, and the judgment itself was not seen. IPC s. 120B is now BNS s. 61 (Chapter 20).†

Class slide 31 reports a Gujarat Police FIR against the chief of Sikhs for Justice for threatening to disrupt the ICC Cricket World Cup. The provisions invoked were not verified, so do not cite it as a s. 66F case.

Correction (Appendix F, item 16). Earlier research for these notes found no Section 66F case; class slide 30 in fact reports a 2022 Mumbai sessions court conviction. Even so, no reported appellate judgment on s. 66F was located.

Exam focus. Because there is no appellate authority, answer s. 66F problems from the text of the section, element by element, and use Anees Ansari only as an illustration.

slides.title: Overlap with the UAPA and the BNS
slides.html:
Terrorism is also defined in UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113, and the choice of statute matters because the UAPA brings harsher procedure.

Section 15 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and, since 1 July 2024, BNS s. 113 also define terrorist acts by reference to the same intent as s. 66F.† Prosecutors therefore often combine them with the IT Act charge.

LawProvisionWhat the notes say
IT Act, 2000s. 66FCyber terrorism; up to life; cognizable, non bailable, not compoundable; investigated by an Inspector
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967s. 15Defines terrorist acts by the same intent;† brings special sanction requirements, extended detention and stricter bail conditions
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023s. 113Since 1 July 2024 also defines a terrorist act, which was formerly defined only in UAPA s. 15†

Why the choice matters. Choosing the UAPA brings special sanction requirements, extended detention and stricter bail conditions that the IT Act does not carry. The same facts can therefore lead to very different pre trial treatment depending on the statute charged.

Unverified (†). The UAPA and BNS overlap, and every BNS section number, rest on secondary knowledge (Appendix G). Check them before citing.

Exam focus. In a problem, charge s. 66F and then expressly note the UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap. Ignoring the UAPA and BNS is a listed mistake.

slides.title: Critical evaluation of Section 66F
slides.html:
Limb (B) is open to attack: it attaches a possible life sentence to accessing "any restricted information" on grounds as wide as decency or defamation.

Limb (B) attaches a possible life sentence to unauthorised access to "any restricted information" where it may be used in relation to decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation or incitement. These grounds are borrowed from Article 19(2).

The danger is overbreadth. Read literally, Limb (B) could catch a researcher or journalist who exceeds authorised access, which is far removed from terrorism.

Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, SC (background)

The Supreme Court struck down s. 66A for vagueness and overbreadth. After that decision, Limb (B) invites a similar critique, although no challenge to it was located.

Limb (A): defensible

It requires terrorist intent and serious harm, so it is far more defensible.

Limb (B): vulnerable

Life sentence, "any restricted information", Article 19(2) grounds, and no terrorist intent: open to a Shreya Singhal style challenge.

Correction (Appendix F, item 18). Section 66A was struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015) and formally omitted from 30 November 2023. Never cite s. 66A as live law.

Exam focus. A critical evaluation question wants three moves: state Limb (B), show its overbreadth with the journalist example, then contrast the safeguards built into Limb (A).

slides.title: Exam guidance: cyber terrorism
slides.html:
Prove each limb element by element, remember "likely to cause" and conspiracy, and never call an attack terrorism without proof of terrorist intent.

Exam focus. Limb (A) needs terrorist intent, a specified cyber act and actual or likely serious harm; Limb (B) needs knowing unauthorised access to restricted information with reason to believe in its misuse; both carry up to life, including for conspiracy.

Common mistakes to avoid:

  1. treating every large attack as terrorism;
  2. forgetting "likely to cause" or conspiracy; and
  3. ignoring the UAPA and BNS.

Worked problem (from the notes)

Ransomware is deployed from abroad. It cuts power to several districts, and the attackers declare that their aim is to show the State's helplessness.

  1. Act: ransomware is a computer contaminant, introduced through unauthorised access.
  2. Harm: cutting power to several districts disrupts essential services.
  3. Intent: the declared aim of showing the State's helplessness is terrorist intent.
  4. Conclusion: Limb (A) is satisfied, with reach over the foreign attackers under s. 75.
  5. Fallback: without proof of intent, ss. 43, 66 and 70 and BNS extortion apply instead.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Four categories of sexual content
slides.html:
Class slide 32 sorts sexual content into four categories, and the law's response rises from protection for erotica to punishment for obscene and extreme content.

This chapter covers the content offences: the obscenity tests, ss. 67, 67A and 67B, the POCSO Act and the special law question. Start with the vocabulary, because each category is treated differently.

Erotica

Art or literature on a sexual theme, not mainly for arousal. Protected by the public good exception.

Pornography

Produced solely for arousal. Sexually explicit material is punished when published electronically.

Obscene material

Material likely to deprave and corrupt. Punished.

Extreme content

Child abuse images and violent or extreme obscenity. Punished.

The law's response in one sentence: obscene and extreme content is punished, sexually explicit material is punished when published electronically, and genuine erotica is protected by the public good exception.

Remember: E-P-O-X, from protected to punished: Erotica, Pornography, Obscene material, eXtreme content.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Hicklin and Miller: the foreign tests
slides.html:
The obscenity test moved from protecting the most vulnerable reader (Hicklin) to judging by the average person and community standards (Miller).

R v Hicklin (1868) LR 3 QB 360 (England)† (class slide 33)

The test asked whether the matter tends to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to immoral influences and into whose hands it may fall. It judged by the most vulnerable reader.

The UK Obscene Publications Act 1959 then substituted the average reasonable person likely to encounter the material, a far less restrictive yardstick.

Miller v California 413 US 15 (1973) (United States)† (class slide 34)

Obscenity is excluded from First Amendment protection where all three parts are met:

  1. the average person, applying contemporary community standards, finds that the work as a whole appeals to the prurient interest;
  2. it depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way; and
  3. as a whole it lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value.

Remember: Miller = P-P-V: Prurient interest, Patently offensive, no serious Value, all judged on the work as a whole.

Both are foreign background. They matter because Indian law later moved from a Hicklin style test towards community standards.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Ranjit Udeshi and IPC section 292
slides.html:
India first adopted a modified Hicklin test in Ranjit Udeshi, upholding IPC s. 292, which deems material obscene on three alternative grounds.

Ranjit D. Udeshi v State of Maharashtra, AIR 1965 SC 881† (class slide 35)

The Supreme Court upheld IPC s. 292 under Article 19(2) (decency and morality) in a prosecution for selling Lady Chatterley's Lover.

It applied a modified Hicklin test: obscenity without a preponderating social purpose is unprotected, the law protecting those whose prurient minds delight in erotic writing.

IPC s. 292(1) (class slide 36). Material is deemed obscene if it:

  1. is lascivious;
  2. appeals to the prurient interest; or
  3. taken as a whole, tends to deprave and corrupt its likely audience.

Why this matters for the IT Act: the ingredients of s. 67 mirror s. 292(1), so the obscenity case law built on s. 292 also governs electronic obscenity.

Law update. IPC s. 292(1) is now BNS s. 294.† The IPC was repealed from 1 July 2024. The Hicklin based approach applied in Ranjit Udeshi has since been replaced by the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar (2014).

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Context and community standards
slides.html:
Later cases judged obscenity in context and by contemporary standards, until Aveek Sarkar (2014) finally replaced Hicklin with the community standards test.

Bobby Art International v Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996) 4 SCC 1, SC†

The Court judged the scenes of Bandit Queen in the context of the film's message about violence against a woman.

Ajay Goswami v Union of India (2007) 1 SCC 143, SC†

The Court required contemporary mores and national standards.

Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal (2014) 4 SCC 257, SC (class slides 37 and 38)

The Court replaced Hicklin with the community standards test. A nude photograph of a tennis player and his fiancée, published to oppose racism, was not obscene under s. 292 or s. 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986.

The line of development, in order:

  1. Hicklin (1868): the most vulnerable reader.
  2. Ranjit Udeshi (1965): modified Hicklin, with a preponderating social purpose.
  3. Bobby Art (1996): judge the work in context.
  4. Ajay Goswami (2007): contemporary mores and national standards.
  5. Aveek Sarkar (2014): community standards replace Hicklin.
  6. Apoorva Arora (2024): vulgarity is not obscenity (next slide).

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Apoorva Arora: profanity is not obscenity
slides.html:
Apoorva Arora (2024) holds that vulgarity and profanity are not obscenity, and that s. 67A requires a sexually explicit act.

Class slide 43 shows the interim stage of the College Romance case. At that stage the Court protected the director and actors from arrest, and Harish Salve argued that offending content could be taken down but the police should be kept out.

Apoorva Arora v State (Govt of NCT of Delhi), 2024 INSC 223 (Supreme Court, A.S. Bopanna and Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha JJ, 19 March 2024)

Facts
On 6 March 2023 the Delhi High Court held the web series' expletive laden language obscene and likely to corrupt young minds, and upheld an FIR under ss. 67 and 67A.
Held
The appeals were allowed and the FIR quashed. (1) Vulgarity and profanity are not by themselves obscene. (2) Obscenity concerns material that arouses sexual and lustful thoughts, judged under the Aveek Sarkar community standards test on the work as a whole and in context. (3) Section 67A requires a sexually explicit act, which was absent.
Significance
Sections 67 and 67A cannot be used against content that is merely crude or offensive.

Correction (Appendix F, item 15). Class slide 43 shows only the interim protection. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR on 19 March 2024 (2024 INSC 223).

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Section 67: obscene material in electronic form
slides.html:
Section 67 punishes publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically, using the three-part definition in IPC s. 292(1), with heavier penalties on a repeat conviction.

s. 67, IT Act. Whoever publishes or transmits, or causes to be published or transmitted, in electronic form material that is lascivious or appeals to the prurient interest, or tends to deprave and corrupt persons likely to read, see or hear it, is punishable as below.

ConvictionImprisonmentFine
FirstUp to three yearsUp to five lakh rupees (₹5 lakh)
SubsequentUp to five yearsUp to ten lakh rupees (₹10 lakh)

Ingredients (class slide 39). They mirror IPC s. 292(1) except for the punishment, so the obscenity case law applies. Break the section into three questions:

  1. Did the accused publish or transmit the material, or cause it to be published or transmitted?
  2. Was it in electronic form?
  3. Is the material lascivious, prurient, or likely to deprave and corrupt its likely audience, judged by community standards (Aveek Sarkar, Apoorva Arora)?

The punishment also drives procedure. A first conviction (three years) is bailable, while a subsequent conviction (five years) is non bailable and cannot be compounded (Chapter 20).

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Imran Khan: a like is not publication
slides.html:
Imran Khan (2025) holds that "liking" a post is neither publishing nor transmitting, and that s. 67 targets obscene content, not merely provocative content.

Imran Khan v State of Uttar Pradesh, 2025:AHC:56788; 2025 SCC OnLine All 2303 (Allahabad High Court, Saurabh Srivastava J, 17 April 2025; class slide 40)

Facts
The applicant was charged under IPC ss. 147 to 149 and IT Act s. 67 after a provocative post allegedly led 600 to 700 people to gather for an unauthorised procession. But he had only "liked" another person's post.
Held
The proceedings were quashed. Liking is neither publishing nor transmitting, and s. 67 punishes obscene (lascivious or prurient) material, not merely provocative content.

The case therefore fails on two separate ingredients of s. 67: there was no publication or transmission, and the content was provocative rather than obscene.

Unverified (†). An earlier 2023 decision of the same court reportedly took the same view of likes while treating sharing or reposting as transmission.†

Remember: Like = not publication. Share or repost = transmission.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Section 67A: sexually explicit material
slides.html:
Section 67A punishes electronic publication of a sexually explicit act more heavily than s. 67, and no tendency to deprave need be shown.

s. 67A, IT Act (class slide 41). Whoever publishes or transmits in electronic form material containing a sexually explicit act or conduct is punishable as below.

ConvictionImprisonmentFine
FirstUp to five yearsUp to ten lakh rupees
SubsequentUp to seven yearsUp to ten lakh rupees

No tendency to deprave need be shown. That is the key difference from s. 67: once a sexually explicit act is depicted, the obscenity tests are unnecessary.

State of West Bengal v Animesh Boxi (Tamluk court, 2018; class slide 41)†

Facts
A "revenge porn" case. After a three year relationship, the accused obtained intimate images (allegedly by hacking the victim's phone), threatened to publish them, and uploaded them to a pornographic site with her and her father's identities.
Held
Convicted under ss. 66E, 66C, 67 and 67A, he was sentenced by the Tamluk magistrate to five years and a ₹9,000 (9,000 rupee) fine.†

Akshay Sripad Rao v State of Maharashtra (2017; class slide 42)†

The FIR alleged that the accused disrobed the victim, photographed her naked and uploaded the images to 145 pornographic websites, as forensic analysis confirmed. The court found a prima facie case under ss. 67 and 67A and IPC ss. 354A and 354D.†

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: The public good and heritage exceptions
slides.html:
Sections 67, 67A and 67B do not reach material proved to serve the public good, or kept for bona fide heritage or religious purposes; the accused must prove it.

Exception to s. 67A (applying to ss. 67 and 67A) and the identical proviso to s. 67B (class slide 44). The offences do not extend to electronic books, writings, drawings, paintings, representations or figures:

  1. proved to be justified as being for the public good in the interest of science, literature, art, learning or other objects of general concern; or
  2. kept or used for bona fide heritage or religious purposes.

Examples: medical texts, sex education and classical or religious art.

Burden of proof. The person relying on the exception bears the burden of proving it. The prosecution proves the offence; the accused then proves that the material is justified.

This exception is how the law protects genuine erotica (class slide 32) while still punishing obscene and explicit material.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Section 67B: child sexual abuse material
slides.html:
Section 67B goes far beyond publication: creating, collecting, browsing, downloading, grooming, facilitating and recording child sexual abuse are all covered.

s. 67B, IT Act. Whoever:

  1. (a) publishes or transmits material depicting children in sexually explicit acts;
  2. (b) creates text or digital images, collects, seeks, browses, downloads, advertises, promotes, exchanges or distributes material depicting children in an obscene, indecent or sexually explicit manner;
  3. (c) cultivates, entices or induces children into online relationships for sexually explicit acts or in a manner that may offend a reasonable adult;
  4. (d) facilitates abusing children online; or
  5. (e) records in electronic form his own or others' abuse involving sexually explicit acts with children.
PointRule
Who is a child?A person under eighteen
PunishmentMatches s. 67A: five years and ten lakh rupees; seven years and ten lakh rupees on repetition
GroomingClause (c) criminalises online grooming before any image exists

Remember: P-C-C-F-R for clauses (a) to (e): Publish, Create or collect, Cultivate (groom), Facilitate, Record.

Exam focus. Do not treat s. 67B as requiring publication. Clause (b) reaches browsing and downloading.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: POCSO: child pornography and sections 14 and 15
slides.html:
The POCSO Act adds a wide definition of child pornography, punishes using children for it (s. 14), and punishes storing or possessing it (s. 15).

The POCSO (Amendment) Act, 2019 (class slides 44 and 45) defines child pornography as any visual depiction of sexually explicit conduct involving a child, including photographs, videos and digital or computer generated images indistinguishable from, or modified to appear to depict, a child.

POCSO s. 14. Using children for pornographic purposes: at least five years with fine; seven on repetition.

POCSO s. 15 (as substituted) punishes three forms of storing or possessing such material:

Storing or possessing…Punishment
without deleting, destroying or reporting it, with intent to shareA fine of at least ₹5,000 (5,000 rupees), or ₹10,000 on repetition
for transmitting, displaying or distributing, except for reporting or court evidenceUp to three years, fine, or both
for commercial purposesThree to five years, fine, or both; five to seven years with fine on repetition

Read POCSO s. 15 together with IT Act s. 67B. Section 67B catches the online acts (browsing, downloading, distributing), while s. 15 catches keeping the material, which is where the next case comes in.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Just Rights for Children Alliance: possession and viewing
slides.html:
Just Rights for Children Alliance (2024) holds that downloading and keeping child sexual abuse material can itself be an offence, without any publication.

Just Rights for Children Alliance v S. Harish, 2024 INSC 716 (Supreme Court, 23 September 2024; class slide 46)

Facts
The Madras High Court had quashed proceedings against a man who downloaded and kept child sexual abuse material on his phone. It held that downloading and viewing without publication or transmission was not an offence under s. 67B or POCSO s. 15.
Held
The order was set aside and the proceedings restored. Storage or possession without deletion or reporting can itself indicate the intention required by POCSO s. 15, and s. 67B covers creating, collecting, seeking, browsing and downloading, not only publication. The Court urged Parliament to replace "child pornography" with "child sexual exploitative and abuse material" (CSEAM) and directed courts to use that term.
Significance
The leading authority on possession and viewing offences.

Exam focus. Use the term CSEAM in your answers, as the Supreme Court directed, and cite this case whenever a problem involves downloading, viewing or keeping such material.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: The special law: Sharat Babu Digumarti
slides.html:
Where obscene material is in electronic form, s. 67 with ss. 79 and 81 is a special scheme, so IPC s. 292 cannot be invoked for the same conduct.

Sharat Babu Digumarti v Government (NCT of Delhi), (2017) 2 SCC 18 (Supreme Court, Dipak Misra and Prafulla C. Pant JJ, 14 December 2016)

Facts
An obscene clip was listed for sale on Baazee.com in 2004. An officer of the company, discharged under s. 67, still faced IPC s. 292.
Held
Where the offence concerns obscene material in electronic form, s. 67, read with ss. 79 and 81, is a special scheme that excludes s. 292, so the general law cannot be invoked for the same conduct.
Significance
The leading authority on the IT Act and the general law, now read with the Bombay High Court Full Bench's ingredient test (Chapter 16).

Section 81 is the hook: it gives the IT Act overriding effect, which is why the special scheme displaces the general obscenity offence (Chapter 20).

Current position (Chapter 16). In the Bombay High Court, compare ingredients and allow the general offence alongside the IT Act where it has an additional ingredient; Sharat Babu still governs where both provisions cover the same conduct. The question is unsettled nationally and must now be answered against the BNS.

slides.part: Chapter 19: Obscene and Sexually Explicit Material: Sections 67, 67A and 67B
slides.title: Exam guidance: the content offences
slides.html:
Match the content to the right section, judge obscenity by community standards, and remember that s. 67B reaches browsing and downloading.

Exam focus. Section 67 covers electronic obscenity judged by community standards (Aveek Sarkar, Apoorva Arora), s. 67A sexually explicit material, and s. 67B a wide range of conduct involving children, including browsing and downloading (Just Rights for Children Alliance).

Common mistakes to avoid: treating

  1. profanity as obscenity;
  2. a like as publication;
  3. s. 67B as requiring publication; or
  4. the general obscenity offence as available alongside s. 67 for the same material.

Worked problem (from the notes)

A man shares a former partner's intimate videos in a group, and a member reposts them. Another member merely likes the post.

  1. The sharer and the reposter both commit ss. 66E and 67A: sharing and reposting are publication or transmission.
  2. Section 67A is non bailable.
  3. Section 66E is not compoundable because the victim is a woman.
  4. The member who merely likes the post commits neither (Imran Khan).

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Cognizable and bailable: section 77B
slides.html:
Under s. 77B, IT Act offences punishable with three years or more are cognizable, and those punishable with three years are bailable.

This chapter covers procedure, jurisdiction, corporate liability and the relationship with the new criminal codes. Begin with the rule that decides how every offence is handled.

s. 77B, IT Act. Notwithstanding the CrPC (now read with the BNSS†), offences punishable with three years and above are cognizable and those punishable with three years are bailable.

ProvisionCognizable?Bailable?
ss. 65, 66, 66B, 66C, 66D and 66EYesYes
s. 67, first convictionYesYes
s. 67, subsequent convictionYesNo
ss. 67A and 67BYesNo
s. 66FYesNo
s. 43Civil contravention, not an offenceNot applicable

Why the line falls here: every offence in the first two rows carries a maximum of three years, so it is bailable. A repeat s. 67 offence (five years), ss. 67A and 67B (five or seven years) and s. 66F (life) all exceed three years, so they are non bailable.

Exam focus. Do not call s. 66E or a first s. 67 offence non bailable.

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Compounding: section 77A
slides.html:
Section 77A allows compounding only for offences up to three years, and never for repeat offenders, socio-economic offences, or offences against women or children.

s. 77A, IT Act. Courts may compound offences other than those punishable with life or more than three years, but not where:

  1. a previous conviction attracts enhanced or different punishment; or
  2. the offence affects socio economic conditions, or is committed against a child under eighteen or a woman.
ResultProvisions
Compoundabless. 65, 66, 66B, 66C and 66D
Compoundable only where the victim is not a woman or childs. 66E, and s. 67 on a first conviction
Not compoundabless. 66F, 67A and 67B, and s. 67 on a subsequent conviction

Contrast the civil track: s. 43 contraventions are compoundable under s. 63, a separate provision.

Exam focus. Do not compound s. 66E committed against a woman.

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Investigation, search and territorial reach
slides.html:
An Inspector investigates (s. 78), may search public places and arrest without warrant (s. 80), and the Act reaches conduct abroad involving Indian computers (s. 75).

ProvisionRule
s. 78Offences are investigated by an officer not below the rank of Inspector, lowered from Deputy Superintendent in 2008.
s. 80†Such an officer, or another authorised officer, may enter a public place, search it and arrest without warrant anyone reasonably suspected of an offence under the Act.
s. 75The Act applies to offences and contraventions committed outside India by any person if they involve a computer, system or network in India.

How they fit together. Section 78 decides who investigates, s. 80 gives that officer powers on the ground, and s. 75 decides how far the Act reaches. The 2008 change to s. 78 widened the pool of officers who can investigate.

Remember the limit on s. 75 from Chapter 18: reach over a foreign offender does not guarantee a trial, which still depends on extradition and international cooperation.

Unverified (†). The wording of s. 80 rests on secondary knowledge and was not checked against the primary text (Appendix G).

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: Companies, intermediaries and the overriding effect
slides.html:
Section 85 makes those in charge of a company liable for its offences, s. 79 shields diligent intermediaries, and s. 81 gives the Act overriding effect.

s. 85, IT Act (companies). Persons in charge of and responsible to a company for its business are deemed guilty of its offences unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence. Directors or officers whose consent, connivance or neglect is proved are also liable.

Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels and Tours (2012) 5 SCC 661, SC†

Held under an analogous provision that the company itself must be arraigned. The reasoning was applied in the Baazee.com litigation.†

s. 79, IT Act (intermediaries; background). Intermediaries are protected for third party content if they observe due diligence, do not initiate transmissions, select receivers or modify content, and act on actual knowledge, which Shreya Singhal (2015) 5 SCC 1 read down to mean a court order or government notification.

s. 81, IT Act (overriding effect). The Act has overriding effect, while saving rights under the Copyright Act, 1957 and the Patents Act, 1970 (and the DPDP Act from 13 May 2027).

Section 81 is the basis of Sharat Babu: because the IT Act overrides, its special scheme for electronic obscenity displaces IPC s. 292.

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: The offences at a glance
slides.html:
Learn each offence with its punishment, because the punishment decides whether it is bailable and whether it can be compounded.

ProvisionPunishment
s. 43Uncapped civil compensation; compoundable under s. 63
s. 65Three years or two lakh rupees or both
s. 66Three years or five lakh rupees or both
s. 66BThree years or one lakh rupees or both
ss. 66C and 66DThree years and one lakh rupees
s. 66EThree years or two lakh rupees or both
s. 66FUp to life
s. 67Three years and five lakh rupees; on repetition, five years and ten lakh rupees
ss. 67A and 67BFive years and ten lakh rupees; on repetition, seven years and ten lakh rupees

Watch the conjunctions. Sections 65, 66, 66B and 66E say "or … or both", while ss. 66C and 66D say imprisonment and fine.

Cognizability, bail and compounding follow section 20.2: three years and above is cognizable, three years is bailable, and compounding is limited by s. 77A.

Remember: Three is the magic number. Every offence from s. 65 to s. 66E, and a first s. 67 offence, tops out at three years: cognizable, bailable, and usually compoundable.

slides.part: Chapter 20: Procedure, Jurisdiction and the General Criminal Law
slides.title: The IT Act and the new criminal codes
slides.html:
Since 1 July 2024 the BNS, BNSS and BSA have replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act; IT Act offences are unchanged, but every IPC reference needs its BNS equivalent.

IT Act offences are unchanged, but the class slides' IPC references must be updated. Check the numbers before citing.†

IPC provision (class slide)SubjectBNS equivalent†
IPC ss. 24 and 25 (class slide 14)"Dishonestly" and "fraudulently"BNS ss. 2(7) and 2(9)
IPC s. 411 (class slide 19)Receiving stolen propertyBNS s. 317
