quiz.why: Hashing is one way, unlike encryption, which is reversible with the key, but even a hash of a phone number can be reversed by hashing every possible number and matching the results, so hashing alone rarely anonymises. The firm can do exactly that without any key or list from the retailer, so the hashes remain personal data in its hands; at most the hashing pseudonymises them, while anonymisation needs techniques such as aggregation, generalisation, suppression or added noise. The 'no key' option repeats the firm's mistake, and the encryption option reaches the right answer for the wrong reason, since hashing and encryption differ.

quiz.concept: Key holder's duties after EDPS v SRB
quiz.q: A public body collects comments from people affected by one of its decisions, replaces their names with codes, keeps the key, and sends the coded comments to an outside consultant that cannot reasonably reidentify anyone. Respondents were never told that the consultant would receive them. The body argues it owed them no information about this, since the comments are not personal data in the consultant's hands. Is the argument sound after EDPS v SRB?
quiz.ok: No. As the key holder, its information duties are judged from its own perspective at collection.
no: Yes. Once the names are replaced by codes, the comments are anonymous for everyone, the body included.
Yes. Information duties are judged from the recipient's perspective at the moment of transfer.
No. Pseudonymised data remain personal data for every recipient, whatever its means of reidentifying.
quiz.why: In EDPS v SRB (Case C 413/23 P, 4 September 2025) the Court held that pseudonymised data are not personal data in all cases and for every person: for a recipient unable reasonably to reidentify they may not be, but they remain personal data for the key holder, whose information duties are judged from its own perspective at collection. The body kept the key, so its duties to respondents applied when it collected the comments, whatever their status in the consultant's hands. The option saying pseudonymised data stay personal data for every recipient reaches the right result for the wrong reason, because since EDPS v SRB coded data are not personal data for every recipient regardless of its means.

quiz.concept: Functional test and joint answerability
quiz.q: A retailer's contract calls its analytics vendor a mere processor acting on instructions, but in practice the two jointly decide which customer data are collected and why. The contract also says only the retailer will handle customers' rights requests. When a customer sends an access request to the vendor, it refuses, citing its processor label and the contract. Is the refusal justified?
quiz.ok: No. It is a joint controller because it decides purposes and means, and it stays answerable to her.
no: Yes. The contract makes it a processor, and processors answer only to the controller that instructs them.
Yes. Even as a joint controller it may rely on the agreed allocation, which binds customers too.
No, but only because it holds her data, and whoever holds personal data is a controller.
quiz.why: Controllership is functional: whoever actually decides why and how data are processed is a controller, alone or jointly, whatever a contract says, so a processor label cannot change what the vendor in fact does (Articles 4(7) and 26). Joint controllers must transparently allocate their responsibilities, but each remains answerable to each data subject individually, so the vendor cannot turn the customer away by pointing to the allocation. The option resting on the vendor holding her data gives a wrong reason, because controllership turns on deciding purposes and means, not on holding the data.

quiz.concept: Stage-limited joint control in Fashion ID
quiz.q: An online shop embeds a social network's plugin, which sends each visitor's IP address and browser details to the network as soon as a page loads; the network later uses the data for its own profiling. Assume that consent is not required for the collection. The shop wants to rely on legitimate interests. For what is the shop a joint controller, and what must it show?
quiz.ok: Only for collection and transmission, and for that share it needs a legitimate interest of its own.
no: For everything, including the later profiling, and it may rest on the network's legitimate interest.
Only for collection and transmission, but for that share it may borrow the network's legitimate interest.
For nothing, as the network alone receives the data, so the shop needs no lawful basis at all.
quiz.why: In Fashion ID (Case C 40/17) the website operator was a joint controller with Facebook Ireland only for the collection and disclosure by transmission of visitors' data, not for Facebook's later processing, over which it had no influence. Each joint controller had to pursue a legitimate interest of its own, and Fashion ID's was the commercial benefit of publicity for its goods. The shop therefore answers only for its own stage and on its own interest, and the 'for nothing' option fails because embedding the plugin decisively influences collection and transmission.

quiz.concept: Fiduciary stays responsible for processors
quiz.q: An Indian online retailer, a Data Fiduciary, hires a cloud company to store and process its customers' data. Their contract says that the cloud company alone is responsible for complying with the DPDP Act for that processing. After the cloud company mishandles the data, the retailer says the contract shifts responsibility away from it. Assuming the Act is fully in force, is the retailer right?
quiz.ok: No. A Data Fiduciary stays responsible for its processor's processing, whatever their contract says.
no: Yes. A valid contract can transfer the fiduciary's responsibility to the processor that caused the harm.
Yes. By accepting the clause the cloud company became the fiduciary, so responsibility passed to it.
No, but only because the contract needed the Board's approval before any processor could act under it.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act mirrors controller and processor as Data Fiduciary and Data Processor (s. 2(i) and (k)): the fiduciary may engage a processor only under a valid contract (s. 8(2)), but it remains responsible for processing carried out on its behalf regardless of any contract (s. 8(1)). The clause therefore cannot move the statutory responsibility away from the retailer. The cloud company does not become the fiduciary by accepting a clause, because it still processes on the retailer's behalf rather than determining purpose and means, and the Act requires a valid contract but no approval by the Board.

quiz.concept: Lawful basis and principles both required
quiz.q: A gym relies on the contract basis for members' contact and payment details, which the membership contract makes necessary. It also collects members' full employment histories, which it never uses, and keeps every record forever. Its privacy notice explains both practices clearly. The manager says that a valid lawful basis and a clear notice mean the GDPR is satisfied. What is wrong with that view?
quiz.ok: Minimisation and storage limitation are separate duties that neither a basis nor a notice can meet.
no: Nothing: with a lawful basis and a clear notice, the remaining principles are only good practice.
Only the employment histories are a problem, as disclosing indefinite retention in the notice cures that.
Only the retention is a problem, as the contract basis covers whatever data the gym asks for.
quiz.why: Chapter II requires every processing operation both to rest on one of the six lawful bases in Article 6 and to comply with all seven principles in Article 5, and infringing the principles attracts the highest tier of fines. Collecting employment histories the gym never uses breaches data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c)), and keeping every record forever breaches storage limitation (Article 5(1)(e)); a clear notice serves transparency but cures neither breach. The 'histories only' option treats transparency as if it could satisfy storage limitation, and the 'retention only' option forgets that necessity for a contract is judged objectively.

quiz.concept: Lawfulness includes compliance with other law
quiz.q: A company records its staff's phone calls, relying on legitimate interests after a careful balancing test that favours it. A national employment statute, however, forbids employers to record such calls. The company argues that the recording is lawful under the GDPR because it has a valid lawful basis. What is the flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: The flaw is that lawfulness also needs compliance with other law, and the statute is breached.
no: There is no flaw: lawfulness under the GDPR means having a valid lawful basis and nothing more.
The flaw is that legitimate interests is closed to employers, who must rely on consent.
The flaw is one of fairness only, since the statute merely shapes what staff can expect.
quiz.why: Article 5(1)(a) bundles lawfulness, fairness and transparency, and lawfulness means both an Article 6 basis (plus an Article 9 condition for special data) and compliance with other law. A sound legitimate interests assessment therefore cannot make lawful a recording that a national statute forbids. The fairness option is tempting because fairness protects reasonable expectations, but breach of another law goes to lawfulness itself, and legitimate interests is withheld from public authorities performing their tasks, not from private employers.

quiz.concept: Choosing a basis for a public authority
quiz.q: A city council must collect a local tax that national law requires it to levy, and it needs residents' data to do so. One officer wants to ask every resident for consent, as the safest basis; another prefers legitimate interests, since residents benefit from the tax. Which approach is correct?
quiz.ok: Use legal obligation or public task, which fit a duty that national law imposes on the council.
no: Ask every resident for consent, since it is the strongest basis and best protects the council.
Use legitimate interests, since the balancing test clearly favours a tax that benefits all residents.
Use whichever basis suits, choosing it once processing has begun, since the bases have no hierarchy.
quiz.why: Article 6(1) sets out six bases with no hierarchy, consent is not the default, and the basis should be fixed before processing begins. A tax that national law requires the council to levy fits legal obligation, an obligation laid down by Member State law, or public task with a basis in law, while legitimate interests is unavailable to public authorities performing their tasks. Consent is no stronger than any other basis, and the option that picks a basis once processing has begun misreads 'no hierarchy': it means no basis is preferred, not that the choice can wait until processing is under way.

quiz.concept: The three-step legitimate interests test
quiz.q: An online shop plans to keep a scan of every customer's passport to prevent fraud, although its existing card and address checks already stop fraud just as well. Its adviser argues: 'Fraud prevention is a legitimate interest, and customers expect anti-fraud checks, so their interests do not override ours. Legitimate interests therefore applies.' What is the flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: It skips necessity: the scans are not needed when existing checks already achieve the same aim.
no: Fraud prevention cannot be a legitimate interest, since it serves the shop rather than its customers.
There is no flaw: a legitimate interest that survives the balancing test is all the basis requires.
Legitimate interests is closed to the shop, which must rely on consent for any anti-fraud checks.
quiz.why: Legitimate interests has three steps: a legitimate interest, necessity of the processing for it, and balancing against the data subject's interests (Article 6(1)(f)). Fraud prevention is a legitimate interest (Recital 47), and the adviser deals with balancing, but skips necessity: processing is necessary only if its purpose cannot reasonably be achieved by other means (Recital 39), and the existing checks already achieve it, so the passport scans fail before any balancing is reached. The 'no flaw' option drops the middle step, and the basis is withheld only from public authorities performing their tasks, not from shops, while consent is not the default.

quiz.concept: Limits of the vital interests basis
quiz.q: A supermarket's app infers from a customer's purchases that she probably has diabetes. Without asking her, the supermarket sends her name and the inference to a private clinic so that it can offer her a check-up, saying this protects her vital interests. She is well and can easily be contacted. Can the supermarket rely on vital interests?
quiz.ok: No. The basis covers life or death situations, and for health data only where consent is impossible.
no: Yes. Health is a vital interest, so processing that may protect her health is enough to qualify.
Yes, provided the check-up might detect a condition that could later become dangerous to her.
No. Vital interests is reserved for public authorities, so a supermarket can never rely on it.
quiz.why: Vital interests is a lawful basis for life or death situations (Article 6(1)(d)), and where special category data are involved Article 9(2) lifts the prohibition on that ground only where consent is impossible. An inferred diabetes diagnosis is health data, since purchases may reveal health and what counts is what data reveal; she is well, so nothing is a matter of life or death, and she can easily be asked. A possible future illness does not turn a sales referral into a life or death situation, and the basis is not confined to public authorities: it is legitimate interests that public authorities cannot use for their tasks.

quiz.concept: Factors in the compatibility test
quiz.q: A gym collected members' attendance logs to run its class booking system. Without asking for consent, it now wants to analyse the logs to decide which members to approach with offers of paid personal training. Which change in the facts would do most to support treating the new use as compatible?
quiz.ok: The analysis would use pseudonymised logs, reidentifying only the members chosen for offers.
no: The new use would earn the gym far more money than its booking system has ever brought in.
The logs would be combined with members' injury records so that each offer suits the member.
The gym already holds the logs, so the analysis would involve no fresh collection of any data.
quiz.why: Where further processing rests on neither consent nor a law, Article 6(4) weighs the link between purposes, the context and relationship, the nature of the data, the possible consequences and safeguards such as encryption or pseudonymisation. Analysing pseudonymised logs and reidentifying only the members selected is a listed safeguard, so it counts in favour of compatibility. Injury records work the other way, because they are health data, a special category, and the nature of the data counts especially against compatibility where special category data are involved, while profit and the fact that the data are already held are not factors at all.

quiz.concept: Storage limitation and anonymised data
quiz.q: An online retailer closes customer accounts after two years of inactivity. It wants to keep, indefinitely, figures built from those customers' order histories showing how sales of each product varied by region and season, aggregated so that no customer can be identified from them. Its data protection officer says storage limitation requires it to destroy everything derived from the closed accounts. Is the officer right?
quiz.ok: No. The principle limits keeping data in identifiable form, so anonymised figures may be kept.
no: Yes. The principle bars keeping any figures derived from personal data once their purpose ends.
No. The principle does not reach closed accounts, so the full order histories may be kept as well.
No. Using data for statistics switches the principle off, and no safeguards are then required.
quiz.why: Storage limitation forbids keeping data in a form that permits identification for longer than necessary, subject to archiving, research and statistics with safeguards (Article 5(1)(e)). Information that no longer relates to an identifiable person is anonymous and outside the GDPR altogether, including for statistical purposes (Recital 26), so aggregated figures from which no customer can be identified may be kept. The officer over-reads the principle, and the statistics option fails because that exception applies to identifiable data and still requires safeguards.

quiz.concept: Risk tiers and the breach clock
quiz.q: A retailer operating in the EU and India misconfigured a server in March, exposing customers' names and email addresses in both places, but discovered the exposure only on 1 June. It rightly assesses the breach as likely to result in a risk to customers, but not a high risk. Assuming the DPDP breach rules are in force, which statement describes its duties?
quiz.ok: In the EU, the supervisory authority alone, with time running from 1 June; in India, the Board and each affected customer.
no: In the EU, the supervisory authority alone, with time running from March; in India, the Board alone, as the risk is not high.
In the EU, the supervisory authority and the customers, with time running from 1 June; in India, the Board alone.
In the EU, the supervisory authority and the customers, with time running from March; in India, the Board and each affected customer.
quiz.why: The GDPR filters notification by risk: under Article 33 the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach unless it is unlikely to result in a risk, while Article 34 requires communication to data subjects only where the risk is high. A risk that is real but not high therefore calls for notice to the authority alone, and the clock started on 1 June, when the retailer became aware, not in March, when the exposure began. The DPDP regime has no risk threshold: s. 8(6) and Rule 7 require every breach to be intimated to the Board and to each affected Data Principal, so the 'Board alone' options wrongly carry the GDPR's risk filter over to India.

quiz.concept: Accountability duties stand on their own
quiz.q: A regulator finds that a controller's high-risk processing is sound in substance, but the controller keeps no records of processing and never carried out the impact assessment such processing requires. It argues that, as no principle has been breached and no one harmed, it has committed no infringement. What is the flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: The flaw is that accountability makes records and impact assessments duties in their own right.
no: There is no flaw: accountability is met by actual compliance, with or without records or impact assessments.
There is no flaw: without harm to anyone, a failure to keep records cannot be an infringement.
The flaw is that a data protection officer must approve every operation before it may begin.
quiz.why: Accountability under Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for compliance and able to demonstrate it, and it is implemented through appropriate measures (Article 24), protection by design and by default (Article 25), records of processing (Article 30), impact assessments for high risk processing (Article 35) and data protection officers (Articles 37 to 39). Because the controller must be able to prove compliance, keeping records and carrying out a required impact assessment are legal duties in their own right, so their absence is an infringement even if the processing is otherwise sound. Accountability is itself one of the seven principles, so the claim that no principle was breached is wrong, and the 'no harm' option misses that these duties stand on their own.

quiz.concept: No legitimate interests basis in DPDP
quiz.q: A bank operating in both the EU and India runs the same transaction-monitoring analytics in each. In the EU it relies on legitimate interests after a balancing test. Its compliance team proposes to rely on the same balancing test in India. Assuming the DPDP Act is fully in force, what is wrong with the proposal?
quiz.ok: The Act has no legitimate interests basis, so the bank needs consent or a legitimate use.
no: Nothing is wrong: the Act's legitimate uses include a general legitimate interests ground.
The test must add a fairness review, as the Act's fairness principle governs balancing.
The Act demands consent for every processing operation, so no other ground exists in India.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act has no list of principles: lawfulness under s. 4 means a lawful purpose plus consent or a legitimate use, and the Act has neither a legitimate interests basis nor a fairness principle. A GDPR-style balancing test cannot by itself justify the processing in India, so the bank must fit it within consent or a legitimate use. Crediting the Act with a legitimate interests ground or a fairness principle is a common error, and the consent-only option forgets that legitimate uses exist.

quiz.concept: Informed consent needs the controller's identity
quiz.q: A puzzle app shows a pop-up: 'Tap Accept to let us use your location to show you local restaurant adverts.' Users can tap Accept or Decline, and the puzzles work either way. The pop-up is run by an advertising network, which collects the location data and decides how they are used, but it is named nowhere in the app, and users assume 'us' means the app maker. Is consent given by tapping Accept valid?
quiz.ok: No, because users do not know who the controller is, so the consent is not informed.
no: No, because tapping a button is not the kind of clear affirmative act that consent requires.
No, because location-based advertising is too vague a purpose for the consent to be specific.
Yes, because users had a genuine choice and the purpose was stated in plain, concrete words.
quiz.why: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous (Article 4(11)), and Recital 42 requires the data subject to know at least the controller's identity and the purposes. Here Decline costs nothing, the purpose is concrete and tapping Accept is a clear affirmative act, but users cannot know that the unnamed advertising network, which decides how the data are used, is the controller. The 'Yes' option is tempting because three elements are met, but each element is a separate condition, and not knowing who is processing the data defeats the consent.

quiz.concept: Buried consent request is not binding
quiz.q: A gym's six-page membership form includes, in the middle of a paragraph on opening hours, a sentence saying the member consents to her data being shared with partner brands for marketing. Nadia signs the form, and the gym keeps the signed copy. When she complains about emails from partner brands, the gym says her signature proves she consented. Is the gym right?
quiz.ok: No, because a consent request buried among other matters is not binding, whatever she signed.
no: Yes, because the gym must be able to prove consent, and the signed form does exactly that.
Yes, because by signing the whole form she accepted every term in it, including the sharing.
No, because the buried sentence makes the whole membership form void, so none of it binds her.
quiz.why: Article 7(2) requires a consent request in a written declaration that also covers other matters to be clearly distinguishable, intelligible, easily accessible and in plain language, and any part that infringes this is not binding. A sentence hidden in a paragraph on opening hours fails that test, so Nadia's signature does not turn it into binding consent. The proof option confuses Article 7(1), which puts the burden of demonstrating consent on the controller, with validity, since proving she signed does not prove valid consent; and the 'whole form void' option over-generalises, because only the infringing part falls.

quiz.concept: Children's consent rule leaves contract law alone
quiz.q: Mia, aged 16 and living in a Member State that has kept the default age, signs up for a paid gaming subscription aimed at teenagers and ticks a box consenting to the processing of her data. When her parents dispute the fees, the company argues that because she was old enough to consent under the GDPR's rule on children's consent, the subscription contract binds her. What is wrong with this argument?
quiz.ok: That rule settles only whether her consent to processing is valid, not whether her contract binds her.
no: Nothing, because once she can validly consent to processing, the subscription contract also binds her.
She is below the age for valid consent, so both her consent and the subscription contract are void.
That rule also requires a parent to approve any paid contract a minor makes, which did not happen here.
quiz.why: Article 8 decides when a child's consent to processing for information society services is valid (from 16, or a national age not below 13), but it leaves national contract law unaffected. Mia's consent to processing is therefore valid at 16, while whether the subscription binds her is a question for national rules on minors' contracts. The 'nothing is wrong' option merges the two questions, treating capacity to consent to processing as capacity to contract, and the parental approval option makes the same merger in reverse by reading a contract rule into a rule about consent to processing.

quiz.concept: Targeted adverts to children: DPDP against GDPR
quiz.q: A gaming app offered directly to children has 12-year-old users in Germany and in India. For each child it obtains verified parental consent, and it then shows them adverts targeted on their in-game behaviour. Assuming the DPDP Act is fully in force, how do the DPDP Act and the GDPR's rule on children's consent treat the targeted advertising?
quiz.ok: The DPDP Act bans it despite parental consent; the GDPR's children's consent rule has no such ban.
no: Both laws allow it, because verified parental consent has been obtained for each child user.
Both laws ban it, because the GDPR's children's consent rule also forbids profiling children for adverts.
The GDPR bans it outright, while the DPDP Act allows it once verifiable parental consent is given.
quiz.why: Under DPDP s. 9, tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are banned, so verifiable parental consent cannot make the Indian adverts lawful. GDPR Article 8 only requires parental consent below 16 (or the national age, never below 13) for consent-based services offered directly to children; it contains no advertising ban, though Recital 38 seeks specific protection for children against marketing and profiling. The 'both allow it' option treats the DPDP ban as a consent requirement that parents can satisfy.

quiz.concept: One-stop shop and the lead authority
quiz.q: Two US app companies each face a forced consent complaint filed with the Belgian supervisory authority. Alpha's main EU establishment is in Ireland. Beta has sales offices in the EU but no main EU establishment. Applying the reasoning of the forced consent cases, which authority should decide each complaint?
quiz.ok: Alpha's goes to the Irish lead authority, while the Belgian authority decides Beta's itself.
no: The Belgian authority decides both, since a complaint is always decided where it was filed.
The Irish authority decides both, since it is the lead authority for every US technology company.
Alpha's goes to the Irish authority, and Beta's must wait until Beta names a main EU establishment.
quiz.why: Under the one-stop shop, a cross-border complaint goes to the lead authority of the controller's main EU establishment, which is why noyb's complaints against Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, filed in Austria, Belgium and Germany, went to the Irish DPC. Where there is no EU main establishment, no lead authority displaces the authority that received the complaint: the Conseil d'État (19 June 2020) held the CNIL competent to fine Google LLC 50 million euros for exactly that reason. So Ireland leads on Alpha's complaint and Belgium decides Beta's; the 'always where filed' option ignores the lead authority rule that sent the Meta complaints to Ireland, and the 'must wait' option ignores the Google ruling.

quiz.concept: DPDP consent limited to necessary data
quiz.q: Asha, in India, signs up for a food delivery app. To deliver her orders, the app asks her, through two separate ticks, to consent to the processing of her address and order details and to it reading her phone contacts, and she ticks both. Assuming the DPDP Act is in force, what does her consent cover?
quiz.ok: Only her address and order details, since consent is limited to the data that purpose needs.
no: All of it, since each separate tick was a free and clear affirmative act that she was able to refuse.
None of it, since asking for unnecessary data invalidates the whole of the consent she has given.
All of it, though she may later withdraw the contacts part as easily as she gave it.
quiz.why: DPDP s. 6(1) requires consent for the specified purpose and limited to the personal data necessary for it; the Act's own illustration is a telemedicine app whose consent covers telemedicine but not access to phone contacts. Reading Asha's contacts is not needed to deliver her orders, so her second tick does not extend her consent to them, though the rest of her consent stands. The 'separate tick' option treats necessity as only a factor in judging whether consent is free, which is the GDPR's approach (Article 7(4)); under the DPDP Act necessity is built into consent itself.

quiz.concept: Effects of withdrawing consent under DPDP
quiz.q: Ravi withdraws his consent on an Indian shopping platform while an order he has already paid for is still undelivered. The platform cancels that order, and tells him that its outsourced email processor, which keeps sending him promotions, is not its responsibility. Assuming the DPDP Act is in force, how has the platform acted?
quiz.ok: Wrongly on both counts: it must complete the paid order and must make its processor stop.
no: Rightly on both counts: withdrawal ends the relationship, and the processor answers for itself.
Rightly on the order, since withdrawal undoes all earlier processing, but wrongly on the emails.
Wrongly on the order, but rightly on the emails, since only the fiduciary itself must stop processing.
quiz.why: Under DPDP ss. 6(4) to (6), withdrawal does not affect earlier processing and the Data Principal bears its consequences, so a shopping platform may refuse new orders but must complete orders already paid for. The fiduciary must also, within a reasonable time, stop processing and make its processors stop, so the email processor is the platform's responsibility. The option saying withdrawal undoes earlier processing makes the classic retroactivity mistake.

quiz.concept: Broad consent for scientific research
quiz.q: A university biobank asks donors to consent to their samples and data being used for research into heart disease, in line with recognised ethical standards, and lets them opt out of particular types of study. A critic says the consent is invalid because the future projects cannot yet be named, so it is not specific. What is the strongest response?
quiz.ok: Broad consent to an area of research is allowed if it meets ethical standards and permits partial consent.
no: The critic is right, because consent must name each defined purpose and research is no exception.
Specificity is irrelevant here, because research that follows ethical standards is exempt from the consent rules.
The consent is valid only if donors are asked again before each new project, as specificity requires.
quiz.why: Specificity normally ties consent to defined purposes, but Recital 33 allows consent to certain areas of scientific research in line with recognised ethical standards ('broad consent'), with the option of consenting to parts only. The biobank's consent to heart disease research, with opt-outs by type of study, fits that pattern. The critic over-generalises the specificity rule, while the 'exempt altogether' option over-generalises the research allowance, which still works through consent.

quiz.concept: Contractual necessity cannot carry ad personalisation
quiz.q: A social network's consent to ad personalisation is held invalid because sign-up depended on it. The network drops the consent request and now says personalised adverts are part of the service users contract for, so it can rely on contractual necessity instead. Users must still accept the new terms to join. Does the switch cure the problem?
quiz.ok: No, because ad personalisation is not necessary to perform a social network contract.
no: Yes, because users who accept terms describing personalised adverts have agreed to that processing.
Yes, provided users are also told of a right to object to the advertising at a later stage.
No, because a social network can never rely on contractual necessity for any of its processing.
quiz.why: Contractual necessity (Article 6(1)(b)) covers only processing needed to perform the contract, and the Irish DPC's January 2023 Meta decisions rejected reliance on it for behavioural advertising, because ad personalisation is not necessary for a social network contract. Relabelling the adverts as part of the service does not make them necessary, and treating acceptance of terms as agreement to everything is a classic mistake. The 'never' option over-generalises: contract remains available for processing genuinely needed to provide the service.

quiz.concept: Why special categories start from a ban
quiz.q: A minister proposes to drop the general ban on processing special category data and rely instead on the ordinary rules on how processing must be carried out, enforced by fines after any misuse. What is the strongest objection, given the reason the GDPR starts from a ban?
quiz.ok: Misuse of these data can cause harm, such as discrimination, too severe and hard to undo for fines to cure.
no: These data are secret by nature, and the ban exists to keep them confidential rather than to prevent harm.
These data can never be processed lawfully, so there would be no processing for the ordinary rules to govern.
These data fall outside the ordinary rules altogether, so dropping the ban would leave them unprotected.
quiz.why: Article 9(1) starts from a prohibition because misuse of these data risks discrimination and serious harm: for ordinary data the law regulates how processing happens, but here the harm can be severe and hard to undo, so the starting point is a ban rather than penalties afterwards. The minister's plan gives up exactly that preventive logic. The 'secret by nature' option mistakes the reason, since data protection regulates processing whether the data are secret or not, and the options saying the data can never be processed or fall outside the ordinary rules ignore the ten Article 9(2) exceptions, the need for an Article 6 basis as well, and the general principles, which still apply (Recital 51).

quiz.concept: Double lock without explicit consent
quiz.q: An employer in a Member State keeps employees' sickness records and medical certificates because national employment and social security law requires it to pay statutory sick pay. Its HR manager insists on every employee's explicit consent, saying that is the only way to process health data. Which analysis is best?
quiz.ok: Legal obligation supplies the lawful basis, and the employment and social security exception lifts the ban.
no: Explicit consent is required, as it is the only exception that can lift the ban on processing health data.
Legal obligation is enough on its own, because health data need only a lawful basis, like any other data.
The employment law exception is enough on its own, because lifting the ban also makes the processing lawful.
quiz.why: Special category data need two grounds, an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception, and explicit consent is only one of ten exceptions. Keeping sickness records to meet a statutory sick pay duty rests on legal obligation under Article 6, while the exception for employment, social security and social protection law lifts the Article 9(1) ban. The HR manager's view is the classic mistake of treating explicit consent as the only key, and the two 'enough on its own' options each drop one half of the double lock.

quiz.concept: Conviction data sit outside special categories
quiz.q: A private security firm in a Member State wants a database of job applicants' past criminal convictions. Its lawyer advises that convictions are a special category of data, so the firm can lift the ban by obtaining each applicant's explicit consent. What is the main flaw in this advice?
quiz.ok: Conviction data have their own regime, which needs official authority or an authorising law with safeguards.
no: Explicit consent is too weak for this, so the firm must rely instead on the convictions having been made public in court.
Conviction data are not protected data at all, so the firm needs no ground beyond its own interests.
It omits that the firm must keep a record of each consent, since the burden of proving consent is on the firm.
quiz.why: Criminal convictions are not on the Article 9(1) list; Article 10 governs them separately, allowing processing only under official authority or where an authorising law provides safeguards. So the firm cannot open the door with explicit consent under Article 9(2) and needs an authorising law with safeguards. The record-keeping option is tempting because a controller must be able to prove consent (Article 7(1)), but it accepts the advice's mistaken premise that consent is the route at all.

quiz.concept: Lindqvist's three readings applied
quiz.q: Eva, in Austria, writes on her personal blog, hosted on an EU server and readable worldwide, that a named teammate 'is off for six weeks with a sprained wrist'. The regulator alleges unlawful processing of health data and unlawful transfers to third countries. Eva says a sprain is too minor to be health data and that her blog is a private hobby. Applying Lindqvist, how should the case be decided?
quiz.ok: She processed health data outside the household exemption, but made no transfer to third countries.
no: She processed health data and also made a transfer to every third country where the blog can be read.
She is covered by the household exemption, because a personal blog is a purely private activity.
She processed only ordinary personal data, because a passing sprain is not a medical condition.
quiz.why: Lindqvist read health data to cover all physical and mental aspects of health, held that publication on the internet to an indefinite audience is not household activity, and held that loading data onto an EU hosted page accessible worldwide is not a transfer to a third country. Eva's note about a sprained wrist is therefore health data, and her public blog falls outside the household exemption, but her upload is not a transfer. The 'transfer to every country' option is tempting, but if uploading counted, every page visible worldwide would be a transfer to every country, which is the practical sense of the ruling.

quiz.concept: Ordinary data can reveal special categories
quiz.q: A ride-hailing company stores only pick-up and drop-off points, which it treats as ordinary location data. Its analytics team then lists riders who travel to a mosque every Friday, and riders who visit a clinic that offers only HIV treatment, in order to target offers. How should the company classify those lists?
quiz.ok: As special category data, since the trips reveal religion and health, whatever the data are called.
no: As ordinary location data, since pick-up and drop-off coordinates do not appear on the list of special categories.
As special category data only once riders have confirmed their religion or diagnosis to the company.
As ordinary data, since inferences drawn from data fall outside the GDPR altogether.
quiz.why: Article 9(1) covers data revealing religious beliefs and data concerning health, and what counts is what the data reveal or allow to be inferred, not what they are called: location may reveal religion, and purchases may reveal health. Regular Friday trips to a mosque and visits to an HIV-only clinic reveal exactly those facts, so the lists are special category data needing a double lock. The 'not on the list' option looks only at the label, the mistake that the indirect revelation principle exists to prevent.

quiz.concept: No sensitive category under the DPDP Act
quiz.q: Assuming the DPDP Act is in force, an Indian diabetes app relies on consent to process the blood-sugar readings of adult users and of users aged 16. Its trainee lawyer advises that blood-sugar readings are sensitive data under the Act, so every user must give explicit consent. What is the better view?
quiz.ok: There is no sensitive category, so adults give ordinary consent, but 16-year-olds need verifiable parental consent.
no: The trainee is right, since the Act requires explicit consent for health data such as blood-sugar readings.
There is no sensitive category, so ordinary consent from every user is enough, the 16-year-olds included.
The trainee is right once the app is notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, since health data then become sensitive.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act has no sensitive category: its only extra protection is for children and persons with disability who have lawful guardians (s. 9), and sensitivity appears only as a factor, with volume, in notifying Significant Data Fiduciaries (s. 10(1)(a)). So the adults' blood-sugar readings need ordinary consent under s. 6, while every user under 18 needs verifiable parental consent, whatever the data. The 'ordinary consent for everyone' option applies the GDPR's age of 16 in India, and the Significant Data Fiduciary option turns a factor for notification into a sensitive category, which the Act does not have.

quiz.concept: Made public by the data subject herself
quiz.q: A hospital employee leaks the cancer diagnosis of Meera, a well-known actor, and the story is reported across the national press. A data broker adds the diagnosis to its celebrity profiles, relying on the exception for data manifestly made public. Which change in the facts would allow the broker to rely on that exception?
quiz.ok: Meera had herself disclosed the diagnosis in a televised interview before the broker collected it.
no: The story had stayed in the news for months, so that the diagnosis became common public knowledge.
The broker had taken the diagnosis from a reputable newspaper rather than from a gossip website.
The employee had posted the diagnosis on a public website instead of passing it to the press.
quiz.why: The Article 9(2) exception for data manifestly made public applies only where the data subject herself has made them public; the fitness app worked problem turns on users not having published their own health data. A leak and press coverage are publication by others, however widespread, so only Meera's own public disclosure would open that exception, and the broker would still need an Article 6 basis. The 'common knowledge' option is tempting, but how far information spreads does not matter when the data subject did not publish it.

quiz.concept: Free access and identity checks
quiz.q: An access request arrives from the email address registered to Sara's customer account, and nothing suggests anyone else sent it. The retailer replies that it will act only once she sends a copy of her passport and pays a handling fee, since access requests are costly to deal with. Can the retailer insist on either condition?
quiz.ok: Neither: identity checks need reasonable doubt, and a fee needs a manifestly unfounded or excessive request.
no: Both, because controllers may always verify identity and may charge a reasonable fee to cover their costs.
Only the passport, because identity must be verified for every request, although access itself is free of charge.
Only the fee, because a controller may charge for any request that is costly for it to answer.
quiz.why: Article 12 makes action on a request free unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, when a reasonable fee or refusal is possible with the burden on the controller, and allows identity to be verified only where there is reasonable doubt. A request from Sara's registered email address, with nothing to suggest anyone else sent it, raises no reasonable doubt, and an ordinary request that is merely costly to answer is not excessive. The 'only the passport' option is tempting because controllers may check identity, but only where there is reasonable doubt, not for every request.

quiz.concept: Timing of information depends on source
quiz.q: Firm A collects customers' details through its own sign-up form and emails them its privacy information the next day. Firm B buys a list of contacts from a data broker and sends each person the required information three days later, before using the list for anything else. Which firm has failed its duty to inform?
quiz.ok: Only Firm A, because information is due at collection when data come from the person herself.
no: Only Firm B, because data obtained from a third party call for information at the very moment they are obtained.
Both firms, because the information must always be given before any personal data are processed.
Neither firm, because each gave the information promptly and well within the one-month outer limit.
quiz.why: Under Article 13, where data are collected from the data subject, the information must be given at the time of collection; under Article 14, where data come from elsewhere, it is due within a reasonable period and at most one month. Firm A's email the day after sign-up is therefore late, however short the delay, while Firm B's notice three days after acquiring the list falls within a reasonable period. The 'neither' option applies the period for data from elsewhere to data collected directly from the person, and the 'only Firm B' option reverses the two rules.

quiz.concept: Erasure after withdrawal yields to legal duties
quiz.q: Lena gave an online shop consent to send her marketing emails, and she has also bought goods from it. She withdraws her consent and demands erasure of everything the shop holds about her, including her invoices, which tax law requires the shop to keep. What must the shop do?
quiz.ok: Erase the marketing data but keep the invoices, since erasure yields to the legal duty to retain them.
no: Erase everything, including the invoices, since her withdrawal leaves the shop no basis for any processing.
Erase nothing, since withdrawing consent does not affect processing carried out before the withdrawal.
Refuse the whole request, since a demand that covers records kept by law must be rejected in full.
quiz.why: Under Article 17(1), withdrawal of consent makes erasure due only where there is no other legal basis, and Article 17(3) makes erasure yield to legal obligations. So the shop must erase the data it held only for consent-based marketing, but may keep the invoices that tax law requires. The 'erase everything' option ignores the need for no other basis to remain, and the 'erase nothing' option misreads the non-retroactivity of withdrawal, which protects past processing but does not justify keeping data for the future.

quiz.concept: Public role limits delisting
quiz.q: A serving government minister asks a search engine to remove, from searches on his name, links to accurate newspaper reports from last year about his conduct in office. He relies on Google Spain. Which response is most consistent with that judgment?
quiz.ok: The links may stay, because his public role gives the public a preponderant interest in access to them.
no: The links must go, because privacy and data protection rights always override the public's interest in access.
The links may stay, because Google Spain applies only to information that was unlawfully published in the first place.
The links must go, and the newspaper must also remove the reports from its own online archive.
quiz.why: Google Spain requires delisting of name-search links to information that is inadequate, irrelevant or no longer relevant, and holds that Charter Articles 7 and 8 override the operator's and the public's interests as a rule, unless the person's role in public life justifies a preponderant public interest in access. Recent, accurate reports about a serving minister's conduct in office fall within that exception. The 'unlawfully published' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason, since the duty applies even to lawfully published pages.

quiz.concept: Restriction preserves data for legal claims
quiz.q: A gym deletes CCTV footage when its retention period ends. The period is about to end for footage of a fall in which a member, Omar, was injured, and Omar, who is suing the equipment supplier, asks the gym to keep it. The gym replies that storage limitation obliges it to delete. What can Omar require?
quiz.ok: Restriction: the gym keeps the footage for his claim but may use it only in limited cases.
no: Nothing: once the gym no longer needs the footage, storage limitation requires its deletion.
Portability: the gym must transmit the footage to his lawyer in a machine-readable format.
Objection: the gym must stop processing and hold the footage until he withdraws the objection.
quiz.why: Article 18 allows restriction where the controller no longer needs the data but the data subject needs them for legal claims: the data are kept but marked, and otherwise used only with consent, for legal claims, to protect others' rights or for important public interest. Omar can therefore stop the deletion and freeze the footage, and the gym must tell him before lifting the restriction. The storage limitation option misses that restriction is the pause button for exactly the moment when deletion would be premature.

quiz.concept: Portability covers only provided data
quiz.q: Ravi is moving to a new bank. He asks his old bank to send the new one three things: the list of payees he set up in online banking, the credit risk score the bank calculated about him, and the identity records the law requires it to keep. The bank runs his account under its contract with him. Which of these does the right to data portability cover?
quiz.ok: Only the payee list, since it is data he provided and is not kept to meet a legal duty.
no: All three, since portability covers all the personal data that the bank holds about him.
The payee list and the risk score, since both are drawn from his own dealings with the bank.
The payee list and the identity records, since he supplied the information in both himself.
quiz.why: Portability under Article 20 covers data the data subject provided, where processing is automated and based on consent or contract, and lets him receive them in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format or have them sent to another controller where technically feasible; it excludes inferred data and processing for legal obligations or public tasks. Ravi supplied the payee list and the bank processes it under contract, so it is covered, but the risk score is the bank's own inference and the identity records are kept because the law requires them. The identity records option is tempting because Ravi supplied that information, but the exclusion turns on why the bank processes the data, not on who supplied them.

quiz.concept: Objection or withdrawal depends on basis
quiz.q: A loyalty scheme analyses members' purchase data to plan its stock. It does so for Anna on the basis of her consent, and for Ben on the basis of its legitimate interests. Both now want the analysis of their data to stop. What is the correct route for each?
quiz.ok: Anna withdraws consent; Ben objects, and the scheme stops unless it shows compelling grounds.
no: Both object, and the scheme must stop at once in each case, since objection is an absolute right.
Both withdraw consent, but the scheme may refuse Ben's withdrawal if it shows compelling grounds.
Anna objects and must give her reasons; Ben withdraws consent, which the scheme cannot refuse.
quiz.why: Objection under Article 21 answers processing based on a public task or legitimate interests, whereas consent-based processing is ended by withdrawal under Article 7(3). Ben gives grounds relating to his situation, and the scheme must then stop unless it shows compelling legitimate grounds overriding his interests or needs the data for legal claims, with Recital 69 putting that burden on it. The 'absolute right' option borrows the direct marketing rule, which does not cover analysis for stock planning.

quiz.concept: Automated decisions using health data
quiz.q: An online insurer's system refuses some applicants automatically, with no human involvement, using health data they enter in the form. The insurer says the refusals are necessary for entering into the insurance contract, and it offers human intervention and a chance to express a view and contest each refusal. What does the insurer still need?
quiz.ok: Explicit consent or a substantial public interest ground, because the refusals rest on health data.
no: Nothing more, since contractual necessity plus those safeguards meets every condition for such decisions.
A token human sign-off on each refusal, so that the decisions fall outside the automated decisions rule.
A human to make every decision, since health data can never be used in automated decision-making.
quiz.why: Article 22(4) adds a condition for decisions based on special category data: they may be made only with explicit consent or on substantial public interest grounds. The contract exception and the Article 22(3) safeguards are therefore not enough where the refusals rest on health data, so the insurer needs applicants' explicit consent. The 'never' option over-generalises, since Article 22(4) permits such decisions on those two grounds, and the sign-off option fails because a token human sign-off is not meaningful involvement and leaves the decisions within Article 22.

quiz.concept: No express right, but information on the logic
quiz.q: A Dutch lender's fully automated system refuses Nora's credit application, and she asks how the decision was reached. The lender's lawyer replies that no operative provision of the GDPR mentions an explanation, that the only recital which does is not binding in itself, and that Nora is therefore owed nothing about the decision's logic. What is the flaw in this reply?
quiz.ok: The information duties still require meaningful information about the logic involved in the decision.
no: The recital binds the lender, because the Court of Justice applies recitals exactly as it applies the operative text.
The rule on automated decisions expressly grants Nora a right to an explanation of the decision.
There is no flaw: with no provision on explanation, the lender owes her no information about the logic.
quiz.why: No operative GDPR article creates a right to explanation, and only Recital 71 mentions one, but Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 15(1)(h) require meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decisions. So the lawyer's premises are right but the conclusion is wrong: Nora is owed meaningful information about the logic, and that is where any argument for an explanation must start. The 'expressly grants' option is the classic error of reading an explanation right into Article 22, and the recital option overstates recitals, which are not binding in themselves although the Court reads the Articles through them.

quiz.concept: No objection right under the DPDP Act
quiz.q: A Berlin employee and a Bengaluru employee each want their employer to stop processing their attendance data. The Berlin employer relies on legitimate interests; the Bengaluru employer relies on a legitimate use under the DPDP Act, which is in force. What can each employee do?
quiz.ok: Only the Berlin employee can object; withdrawal of consent does not reach a legitimate use in India.
no: Both can object, as each law lets a person challenge processing that rests on the employer's own interests.
Both can withdraw consent, as each law lets a person halt any processing of her data at any time.
The Bengaluru employee can withdraw consent to the legitimate use, but the Berlin employee cannot object.
quiz.why: Article 21 lets a data subject object to processing based on legitimate interests, and the controller must then stop unless it shows compelling legitimate grounds. The DPDP Act has no right to object, and its nearest equivalent, withdrawal of consent, does not reach processing under legitimate uses, which is one reason its rights are called narrower. The 'both can object' option makes the common error of saying that the DPDP Act has an objection right.

quiz.concept: Trade secrets cannot justify total refusal
quiz.q: Priya asks her bank in Spain for access to the data it holds about her, including how its credit scoring treats her. The bank refuses the request entirely, saying any answer would expose its scoring software, which is a trade secret protected by copyright. Is the refusal lawful?
quiz.ok: No, because trade secrets may limit what is disclosed but can never justify a total refusal.
no: Yes, because protecting trade secrets and software copyright overrides the right of access.
No, because access overrides trade secrets, so the bank must also disclose its scoring source code.
Yes, provided the bank offers to answer the request once Priya has paid a reasonable fee for it.
quiz.why: Recital 63 explains that access covers purposes, recipients and the logic of automatic processing, and must respect others' rights, trade secrets and software copyright, but that this must never lead to a total refusal. The bank may hold back what would reveal its protected software, but it must still confirm the processing and give Priya a copy of her data and the required information. The source code option ignores the protection of trade secrets, and the fee option borrows the rule for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, which does not apply here.

quiz.concept: Each responsible party liable in full
quiz.q: A controller ignored warnings about weak passwords, and its processor disregarded the controller's instruction to patch a server. Together the two failures caused a breach that harmed Kai, who sues only the processor for his full loss. What is the processor's position?
quiz.ok: It is liable for the entire damage, but may then recover the controller's share through recourse.
no: It is liable only for its own share, since compensation is always divided according to fault.
It is not liable at all, since only controllers owe compensation to data subjects harmed by a breach.
It is liable in full only if Kai first shows that the controller cannot pay the compensation.
quiz.why: Recital 146 (Article 82) requires full and effective compensation, exempts only a party not in any way responsible, and makes each responsible party liable for the entire damage, with apportionment possible in joined proceedings and recourse among them afterwards. Both parties were at fault and Kai sued only the processor, so it must pay his full loss and then recover the controller's share. The 'own share' option misplaces apportionment, which happens in joined proceedings or through recourse, not by cutting down Kai's claim.

quiz.concept: Foreign orders need an international agreement
quiz.q: A court in Country Z, outside the EU, orders Kessel GmbH, a German company, to send it EU customers' data held in Germany for a criminal investigation. No mutual legal assistance treaty or other international agreement links Country Z with the EU or Germany. Kessel's lawyer says the order itself makes the transfer lawful. Is she right?
quiz.ok: No, because foreign orders to transfer are recognised only where based on an international agreement.
no: Yes, because complying with a court order is a legal obligation that the company is bound to obey.
Yes, provided the company first tells the affected customers that it is complying with the order.
No, because without an international agreement, no transfer of these data to Country Z can ever be lawful.
quiz.why: Article 48 recognises a third-country court's or authority's order to transfer personal data only where it is based on an international agreement such as a mutual legal assistance treaty. With no such agreement, the order does not itself make the transfer lawful, so the lawyer is wrong. The 'legal obligation' option treats a foreign order as self-justifying, which is exactly what this boundary rule prevents, and the option saying no transfer could ever be lawful over-generalises, since Chapter V still allows transfers through adequacy, safeguards or derogations.

quiz.concept: Authorities investigate; only the Court invalidates
quiz.q: A supervisory authority receives a complaint that an adequacy decision for Country Y fails to protect transferred data, because Y's agencies have generalised access to the content of communications. The authority's chair proposes either to dismiss the complaint as barred by the decision, or to declare the decision invalid herself. Following Schrems I, what should the authority do?
quiz.ok: Examine the complaint independently, leaving any ruling on the decision's validity to the Court of Justice.
no: Dismiss the complaint, since an adequacy decision binds the authority and bars any examination of it.
Declare the decision invalid itself, since independent authorities may set aside Union acts they examine.
Pass the complaint to the Commission, since only the Commission may assess whether a country is adequate.
quiz.why: Schrems I held that national supervisory authorities must examine complaints about an adequacy decision independently, but that only the Court of Justice can invalidate it. The authority therefore can neither hide behind the decision nor strike it down itself; it must investigate and leave invalidity to the Court. The 'dismiss' option is the Irish Commissioner's own position, which the Court rejected, and the 'declare it invalid' option confuses the power to investigate with the power to annul a Union act.

quiz.concept: Clauses bind only the parties
quiz.q: After Schrems II, an exporter's lawyer argues: 'The Court upheld the standard contractual clauses, so once we sign them with our importer abroad, our transfers are safe whatever that country's law says.' What is the main flaw in this argument?
quiz.ok: Clauses bind only the parties, so they work only where the destination's law lets them be honoured.
no: The Court struck down the clauses along with the Privacy Shield, so they cannot support any transfer now.
The clauses can be used only for transfers to countries that already have an adequacy decision.
The importer abroad is not a party to the clauses, so it is never obliged to honour any of them.
quiz.why: Schrems II upheld the standard clauses decision but held that exporters must check case by case whether the destination's law allows compliance, adding supplementary measures or suspending transfers, and that supervisory authorities must suspend transfers where the clauses cannot be honoured. The reason is that a contract binds only its parties and cannot restrain a foreign State's intelligence services, so signing is not enough, as the Irish DPC's 1.2 billion euro fine on Meta Ireland in May 2023 shows. The 'struck down' option repeats the classic error: Schrems II invalidated the Privacy Shield, not the clauses.

quiz.concept: Review Court independence answers Schrems II
quiz.q: A student argues that the EU-US Data Privacy Framework is bound to fall for the same reason as the Privacy Shield, because nothing about redress has changed. Which point from the case law most directly answers the student on redress?
quiz.ok: Schrems II faulted the Ombudsperson's lack of independence; Latombe found the Review Court independent enough.
no: Schrems II faulted only the breadth of US surveillance, so redress was never one of the Privacy Shield's defects.
Latombe found the Review Court independent, and that finding now binds the Court of Justice on the appeal.
Schrems II faulted redress under the standard clauses, which the newer modular clauses have since cured.
quiz.why: Schrems II struck down the Privacy Shield because US surveillance was not limited to what is strictly necessary and because the Ombudsperson was neither independent nor able to bind the intelligence services. In Latombe (3 September 2025) the General Court dismissed an annulment action against the Data Privacy Framework, finding the Review Court sufficiently independent, which answers the student's premise; but an appeal is pending, so the framework stands without being beyond challenge. The 'binds the Court of Justice' option ignores that pending appeal, and the clauses option repeats the classic error: Schrems II upheld the standard clauses and struck down the Privacy Shield.

quiz.concept: DPDP exemption for outsourced foreign data
quiz.q: A Berlin hospital sends patient billing data to Kiran Billing, a processor in Pune, under a contract between the two. Kiran's Indian counsel says that because the processing happens in India, the DPDP Act applies to it in full. Assuming the Act is in force, what is the better view, and why?
quiz.ok: It is largely exempt: the Act spares foreigners' data processed under foreign contracts, to protect outsourcing.
no: It is fully covered: the Act protects all digital personal data processed anywhere within India.
It is largely exempt: the GDPR displaces Indian law wherever the personal data of EU patients are concerned.
It is fully covered, and Kiran may hold the data only if Germany is a notified, approved country.
quiz.why: DPDP s. 17(1)(d) exempts processing in India of foreigners' data under foreign contracts, protecting the outsourcing industry, so Kiran's work for the Berlin hospital is largely outside the Act. The EU side is unaffected: the hospital still needs controller-to-processor clauses with an assessment of Indian law, an Article 28 contract and an Article 9(2) exception for the health data. The 'GDPR displaces Indian law' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason, and the 'notified country' option misreads s. 16, a negative list for transfers out of India rather than an approval system.

quiz.concept: Limits on transfers from public registers
quiz.q: A Member State's register of licensed pharmacists is open only to people who show a legitimate interest. The registry plans, on its own initiative, to send the entire register to a marketing firm in a third country with no adequacy decision, relying on the derogation for transfers from public registers. Which change would make the transfer fit that derogation?
quiz.ok: Sending only an extract, at the request of a person abroad who has a legitimate interest in it.
no: Sending the whole register, but only once the firm asserts a legitimate interest in receiving it.
Sending the register in monthly instalments, so that no single transfer covers all of it.
Sending the register to the firm's EU office, which then forwards it to the head office abroad.
quiz.why: The derogation for transfers from public registers, explained by Recital 111, may not cover an entire register, and where access is limited to persons with a legitimate interest, the transfer may be made only at their request. An extract sent at the request of someone with a legitimate interest fits; a routine export of the whole register on the registry's own initiative does not. Splitting the register into instalments still sends all of it, and routing it through an EU office fails because Chapter V also governs onward transfers (Article 44).

quiz.concept: Privacy as a qualified right
quiz.q: After Puttaswamy, a petitioner argues that any statute letting the State process personal data without the individual's consent must be void, because informational privacy is now a fundamental right. What is the flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: Privacy may yield to a law with a legitimate aim and proportionate means, so each statute must be tested.
no: There is none, because the Court made informational privacy an absolute right that no statute may limit.
The Court protected bodily privacy and privacy of choice, but it left informational privacy to Parliament.
The later Aadhaar ruling held that State processing of personal data need not satisfy the privacy test.
quiz.why: Puttaswamy (2017) held privacy, including informational privacy, to be a fundamental right under Article 21 and the Part III freedoms, but one that a lawful, proportionate intrusion can limit. A statute allowing State processing without consent is therefore not void for that reason alone; it must pass legality, legitimate aim and proportionality. The 'absolute right' reading fails because the plurality itself set out those three tests, and the 2018 Aadhaar judgment applied them rather than dispensing with them.

quiz.concept: Aadhaar ruling upheld the scheme with limits
quiz.q: A petitioner challenging the State benefits legitimate use argues that, since Puttaswamy, any State data scheme that intrudes on informational privacy must be struck down in its entirety. How does the 2018 Aadhaar judgment bear on her argument?
quiz.ok: It cuts against her: applying proportionality, it upheld Aadhaar in substance and struck down only a part.
no: It supports her: having recognised privacy as a fundamental right, it struck the Aadhaar scheme down entirely.
It cuts against her: it revived the older rulings that had denied privacy the status of a fundamental right.
It cuts against her: it upheld Aadhaar in full, leaving private authentication under contract intact.
quiz.why: Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018), decided by five judges, applied the 2017 proportionality test, upheld Aadhaar in substance and struck down Aadhaar Act s. 57 only to the extent that it let private entities demand authentication under contract. It therefore shows that a State data scheme can survive the test with only a part struck down, which answers an all-or-nothing argument. The option crediting the 2018 ruling with recognising privacy merges the two rulings, since the nine-judge Bench did that in 2017, and the option saying Aadhaar was upheld in full misses the partial strike-down.

quiz.concept: The 2018 draft is history, not law
quiz.q: In 2028, a petitioner argues that the legitimate use for State functions is invalid simply because it departs from the draft bill that the Srikrishna Committee proposed in 2018. What is the main flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: The draft never became law, so departing from it cannot by itself make a clause invalid.
no: It relies on the 2018 draft, when only the 2019 Bill that replaced it could bind Parliament.
It ignores that the Joint Parliamentary Committee's report replaced the draft as the test of validity.
It overlooks that the draft binds only where the Act is silent, and here the Act speaks expressly.
quiz.why: The Srikrishna Committee was set up by the government on 31 July 2017, weeks before Puttaswamy was decided, and its draft Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018 never became law; nor did the 2019 Bill, withdrawn in 2022, or the Joint Parliamentary Committee's 2021 report, and the notes warn against treating the 2018 or 2019 texts as law. A clause such as s. 7(c) that lets privacy yield is measured against Puttaswamy instead: it must rest on a law, pursue a legitimate aim and be proportionate. The option letting the draft fill gaps where the Act is silent still treats the draft as law, which it never was.

quiz.concept: Non-personal data left outside the Act
quiz.q: A Bengaluru start-up analyses anonymised traffic flows from which no individual can be identified. A trainee advises that the DPDP Act governs this, because the Joint Parliamentary Committee recommended a single law for personal and non-personal data. How should the advice be corrected?
quiz.ok: That single-law idea did not survive; the Act covers only data about an identifiable individual.
no: The advice is right, because the 2023 Act adopted the Committee's model of one law for all data.
The Committee's report binds the start-up only once the government notifies it as significant.
The Act reaches non-personal data only when they are processed abroad in connection with India.
quiz.why: The JPC reported on 16 December 2021 recommending one Data Protection Bill for personal and non-personal data, but that idea did not survive: the 2023 Act regulates only personal data, meaning data about an individual identifiable by or in relation to them (s. 2(t)), and leaves non-personal data unregulated. A committee report is legislative history, not law, so it cannot widen the Act. Data from which no one can be identified therefore fall outside it.

quiz.concept: Assent is not commencement
quiz.q: In March 2026, a company negligently leaks customers' health data, and one customer suffers wrongful loss. A student's answer says the DPDP Act governs her claim, because the Act received assent in August 2023. What is wrong with the answer?
quiz.ok: Assent is not commencement; the duties begin only in May 2027, so the IT Act governs her claim.
no: Nothing; an Act binds from the date of its assent unless a court later suspends its operation.
Only the reason is wrong: the whole Act came into force with the Rules in November 2025, so it does govern.
The DPDP Act never applies to health data, which stay governed by the IT Act's rules on sensitive data.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act received assent on 11 August 2023 as Act No. 22 of 2023, but it commences in phases: definitions and the Board on 13 November 2025, Consent Managers on 13 November 2026, and fiduciaries' duties, penalties and the omission of IT Act s. 43A only on 13 May 2027. A March 2026 leak therefore falls under s. 43A and the SPDI Rules, which let a person suffering wrongful loss from negligent security of sensitive data, such as health data, claim compensation. The 'whole Act in November 2025' option is the trap: only the phase one provisions began then.

quiz.concept: Reliance on executive notification
quiz.q: Critics say the DPDP Act leaves too much to executive rule making. Which pair of decisions does the Act in fact leave to the government?
quiz.ok: Which countries personal data may not be sent to, and which State agencies are wholly exempt.
no: How large a penalty a fiduciary must pay, and whether a complaint has grounds to proceed.
Whether a Board order survives an appeal, and whether a dispute should go to mediation.
Whether to accept a fiduciary's voluntary undertaking, and whether to issue interim orders.
quiz.why: The notes sum up the 2023 Act as a shorter, more permissive law relying on consent and executive rule making. Under s. 16(1) the government may restrict transfers to notified countries, and s. 17(2)(a) exempts State agencies from the whole Act by executive notification, without statutory necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation or oversight. Penalties, the sufficiency of complaints, mediation, undertakings and interim orders are for the Board, an independent adjudicatory body (ss. 28 and 31 to 33), and appeals go to the TDSAT (s. 29), so none of the other pairs shows reliance on the executive.

quiz.concept: No special category for health data
quiz.q: In 2028, HealthPal processes its Indian users' symptom data on the basis of their consent. A trainee says that, because these are health data, the DPDP Act sets a stricter gateway for them than for other personal data. What is the correct position?
quiz.ok: Health data need only the gateways that apply to all data, as the Act has no sensitive data category.
no: Explicit consent is needed, as it is for the special categories of personal data under the GDPR.
A stricter gateway applies, but only once the government notifies HealthPal as a significant fiduciary.
Health data fall outside the Act and stay under the IT Act's rules on sensitive personal data.
quiz.why: The 2023 Act dropped sensitive data as a category, so health data pass through the same gateways as any other personal data: valid consent or a legitimate use (s. 4). Sensitivity matters only indirectly: the government weighs the volume and sensitivity of data when notifying Significant Data Fiduciaries (s. 10(1)), and notification adds duties such as an India based DPO and annual audits, not a stricter gateway. Explicit consent for health data is the GDPR's Article 9 rule, and the IT Act route for sensitive data, s. 43A, is omitted from 13 May 2027.

quiz.concept: Long title balances right and need
quiz.q: In proceedings before the Board, counsel for a fiduciary argues that because the long title speaks of the need to process personal data for lawful purposes, every doubtful duty in the Act must be read in the fiduciary's favour. What is the best reply?
quiz.ok: The title balances that need against the individual's right, so it supports protective readings too.
no: The title carries no interpretive weight, since only the operative sections can decide a case.
The title recognises only the individual's right, so every doubt must be resolved in her favour.
The title treats all processing as banned unless a legitimate use applies, so counsel's argument must fail.
quiz.why: The long title provides for processing 'in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such personal data for lawful purposes'. It frames a balancing law about the manner of processing, not a ban, and supports both a protective purposive reading and weight for genuine processing needs. Counsel's one-sided reading ignores the right, just as the option resolving every doubt in her favour ignores the need.

quiz.concept: No monitoring limb, public data excluded
quiz.q: In 2029, a Singapore firm scrapes the profiles that Indian engineers have themselves made public online, and sells analytics about them to US companies. It offers nothing to anyone in India. Which reasoning on the DPDP Act is correct?
quiz.ok: It is outside: it offers nothing in India, so the foreign reach fails, and self-published data are excluded.
no: It applies, because profiling Indian engineers online counts as monitoring their behaviour in India.
It applies, because the Act follows the data of Indian Data Principals wherever in the world they are processed.
It is outside, but only because the firm carries out all of its processing beyond India's territory.
quiz.why: Section 3(b) reaches processing abroad only where it is connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India, and there is no monitoring limb like GDPR Article 3(2)(b). Separately, s. 3(c) excludes data that the Data Principal herself made public. The firm is outside on both counts, but not merely because it is abroad: a foreign firm offering services to people in India would be caught.

quiz.concept: Only digital personal data are covered
quiz.q: In 2028, a Delhi clinic keeps its patient records only on paper forms filed in a cabinet. Which change in the facts would bring those records within the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: The clinic scanned the forms into its computer system and went on to process the scanned copies.
no: The forms began to record patients' health conditions as well as their names and contact details.
