The clinic grew large enough for the government to notify it as a Significant Data Fiduciary.
The clinic began to send the paper forms by courier to a diagnostic laboratory in Mumbai.
quiz.why: Section 3(a) applies to digital personal data processed in India, whether collected digitally or collected physically and digitised later, so undigitised paper records fall outside the Act. Scanning the forms and processing the scanned copies brings them within it. The sensitivity of the data, the clinic's size or status, and physical sharing of the paper do not matter while the records stay undigitised.

quiz.concept: Processor or fiduciary depends on purpose
quiz.q: PayEase runs payroll for an employer under a contract, processing staff data only on the employer's instructions. It then starts using the same data to market its own loans to those staff. How does the DPDP Act classify PayEase?
quiz.ok: A processor for the payroll, but a fiduciary for the marketing, whose purpose and means it decides.
no: A processor throughout, because it first received the data under the employer's contract.
A fiduciary throughout, because any business that holds personal data is a fiduciary.
A joint fiduciary with the employer for both activities, because the two share the same data.
quiz.why: A Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing, alone or with others (s. 2(i)), while a Data Processor processes on a fiduciary's behalf (s. 2(k)). For payroll PayEase acts on the employer's behalf, but in marketing its own loans it decides why and how the data are used, so it is a fiduciary for that processing. How it first obtained the data does not fix its role for a new purpose of its own.

quiz.concept: Specified purpose limits retention
quiz.q: In 2028, a fitness app's notice named one purpose: running Riya's workout plans. She cancels and asks for erasure. The app refuses, giving as its only reason that it needs the data for future product research, which its notice never mentioned. Does that reason justify the refusal?
quiz.ok: No: only the specified purpose stated in the notice, or a legal duty, can justify keeping the data.
no: Yes: product research is a lawful purpose, since no law forbids it, so the app may keep the data.
Yes: the erasure right covers only data she provided voluntarily, not data processed on her consent.
No: the erasure right is absolute, so the app must erase whatever reason it gives for keeping the data.
quiz.why: Section 12(3) requires erasure on request unless retention is necessary for the specified purpose or for legal compliance, and s. 2(za) defines the specified purpose as the purpose stated in the notice. Product research was never stated and her workout plans have ended, so it cannot justify the refusal; only a legal duty, such as the one-year retention of logs under Rule 8(3), could justify keeping some data. The 'lawful purpose' option confuses the permissive s. 4 test with the narrower specified purpose, and the 'absolute right' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason.

quiz.concept: Joint fiduciaries without allocation rules
quiz.q: Once the Act's duties apply, an airline and a hotel chain jointly decide what customer data to collect for a shared loyalty programme and how to use them. When a customer complains, each says the other is the fiduciary. How does the DPDP Act treat them?
quiz.ok: Both are fiduciaries, though unlike the GDPR the Act sets no rules for sharing out their duties.
no: Only the firm that collected the data is a fiduciary, and the other is merely its processor.
Both are fiduciaries, and they must divide their duties by an arrangement, as joint controllers must.
Neither is a fiduciary for the programme until the government notifies one of them as significant.
quiz.why: A Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing 'alone or with others' (s. 2(i)), so both firms are fiduciaries for the programme. The notes stress that the Act recognises joint fiduciaries without allocation rules, unlike the GDPR's joint controller regime. Requiring an arrangement that divides their duties imports the GDPR position, and significance is a separate status that matters only for extra duties.

quiz.concept: Lawful purpose is only the first step
quiz.q: In 2029, a data broker's lawyer argues: 'Profiling users to sell insights is not forbidden by any law, so it is a lawful purpose, and our processing is therefore permitted.' What is the main flaw?
quiz.ok: A lawful purpose is necessary but not enough; the broker still needs consent or a listed legitimate use.
no: Profiling for sale is not a lawful purpose, because a lawful purpose must benefit the Data Principal.
The broker must also show that its interests outweigh the users', as a legitimate interests ground requires.
There is no flaw, because the Act's real protection lies in the lawful purpose requirement itself.
quiz.why: Section 4 permits processing only for a lawful purpose, defined as any purpose not expressly forbidden by law, and only with consent or for a legitimate use. Because the lawful purpose test is so permissive, the real contest lies at the consent and legitimate use steps. The balancing option imports the GDPR's legitimate interests ground, which the DPDP Act does not have.

quiz.concept: Notice for old and new consents
quiz.q: After the notice duty commences on 13 May 2027, a bank keeps processing data under a consent Asha gave in 2024 without any notice. A new app takes Bilal's consent in June 2027 and emails him the notice a week later. How do the notice rules treat them?
quiz.ok: The bank must notify Asha as soon as reasonably practicable and may carry on; the app's late notice fails.
no: Both comply, so long as each of them sends its own notice as soon as reasonably practicable after the consent.
The bank must stop processing Asha's data until she consents again after receiving a proper notice.
The bank owes Asha no notice, as her consent predates commencement; the app's late notice fails.
quiz.why: For consents given before commencement, s. 5(2) requires notice as soon as reasonably practicable and lets processing continue until the Data Principal withdraws. For new consents, s. 5(1) requires every request to be accompanied or preceded by notice, so a notice sent a week after Bilal's consent is too late. The option treating both as compliant wrongly extends the transitional rule for old consents to new ones.

quiz.concept: Conditional consent under both regimes
quiz.q: HealthPal, with users in Germany and India, makes consent to personalised advertising a condition of its free plan, although the plan does not need advertising to work. Once both laws apply, how do the GDPR and the DPDP Act treat that consent?
quiz.ok: Both reject it: the GDPR as not freely given, the DPDP Act as conditional and beyond the necessary data.
no: Only the GDPR rejects it, because the DPDP Act lets a free service attach conditions to consent.
Only the DPDP Act rejects it, because the GDPR treats advertising as necessary for providing a free service.
Neither rejects it, because a user who dislikes the condition can simply decline the free plan.
quiz.why: Section 6(1) requires consent to be free, unconditional and limited to the data necessary for the purpose; together these stop a fiduciary from making a service conditional on consent to processing it does not need. Under the GDPR, conditioning the free plan on advertising consent fails Article 7(4) and Recital 43, and the Meta decisions reject advertising as contractually necessary. The model therefore fails under both laws.

quiz.concept: Conditions of the State benefits use
quiz.q: In 2028, a State department wants to enrol Kavita in a prescribed subsidy without asking her, using her data from a departmental database that has never been notified. She has never consented to State processing for any benefit, and the processing otherwise meets the standards set by the Rules. Which change in the facts would let it rely on the legitimate use for State benefits?
quiz.ok: The database holding her data had been notified before the department used it.
no: The department had sent her a notice about the subsidy before it used her data.
She had been told of the proposed use and had raised no objection to it.
The subsidy was valuable enough to make the use proportionate to its benefit for her.
quiz.why: Section 7(b) lets the State process data without consent to provide prescribed subsidies, benefits, services, certificates, licences or permits only where she previously consented to such State processing or the data are in a notified database, subject to Rule 5 standards. A notified database would therefore satisfy the clause. Silence after being told belongs to the voluntary provision use in s. 7(a), and neither a notice nor a favourable balance substitutes for the statutory conditions.

quiz.concept: Disaster use is tied to assistance
quiz.q: During floods in 2028, an NGO relies on the disaster legitimate use to collect stranded residents' phone numbers and locations and guide rescue boats to them. Six months after the floods are over, it texts the same residents to ask for donations. How does the DPDP Act treat the donation appeal?
quiz.ok: It needs consent or another listed use, as the disaster use covers only safety or assistance during the floods.
no: It is covered by the disaster use, since data gathered in a disaster may be reused for related good causes.
It is covered as voluntary provision, since residents who gave their numbers to rescuers may be contacted again.
It needs no basis at all, since a charity's appeal serves the public interest rather than a commercial aim.
quiz.why: Section 7(h) allows processing without consent for safety or assistance during a disaster or breakdown of public order, so it cannot stretch to a fundraising appeal six months after the floods. Voluntary provision under s. 7(a) does not help either: it covers only the specified purpose for which the data were given, here the rescue, and ends with that purpose, as the broker illustration shows. Nor is there any public interest or legitimate interests ground, because s. 4 allows only consent or a listed legitimate use.

quiz.concept: Breach versus unreasonable safeguards
quiz.q: In mid-2028, a fiduciary with encryption, access controls, logging, backups and security clauses in its processor contracts is breached by a novel attack, and it intimates the breach at once. Is it exposed to the highest penalty in the Schedule?
quiz.ok: Only if its safeguards fell short of reasonable; a breach alone is not the failure penalised.
no: Yes, because any breach proves that the fiduciary's safeguards cannot have been reasonable.
No, because a fiduciary that intimates a breach promptly cannot be penalised for it.
Only if children's data were affected, since only those breaches carry the highest penalty.
quiz.why: The top penalty, up to 250 crore rupees, is for failing to take reasonable security safeguards under s. 8(5) and Rule 6, not for suffering a breach. A fiduciary with the Rule 6 minimum measures may still be breached, so the Board must ask whether its safeguards were reasonable. Prompt intimation discharges the separate duty in s. 8(6) but does not answer a security failure if one is shown, and the children's duties carry a lower cap of 200 crore rupees.

quiz.concept: Breach notice under both regimes
quiz.q: In 2029, a Pune company with users in Germany and India suffers a breach that exposes email addresses and poses only a low risk to users. It plans to notify the regulators within 72 hours and to tell no users. Assess the plan under the GDPR and the DPDP Act.
quiz.ok: It meets the GDPR, but the DPDP Act requires each Indian user and the Board to be told without delay.
no: It meets both laws, since neither requires users to be told of a breach that poses only a low risk.
It fails under both laws, since both require every affected user to be told of any breach at all.
It fails only under the GDPR, which requires every affected user to be told, whatever the risk.
quiz.why: Under the GDPR the authority is notified within 72 hours and users are told only where the risk to them is high (Articles 33 and 34), so this low-risk breach needs no user notice. The DPDP Act has no seriousness threshold: s. 8(6) and Rule 7 require every affected Data Principal and the Board to be told without delay, followed by a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours. The plan therefore fails under the DPDP Act, both because users are left out and because 72 hours is the deadline for the follow-up report, not the first intimation.

quiz.concept: Erasure yields to required retention
quiz.q: In 2028, Ravi withdraws his consent from a food delivery app and demands that the app and its cloud processor delete everything about him at once, including the logs of his use. What must the app do?
quiz.ok: Erase his data and have its processor do so too, keeping only what law requires, such as a year's logs.
no: Erase its own copy only, since whatever the processor holds is entirely the processor's own responsibility.
Delete everything at once, because withdrawal of consent overrides any duty to keep the data.
Keep everything for three years, in case he returns to the app and reactivates his account.
quiz.why: On withdrawal of consent, s. 8(7) and Rule 8 require the fiduciary to erase the data and cause its processors to erase them, unless law requires retention. The Rules themselves require every fiduciary to keep personal data, traffic data and logs for at least one year for the Seventh Schedule purposes (Rule 8(3)), so those may be kept. The three year figure belongs to the large platform rule for inactive users, which requires erasure rather than permitting retention.

quiz.concept: Child age under the two regimes
quiz.q: In 2028, HealthPal relies on consent for its 17-year-old users in Germany and in India. Assume that the GDPR age applying in Germany is sixteen, and that no Indian exemption or notified age threshold applies. What does each law require for these users?
quiz.ok: The German user consents herself; the Indian one needs verifiable parental consent and cannot be targeted.
no: Both may consent for themselves, since both users are over sixteen, the age at which childhood ends.
Both need verifiable parental consent, since both laws treat everyone under eighteen as a child.
The Indian user may consent for herself, although no advertising may be targeted at her until she is eighteen.
quiz.why: The GDPR requires parental consent only below sixteen or the national age (Article 8), so the 17-year-old in Germany consents herself. The DPDP Act treats everyone under eighteen as a child (s. 2(f)), so the Indian user needs verifiable parental consent (s. 9(1)) and cannot be tracked or targeted with advertising (s. 9(3)). Setting the Indian age at sixteen is the trap the notes warn against.

quiz.concept: Verifying a lawful guardian
quiz.q: In 2028, a travel booking app is asked to process the data of Arun, a 30-year-old man with an intellectual disability who has a lawful guardian. His cousin, who cares for him, offers her own consent and proves only that she is an adult. What must the app verify before relying on it?
quiz.ok: That she was appointed his guardian by a court, a designated authority or a local level committee.
no: Only that she is an identifiable adult, which is the same check required for a child's parent.
Nothing, because Arun is an adult and must give his own consent to processing in every case.
That she lives with Arun and manages his daily affairs, which in itself makes her his guardian.
quiz.why: Section 9(1) requires the verifiable consent of the lawful guardian before processing the data of a person with disability who has one, and such a guardian counts as the Data Principal (s. 2(j)). Rule 11 requires the fiduciary to verify that the guardian was appointed by a court, a designated authority or a local level committee. The identifiable adult check in Rule 10 is the test for a child's parent, so it is not enough here.

quiz.concept: Significance comes from notification
quiz.q: In 2029, a social media intermediary with five crore registered users in India has never been notified as significant. Its compliance head says it therefore need not appoint a Data Protection Officer or carry out annual impact assessments and audits, nor follow the special erasure rule for large platforms. Is she right?
quiz.ok: Right on the officer and the assessments, but wrong on erasure, which turns on its class and user numbers.
no: Right on all of them, since every extra duty for large platforms depends on notification.
Wrong on all of them, since crossing two crore users makes a platform significant automatically.
Wrong on the officer and the assessments, but right on erasure, which binds only significant fiduciaries.
quiz.why: Significant Data Fiduciaries are notified by the government considering factors such as the volume and sensitivity of data and risk to rights (s. 10(1)); only then must a fiduciary appoint an India based DPO and carry out the annual impact assessments and audits required by s. 10(2) and Rule 13. The large platform erasure rule in Rule 8 and the Third Schedule applies by user numbers alone, two crore registered users for social media intermediaries, so it binds this platform. Treating the user threshold as making a platform significant merges two separate tests.

quiz.concept: Availability breach and parents as Data Principals
quiz.q: In 2028, ransomware locks an online tutoring platform for pupils aged 10 to 15 out of its records for a day, though nothing is copied. The platform says there was no breach because no data left its systems, and that pupils cannot be sent notices anyway. What must it do?
quiz.ok: Treat the loss of access as a breach and tell each pupil's parent and the Board without delay.
no: Nothing, because a personal data breach requires data to be disclosed, copied or acquired by someone.
Tell the Board only, because pupils are children and the Board will decide whether parents should know.
Tell each pupil directly and the Board, because a child remains the only Data Principal for her data.
quiz.why: A personal data breach includes any loss of access that compromises the availability of personal data (s. 2(u)), so a day of lock-out counts even though nothing was copied. The pupils are children, being under eighteen (s. 2(f)), so their parents are their Data Principals (s. 2(j)), and s. 8(6) with Rule 7 requires each affected Data Principal and the Board to be told without delay, followed by the detailed report within 72 hours. There is no seriousness threshold, and the platform also remains exposed on its safeguards and its duties to children.

quiz.concept: Access depends on the gateway
quiz.q: In 2029, Neha asks a pharmacy, to which she voluntarily gave her phone number for receipts, for a summary of the data it holds on her. Her colleague Kabir asks the same of their employer, which processes his data under the employment legitimate use. Who is entitled to a summary?
quiz.ok: Only Neha, since voluntary provision is treated like consent, while the employment use gives no access.
no: Both, because the access right belongs to every Data Principal whatever the fiduciary's ground.
Only Kabir, because the access right attaches to the employment use but not to voluntary provision.
Neither, because the access right arises only where the Data Principal gave express consent to processing.
quiz.why: Section 11 gives the access right against a fiduciary to which she gave consent, including deemed consent under the voluntary provision use in s. 7(a). Where the fiduciary relies on any other legitimate use, such as employment under s. 7(i), there is no access right at all. The 'express consent only' option overlooks that s. 7(a) works like deemed consent, which is why ss. 11 and 12 apply to it.

quiz.concept: State correction only for decisions
quiz.q: In 2028, a State department processes Leela's data under the consent she gave when she registered on its portal for its schemes. It records her occupation wrongly but so far uses the record only to address general circulars to her, and it refuses her request for correction. Which change in the facts would entitle her to the correction?
quiz.ok: The department began using the record to decide whether she is eligible for one of its schemes.
no: She attached documents that verifiably prove her correct occupation to her correction request.
She asked the department to erase the wrong record altogether rather than to correct it.
She first raised a grievance with the department's grievance officer before renewing her request.
quiz.why: Under s. 17(4), the erasure right in s. 12(3) does not apply to the State, and the correction duty in s. 12(2) applies only where the processing includes a decision affecting the Data Principal. Once the record feeds a decision on her eligibility, the department must correct it. Authentic documents and a prior grievance are things she owes or must exhaust, but neither widens the State's limited duty, and erasure on request never binds the State.

quiz.concept: Grievance route for Consent Managers
quiz.q: In 2029, Farah tells her registered Consent Manager to withdraw her consent to a lender, but it never passes the instruction on. She files a complaint about it straight away with the Board. What is the procedural position?
quiz.ok: She must first use the Consent Manager's own grievance redressal; after that the Board can act against it.
no: The Board cannot act at all, since its complaint jurisdiction covers only Data Fiduciaries.
She may go straight to the Board, since the internal step applies only to complaints made against fiduciaries.
She must sue the Consent Manager in a civil court, since it is not a Data Fiduciary under the Act.
quiz.why: Section 13 entitles a Data Principal to grievance redressal from a fiduciary or a Consent Manager, within at most ninety days (Rule 14(3)), and she must exhaust that remedy before approaching the Board. The Board's functions under s. 27 include acting on complaints against both fiduciaries and Consent Managers. Going straight to the Board follows the GDPR model of direct complaint, which the DPDP Act reverses, and civil courts are barred (s. 39).

quiz.concept: Nomination on death or incapacity
quiz.q: In 2028, Meena nominates her son to exercise her rights under the DPDP Act. She later spends a month trekking abroad with no internet access, and a year after that a stroke leaves her unable to manage her affairs. In which situation may her son act as her nominee?
quiz.ok: Only after the stroke: incapacity means inability to act through unsoundness of mind or bodily infirmity.
no: In both situations, since a nominee may act whenever the Data Principal cannot conveniently act herself.
Only after her death, since a nominee's authority under the Act begins only when the Data Principal dies.
Neither yet, since the Act, like the GDPR, leaves nominees and deceased persons' data to the general law.
quiz.why: Section 14 lets a Data Principal nominate an individual to exercise her rights on her death or incapacity, and incapacity means inability to exercise them because of unsoundness of mind or infirmity of body. A month out of contact is neither, but a stroke that leaves her unable to manage her affairs is incapacity. The GDPR, by contrast, leaves the deceased to national law (Recital 27), which is why nomination counts among the DPDP Act's distinctive features.

quiz.concept: Scope of the duty not to suppress
quiz.q: In 2028, Rohan leaves out a material past address when applying online to a State agency for a proof-of-address document. His sister Meera leaves out her middle name when signing up to a shopping app. Who breaches a duty of a Data Principal?
quiz.ok: Only Rohan, since the duty not to suppress covers State documents and identity proofs, not ordinary sign-ups.
no: Both, since a Data Principal must never suppress any information she gives to any fiduciary.
Neither, since the duty to give authentic information arises only when a Data Principal seeks correction or erasure.
Only Meera, since giving an incomplete name to a business amounts to impersonating another person.
quiz.why: Section 15 bars suppressing material information when providing data for State documents, unique identifiers, proof of identity or proof of address, so Rohan's omission is caught and can attract a penalty of up to 10,000 rupees. No duty demands completeness in an ordinary sign-up, and Meera does not pretend to be anyone else, so impersonation is not engaged. The 'authentic information' duty is a separate one, limited to correction and erasure requests.

quiz.concept: Who may be a Consent Manager
quiz.q: In December 2026, a company incorporated in Singapore, with a net worth far above the minimum and directors of proven integrity, applies to the Board to register as a Consent Manager. What is the main obstacle?
quiz.ok: A Consent Manager must be an Indian company, which a Singapore company is not.
no: Registration opens only in May 2027, when the rest of the Act's duties begin.
It must first appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India, as a significant fiduciary must.
A Consent Manager must answer to the fiduciaries it serves, which a foreign firm cannot ensure.
quiz.why: Rule 4 and Part A of the First Schedule require a Consent Manager to be an Indian company with adequate capacity, sound finances, a net worth of at least two crore rupees and directors of integrity. The registration provisions (s. 6(9), Rule 4 and s. 27(1)(d)) operate from 13 November 2026, so timing is no bar in December 2026. A Consent Manager is accountable to and acts for the Data Principal (s. 6(8)), and an India based DPO is a duty of Significant Data Fiduciaries only.

quiz.concept: No portability or restriction rights
quiz.q: In 2028, a music streaming service processes Tara's data on the basis of her consent. She wants to take her listening history to a rival in a reusable form and, meanwhile, to stop the service using her data while she decides. What does the DPDP Act give her?
quiz.ok: A summary of her data and the power to withdraw consent, but no portability or restriction right.
no: A right to have her data sent to the rival in a reusable form, but no right to pause processing.
A right to pause processing while she decides, but no right to have her data moved to the rival.
Only the power to withdraw consent, since a summary is available only for voluntarily given data.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act omits portability, objection, restriction and automated decision rights, so she cannot require transfer to a rival or a pause in processing. She can obtain a summary under s. 11, since the processing rests on consent, and withdraw consent under s. 6, after which processing must stop within a reasonable time. The absence of portability is also why the notes say the Act weakens competition between services.

quiz.concept: Remedies after an algorithmic refusal
quiz.q: In 2029, a bank's automated scoring system refuses Priya a credit card, using data she gave with her consent. She believes it relied on an outdated salary figure. Which course does the DPDP Act support?
quiz.ok: Seek correction of the salary figure, since data used for a decision about her must be accurate.
no: Demand that a human reconsider the refusal, under a right not to be subject to automated decisions.
Complain straight to the Board, which can order the bank to compensate her for the refusal.
Demand a full copy of every record and score held on her, to be handed over in a reusable form.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act gives no right to human review, to contest or to an explanation, but for consent based processing she can obtain correction and updating of her data (s. 12), and the bank must keep data used for decisions about her complete, accurate and consistent (s. 8(3)). If the bank does not act, she must use its grievance redressal (s. 13) before complaining to the Board, which can penalise but not compensate. Access yields only a summary, not a copy, and there is no portability.

quiz.concept: Negative list against GDPR transfers
quiz.q: In 2029, an Indian company and a German company each want to send customer data to a private firm in Country Z. India has not notified Z as restricted, no other Indian law restricts the transfer, the Indian company is not a significant fiduciary, and no GDPR transfer route is yet in place for Z. What is the position of each?
quiz.ok: The Indian firm may send freely; the German one is barred until a route applies, with an impact assessment.
no: Both may transfer freely, since neither law restricts transfers to a country that is not listed.
Both are barred until each has put a transfer route and an impact assessment in place for Country Z.
The Indian firm must first carry out an impact assessment, while the German one may transfer its data freely.
quiz.why: Section 16(1) adopts a negative list: the government may restrict transfers to notified countries, and transfer anywhere else is free, with no impact assessment. The GDPR takes the opposite approach, barring transfers unless a route applies, with an impact assessment. The stem rules out the Indian exceptions: stricter laws preserved by s. 16(2), the Rule 13(4) localisation for Significant Data Fiduciaries, and the Rule 15 conditions on making data available to foreign States or entities under their control.

quiz.concept: Partial exemption drops breach intimation
quiz.q: In 2028, a telecom company processes a former customer's data as necessary to enforce its legal claim against him for unpaid bills, and hackers steal the data. Must the company tell him and the Board about the breach?
quiz.ok: No: that duty is disapplied, though the company must still keep reasonable security safeguards.
no: Yes: every breach must be intimated, since the intimation duty has no seriousness threshold of any kind.
No: processing to enforce a legal claim falls outside the whole Act, security duties included.
It need tell only the Board, since only the former customer's rights fall away under the exemption.
quiz.why: Processing necessary to enforce legal rights or claims is partly exempt under s. 17(1): Chapter II (ss. 4 to 10) except s. 8(1) and (5), Chapter III and s. 16 do not apply. The breach intimation duty in s. 8(6) sits in Chapter II and is not one of the two surviving provisions, so it falls away, while the overarching responsibility in s. 8(1) and the security safeguards in s. 8(5) still bind the company. The 'no seriousness threshold' point is true where the duty applies, but it cannot revive a duty that the exemption has disapplied.

quiz.concept: Partial and total exemptions compared
quiz.q: In 2029, a market regulator processing data in its supervisory functions and a State agency notified for the total exemption both leak data through weak security. Which of them was still bound by the duty to take reasonable security safeguards?
quiz.ok: Only the regulator, since a partial exemption keeps the security duty and a total one removes the Act.
no: Both, because the duty to take reasonable security safeguards survives every exemption in the Act.
Neither, because both are State bodies whose processing is exempt from all of a fiduciary's duties.
Only the notified agency, because regulators in supervisory roles are outside the Act altogether.
quiz.why: Under s. 17(1), processing by regulators performing regulatory or supervisory functions loses most of Chapter II, all of Chapter III and s. 16, but the overarching responsibility and the security safeguards in s. 8(1) and (5) survive, so the regulator was still bound. Under s. 17(2)(a), the whole Act does not apply to a notified State instrumentality, so nothing survives. That contrast, security kept in one tier and nothing in the other, is why the total exemption draws the strongest criticism.

quiz.concept: Start-up exemption keeps consent rules
quiz.q: In 2028, the government notifies a start-up under its power to exempt certain fiduciaries from duties that include the notice duty. The founder reasons: 'With no notice to give, the consent rules no longer bind us, so we may bundle consent to any data we like.' What is the flaw?
quiz.ok: The exemption reaches notice but not valid consent, which must still be limited to necessary data.
no: There is none, since consent cannot be informed without notice, so the consent rules fall away too.
The start-up power covers only non-residents' data processed in India under foreign contracts.
Start-ups can be exempted only from the duties of significant fiduciaries, never from notice.
quiz.why: Section 17(3) lets the government exempt notified fiduciaries, including startups, from ss. 5, 8(3), 8(7), 10 and 11, but not from s. 6. Consent must therefore still be free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, affirmative and limited to necessary data. The non-residents option describes the separate partial exemption in s. 17(1)(d).

quiz.concept: Safeguards missing from the State exemption
quiz.q: Critics say the power to exempt notified State agencies from the whole Act falls short of the end to end safeguards demanded in Big Brother Watch. Which amendment would most directly answer that criticism?
quiz.ok: Requiring each exemption to be necessary and proportionate, independently authorised and overseen.
no: Requiring every exemption notification to be published in the official Gazette before it takes effect.
Extending the exemption to private contractors that process data for the notified agencies.
Allowing exemptions only within five years of commencement, like the power to disapply provisions.
quiz.why: Section 17(2)(a) exempts agencies by executive notification without statutory necessity, proportionality, independent authorisation or oversight, which are the safeguards Big Brother Watch requires and Puttaswamy arguably requires. An amendment supplying them meets the clause's weak point, proportionality, directly. Publication or a time limit leaves that gap untouched, and extending the exemption to contractors would widen it.

quiz.concept: What sets the Board in motion
quiz.q: In 2028, a fiduciary intimates a personal data breach to the Board. Before any Data Principal complains, the Board directs it to take urgent remedial measures and begins an inquiry. The fiduciary objects that an adjudicatory body can act only on a complaint. Is the objection sound?
quiz.ok: No: a breach intimation itself lets the Board direct urgent measures, inquire and impose a penalty.
no: Yes: the Board can act only on complaints made by Data Principals, never on intimations or references.
Yes: only the government may direct urgent measures, and only after a reference from the Board.
No, but only because the Board regulates fiduciaries generally, like a GDPR supervisory authority.
quiz.why: On intimation of a breach the Board may direct urgent remedial or mitigation measures, inquire into the breach and impose penalties (s. 27(1)(a)). It also acts on Data Principals' complaints, government references and court directions, so it is adjudicatory but not confined to complaints. The option likening the Board to a GDPR authority reaches the right answer for the wrong reason: the Board adjudicates on intimations, complaints and references rather than regulating like a GDPR authority.

quiz.concept: Challenging a Board order
quiz.q: In 2029, after an inquiry and a hearing, the Board penalises a fiduciary. The fiduciary files a civil suit asking a civil court to declare the penalty unlawful. What is wrong with this course?
quiz.ok: Civil courts are barred; the fiduciary's remedy is an appeal to the TDSAT within sixty days.
no: Nothing, because Board orders are executable as civil decrees and so are open to civil suits.
It must first ask the Board to direct mediation, which is a precondition of any challenge.
It should petition the High Court, because no tribunal hears appeals against orders of the Board.
quiz.why: Section 39 bars civil courts, and an appeal against a Board order lies to the TDSAT within sixty days, to be decided within six months if possible (s. 29). The TDSAT's role comes from s. 44(1), already in force, which amends the TRAI Act. That Board orders are executable as civil decrees (s. 30) concerns enforcement, not a route of challenge, and mediation under s. 31 is optional, not a precondition.

quiz.concept: Penalty caps are maxima
quiz.q: In 2029, Alpha and Beta each commit the same kind of significant breach of the security duty. Alpha contained its leak within hours; Beta took weeks to contain its leak, to save costs. Beta argues that both must pay the same penalty, because the Schedule fixes one figure for that breach. What is the strongest objection?
quiz.ok: The Schedule sets a cap, and within it Beta's late mitigation and the costs it saved justify a higher penalty.
no: None; the Schedule fixes one amount for each kind of breach, so both must pay exactly the same sum.
Beta should pay more only if its turnover is larger, because penalties are set as a share of turnover.
Both must pay the full maximum, because every breach of the security duty is treated as significant by definition.
quiz.why: Section 33 requires the Board, after a hearing, to weigh the nature, gravity and duration of the breach, the type of data, repetition, gain made or loss avoided, mitigation and its timeliness, proportionality and deterrence, and likely impact. The Schedule caps, such as 250 crore rupees for security failures, are maxima, never linked to turnover. Beta's weeks of delay in containing the leak and the costs it saved, a loss avoided, therefore justify a heavier penalty than Alpha's within the same cap.

quiz.concept: Penalties without compensation
quiz.q: In 2028, a minister says victims of data leaks are well protected, because the Board can fine a fiduciary up to 250 crore rupees for failing to keep data secure. What is the strongest objection?
quiz.ok: Fines go to the State, the Act provides no compensation, and the IT Act route closed in May 2027.
no: The fines are set as a share of turnover, so small fiduciaries that leak data pay almost nothing.
The Board can award compensation to victims only after the TDSAT has confirmed the penalty on appeal.
Fines are paid into a fund for victims, but only those who first complained to the fiduciary may claim.
quiz.why: The Board penalises (s. 33), but penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund (s. 34) and the Act provides no compensation. From 13 May 2027, s. 44(2) omits IT Act s. 43A, so a victim of negligent leakage can no longer claim compensation through the adjudicating officer and must rely on tort or contract. Penalties are fixed caps, never linked to turnover, so the turnover option misstates the scheme.

quiz.concept: Board functions begin in phases
quiz.q: In January 2027, the Board receives two matters: a registered Consent Manager has breached its registration conditions, and an app has bundled consents in breach of the consent rules. What can the Board do?
quiz.ok: Act on the Consent Manager's breach, but not on the app's, since the consent rules start in May 2027.
no: Act on both, since the Board has held its full powers from its establishment in November 2025.
Act on neither, since none of the Board's functions can operate before May 2027.
Act on the app's breach, but not on the Consent Manager's, since registration duties start later.
quiz.why: Commencement is phased. The Board's machinery came into force on 13 November 2025, its power over breaches of Consent Manager registration (s. 27(1)(d)) on 13 November 2026, and the consent rules in s. 6(1) to (8), with the rest of s. 27, only on 13 May 2027. So in January 2027 the Board can act on the Consent Manager's breach, but the app's conduct is not yet a breach of any duty in force.

quiz.concept: RTI amendment in force and unstayed
quiz.q: In April 2026, an information officer refuses a request for an official's personal information under the RTI exemption as rewritten by the DPDP Act. The applicant argues that the rewrite cannot yet apply, because the Act's duties start only in May 2027 and because its validity has been referred to a larger Bench. Assess both points.
quiz.ok: Both fail: the rewrite has applied since November 2025, and the Court declined to stay it.
no: Both succeed: the rewrite starts with the Act's duties, and a reference suspends it meanwhile.
The first fails, but the second succeeds, since a reference to a larger Bench suspends the rewrite.
The first succeeds, since the rewrite starts with the Act's duties, but the second point fails.
quiz.why: Section 44(3), which substitutes RTI Act s. 8(1)(j) to exempt 'information which relates to personal information', has been in force since 13 November 2025, in the first phase of commencement. In Venkatesh Nayak v Union of India the Supreme Court issued notice on 16 February 2026, declined an interim stay and referred the matter to a larger Bench, so the provision remains operative unless stayed. The notes specifically warn against claiming that s. 44(3) is stayed.

quiz.concept: IT Act compensation needs negligence
quiz.q: In 2026, a company that maintained reasonable security practices for its customers' health data is hacked in a sophisticated attack, and one customer suffers wrongful loss. Can she obtain compensation from the company under the IT Act?
quiz.ok: No; the remedy needs negligence in securing the data, and this company was not negligent.
no: Yes; any leak of sensitive personal data that causes wrongful loss must be compensated.
Yes, but she must claim it from the Data Protection Board, which replaced the adjudicating officer.
No; the IT Act remedy ceased to exist once the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025.
quiz.why: Until 13 May 2027, IT Act s. 43A, with the SPDI Rules 2011, makes a body corporate that is negligent in maintaining reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data, such as health data, and so causes wrongful loss or gain, compensate the person affected through the adjudicating officer (s. 46). Liability turns on negligence, so a company whose practices were reasonable is not liable merely because it was hacked. The remedy lasts until s. 44(2) omits s. 43A on 13 May 2027, and the Board never awards compensation.

quiz.concept: Legitimate use replaces only consent
quiz.q: In 2028, an employer processes staff data without consent under the employment legitimate use. It argues that, with no consent to manage, it owes none of a fiduciary's general duties, such as security safeguards, breach intimation and accuracy. What is the flaw?
quiz.ok: A legitimate use replaces consent only; a fiduciary's general duties still apply to the processing.
no: A legitimate use works as deemed consent, so those duties begin only once an employee objects.
There is none, since those duties attach only to processing that rests on the Data Principal's consent.
Those duties bind an employer only if the government has notified it as a significant fiduciary.
quiz.why: Section 4 makes consent and the s. 7 legitimate uses alternative gateways, but the s. 8 obligations bind the fiduciary whichever gateway it uses. As the answer plan puts it, a legitimate use replaces consent, not the fiduciary's s. 8 duties, so the employer must keep the data secure, intimate breaches and keep data accurate where they are used for decisions. Deemed consent and objection belong to the voluntary provision use in s. 7(a), not to employment.

quiz.concept: Anonymity and the attribution problem
quiz.q: A local firm's server is broken into with a cheap, ready-made attack kit that anyone can buy online. Investigators trace the attack only as far as a pensioner's home computer in the same city, which had been secretly taken over and used as a relay, and can get no further. Which feature of cybercrime explains why the prosecution has stalled, and which assumption of ordinary criminal law does it defeat?
quiz.ok: Anonymity, which defeats the assumption that the offender can be found and brought before a court.
no: Accessibility, which defeats the assumption that only a person with real technical skill can commit the crime.
Portability, which defeats the assumption that the owner of a thing loses it when the thing is taken.
Scale, which defeats the assumption that one offender can reach only a few victims at any one time.
quiz.why: The notes explain that each of the five features breaks an assumption of ordinary criminal law: anonymity, through false identities, proxies, encryption and compromised machines, frustrates attribution, although prosecution assumes the offender can be identified and reached. Here the trail ends at a pensioner's hijacked computer, so the obstacle is identifying the real attacker; nothing was copied and only one target was hit, which rules out portability and scale. Accessibility is the tempting option because the cheap kit shows it, but a lowered skill barrier explains how the attack was possible, not why the prosecution stalled.

quiz.concept: Why Gold's acquittal does not travel to India
quiz.q: Defence counsel in an Indian court argues: 'In R v Gold the House of Lords held that dishonestly gaining access to a data bank by a trick is not a crime. My client did the same, using another customer's password obtained by a trick, so he too must be acquitted.' What is the best reply?
quiz.ok: Gold turned on the then lack of any computer offence; Indian statute now punishes dishonest unauthorised access.
no: Gold's result holds in India too, because the IT Act treats access without permission only as a civil wrong.
Indian law now punishes every access without permission, so his dishonesty need not even be proved to convict him.
Gold held only that the trick gave the defendants the account holder's consent, and consent is no defence in India.
quiz.why: In R v Gold the House of Lords upheld the acquittal because no unauthorised access offence then existed and the forgery statute, built for documents, could not be stretched; Lord Brandon said that making such conduct a crime was for Parliament, and legislatures responded with computer-specific laws, in India the IT Act, 2000 and the 2008 amendment. Today access without permission is a s. 43(a) contravention, and done dishonestly it is an offence under s. 66 (dishonestly using another's password is also identity theft under s. 66C), so the gap that saved the Gold defendants no longer exists. The two track options fail in opposite directions: access without permission alone is only a civil contravention under s. 43, which needs no mental element, but s. 66 makes the same act a crime when it is done dishonestly or fraudulently, as here.

quiz.concept: An undefined label cannot decide liability
quiz.q: A student writes: 'Harassing someone by email is a cybercrime, so it can be prosecuted only under the IT Act's own offences, and the general criminal law has no role.' What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.ok: It lets an undefined label decide: the computer is a tool here, so the crime also exists in general law and the issue is overlap.
no: It overlooks that the IT Act defines cybercrime, and the definition covers only attacks in which the computer is the target.
It overlooks that the computer is merely incidental here, so the case raises questions of evidence rather than questions of liability.
It overlooks that the general law always displaces the IT Act where the conduct was already a crime before computers.
quiz.why: The notes stress that 'cybercrime' has no fixed definition and that a label with no legal meaning cannot decide a case, so lawyers classify conduct by the computer's role: target, tool or incidental. Email harassment uses the computer as a tool for an existing crime, often also chargeable under the general law, so the real question is how the two overlap, which is answered by comparing ingredients (Chapter 16). The option treating 'cybercrime' as a defined term repeats one of the three common mistakes the notes flag, and the incidental category is for computers that merely hold evidence, such as a murder victim's phone.

quiz.concept: Budapest categories and cross-border evidence
quiz.q: A gang in one country emails customers of a bank in a second country, posing as the bank to collect their passwords. The emails were routed through servers in a third country, which hold the records investigators need. How does the Budapest Convention's scheme deal with such a case?
quiz.ok: It treats the emails as computer-related forgery and fraud, and its procedure and cooperation rules meet the evidence problem.
no: It treats the emails as computer-related forgery and fraud, but it defines offences only and leaves evidence abroad to states.
It treats the emails as a content-related offence, and its procedure and cooperation rules meet the evidence problem.
It treats the emails as an offence against data and systems, but it defines offences only and leaves evidence to states.
quiz.why: The Budapest Convention, the first multilateral cybercrime treaty, covers substantive law, procedure and international cooperation, which answers the global, transboundary nature of cybercrime, and it sorts offences into four categories, of which computer-related forgery and fraud corresponds to ss. 66C and 66D of the IT Act. Emails impersonating a bank to collect passwords are phishing, which the technique map places under ss. 66C and 66D, so they belong with computer-related forgery and fraud, and records held on servers in a third country are the cooperation problem the Convention's procedural side exists to meet. The 'offences only' options overlook that procedure and cooperation are part of the treaty, and the content-related category covers child pornography (ss. 67 to 67B), not deceptive messages.

quiz.concept: The two tracks are not alternatives
quiz.q: A company recovers compensation from an intruder before the adjudicating officer for accessing and deleting its files without permission. Police later prosecute him, alleging that he acted to cause the company wrongful loss. He argues that, having chosen the civil track, the company cannot also have him punished. How should his argument be answered?
quiz.ok: It fails: the tracks are not alternatives, and the same act can found compensation and, if done dishonestly, punishment too.
no: It is correct: a victim must elect one track at the outset, since one act cannot be both a contravention and an offence.
It is correct: paying compensation and then facing punishment would penalise him twice over for the very same act.
It fails, but only because the claim was within the officer's limit, and only such claims leave the criminal track open.
quiz.why: The notes say the two tracks are not alternatives you choose between: the same act can sit on both, because s. 66 punishes a s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulently. The access and deletion founded compensation under s. 43, and if the prosecution proves an intention to cause wrongful loss, the same act is also an offence under s. 66. The election and 'punished twice' options both treat the tracks as alternatives, and the pecuniary limit only decides which civil forum hears a claim, so it can neither open nor close the criminal track.

quiz.concept: Width of access: a command without login
quiz.q: Meera has no permission to use a factory's systems. Without logging in, she sends a single crafted command over the internet to its networked control computer, which carries the command out. Facing a compensation claim for unauthorised access, she argues that she never entered the system, as she neither logged in nor saw any of its data. Does her argument succeed?
quiz.ok: No: access includes instructing or communicating with a computer's functions, so a command it obeys is access.
no: Yes: access means entry through a login, so a command sent from outside is at most an attempt to gain access.
Yes: access requires some data to be viewed or taken, so a command that shows her nothing cannot be access.
No: any message sent to another's computer is access and a contravention, even one the owner has permitted.
quiz.why: Section 2(1) defines 'access' as gaining entry into, instructing or communicating with the logical, arithmetical or memory function resources of a computer, system or network, and the notes stress that its width means a remote command, not only a login, can be access under s. 43(a). The factory's computer received and carried out Meera's command, so she instructed it without permission, which is access whether or not she logged in or saw any data. The login option confuses access with authentication, which only confirms who a user is, and the option treating even a permitted message as a contravention fails because s. 43 is triggered only by acting without the owner's permission.

quiz.concept: Ransomware on the two tracks
quiz.q: A gang plants ransomware on a hospital's network, encrypting the patient records and offering the key in return for a payment. The ransom is the gang's only aim. The hospital asks how the IT Act treats the attack. Which analysis is best?
quiz.ok: A contravention by contaminant and by damage to data, made an offence too by the gang's aim of wrongful gain.
no: Cyber terrorism as well, because an attack on a hospital's records is in itself proof of a terrorist intent.
A contravention by contaminant only, made an offence by the ransom demand, since encrypting data damages nothing.
The stolen-device offence, because by holding the only key the gang in effect retains the hospital's records.
quiz.why: The technique map links ransomware, which encrypts data for payment, to s. 43(c), (d) and (i) and s. 66, with s. 66F only where there is terrorist intent. Planting the ransomware introduces a contaminant, and encrypting the records alters them, which is damage under Explanation (iv); demanding a ransom shows an intention of wrongful gain, which is dishonest, so s. 66 applies as well. The 'contaminant only' option overlooks that damage includes altering or modifying data, and the cyber terrorism option fails because the gang's only aim was money, and the gravity of the target cannot supply the terrorist intent that s. 66F requires.

quiz.concept: Permission, not intent, triggers liability
quiz.q: A firm instructs an IT contractor in writing to wipe and reformat its old servers, and he does so. After a fee dispute, the firm claims compensation for the lost data, arguing that a civil contravention needs no mental element, but the claim fails. Which change in the facts would give the firm a good claim?
quiz.ok: He also wipes a separate archive drive that the written instruction did not cover.
no: He wipes the servers in a temper, hoping that the firm will regret the dispute.
He also wipes a spare machine that the written instruction listed among the old servers.
He wipes the servers knowing that the firm had never backed up the data on them.
quiz.why: Section 43 applies only where a person does one of the ten acts 'without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge', and the scope of that permission defines liability. The written instruction permitted wiping the servers, and any machine it listed, so that was no contravention however much data was lost, but wiping an archive drive outside the instruction would be deletion, and so damage, without permission. The temper option fails because a bad purpose does not take a permitted act outside the permission, as Bignell shows for access, and his knowledge about backups is equally beside the point, because the trigger is the lack of permission, not the state of mind.

quiz.concept: No intent needed for the first five acts
quiz.q: Without permission, Rohan plugs his own pen drive into his office's server and copies the payroll file onto it. Unknown to him, the drive carries a virus, which passes to the server and makes it crash at random for a week. The firm claims compensation. Which analysis is best?
quiz.ok: He is liable for the copying and also for the virus and the crashes, since none of these acts needs any intent.
no: He is liable for the copying only, since he did not know of the virus, and a contaminant must be knowingly introduced.
He is liable for the copying and the virus, but not the crashes, since a disruption must be intended to be a contravention.
He is liable for nothing, since copying leaves the firm's file in place, and he never meant the server any harm.
quiz.why: Each of clauses (a) to (e) of s. 43 needs only lack of permission, and no clause needs a mental element except clause (j). Rohan's copying is s. 43(b), the virus he brought in is introducing a contaminant under s. 43(c), and the random crashes are disruption under s. 43(e), an unexpected deviation from normal operation, so his ignorance of the virus is no answer to the claim for compensation. The 'knowing contaminant' option reads in a mental element that these clauses do not contain, and copying without permission is a contravention under s. 43(b) whether or not the original survives.

quiz.concept: Diminishing utility without altering data
quiz.q: On his last day, Kabir changes the password of his team's shared server without permission, locking his colleagues out. The files on it become useless to the firm, although none is deleted or changed. Facing a claim for interfering with the firm's information, he argues that the Act's clause on information requires it to be destroyed, deleted or altered, and every file survives exactly as it was. Is his argument a good answer to that claim?
quiz.ok: No: that clause also covers diminishing information's value or utility, which making the files useless did.
no: Yes: that clause needs information to be destroyed, deleted or altered, so only the denial of access remains.
No, but only because the new password altered the files themselves, which that clause treats as alteration.
Yes, unless he meant the files to become useless, because diminishing their value or utility must be intended.
quiz.why: Clause (i) of s. 43, added in 2008 in the wording of the old s. 66 'hacking' offence, covers destroying, deleting or altering information or diminishing its value or utility, and the notes' worked example treats a password change that locks everyone out as a contravention of clauses (d), (f) and (i). The files survive unchanged but have become useless to the firm, which diminishes their utility, so Kabir's argument fails even before the denial of access and the alteration of the system are counted. The option requiring intent repeats the mistake of requiring a mental element for every clause, when only clause (j) needs one.

quiz.concept: Authority measured by data, not purpose
quiz.q: Asha, a bank officer, may view the accounts of all customers at her branch; she looks up a neighbour who banks there, purely out of curiosity. Ravi, assigned only to his own branch's accounts, opens accounts held at another branch. Applying the English cases on misuse by authorised users, whose access is unauthorised?
quiz.ok: Only Ravi's, since authority is measured by the data and kind of access permitted, not by the purpose of use.
no: Both, because a private purpose takes Asha's access outside her permission just as another branch takes Ravi's.
Neither, because both logged in with their own valid credentials to a system they were entitled to use.
Only Asha's, because her purpose was private, while Ravi showed no improper motive in opening the accounts.
quiz.why: In Bignell, police officers who used the Police National Computer for private purposes did not commit unauthorised access because they were authorised to access that data, while in Allison an employee who accessed accounts outside her assignment did. Authority is measured against particular data and kinds of access, so Asha's curiosity does not make her access unauthorised, but Ravi's entry into another branch's accounts does. The option treating Asha's private purpose as decisive applies the very reasoning Bignell rejected; both cases are English and only persuasive in India.

quiz.concept: Forum rules and uncapped compensation
quiz.q: Two victims claim compensation from the same hacker. Nisha lost 40 lakh rupees and files a suit in a civil court because she thinks it will be quicker. Omar lost 7 crore rupees but claims only one crore before the adjudicating officer, believing that is the most anyone can recover. Who has made a mistake?
quiz.ok: Both: Nisha cannot bypass the officer for a claim within his competence, and Omar is wrong that recovery is capped at one crore.
no: Only Nisha: civil courts are barred from claims within the officer's competence, but Omar is right that recovery stops at one crore.
Only Omar: compensation is uncapped, but a claimant may take a claim of any size to a civil court if she prefers.
Neither: a claimant may choose her forum, and compensation for a contravention is still capped at one crore.
quiz.why: Claims up to five crore rupees go to the adjudicating officer under s. 46, and s. 61 bars civil courts from matters within the officer's competence, so Nisha's 40 lakh claim cannot bypass the officer. Compensation under s. 43 has been uncapped since 2008, the one crore limit being the old position, so Omar could claim his full loss, and a claim of 7 crore would go to a civil court. The 'only Nisha' option repeats the outdated cap, one of the four mistakes the notes warn against.

quiz.concept: Custodian liability before and after omission
quiz.q: An online pharmacy negligently fails to maintain reasonable security practices, and a hacker leaks the sensitive personal data it holds, causing a customer loss. In one version, the leak happens in January 2027 and her claim is decided in March 2027; in another, the leak happens in June 2027. What difference does the date make to her IT Act compensation claim against the pharmacy?
quiz.ok: In the first the pharmacy must compensate her for its negligence; in the second it need not, as the Board only penalises.
no: None: in both versions only the hacker must compensate her, since the Act makes the intruder, not the custodian, pay.
None: in both versions the pharmacy must compensate her, since its liability lasts until the Board starts its work.
In the second the Board orders the pharmacy to compensate her, taking over the duty that the omitted provision imposed.
quiz.why: Section 43A makes a body corporate that negligently fails to maintain reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data compensate those who suffer, but DPDP s. 44(2)(a) omits it from 13 May 2027, after which the Data Protection Board penalises without compensating; s. 43, which targets the intruder, is unaffected. The first version runs its whole course while s. 43A is in force, so the negligent pharmacy must compensate her, but a leak in June 2027 leaves her no IT Act claim against it. The 'intruder only' option forgets that s. 43A targets the custodian, the 'until the Board starts work' option invents a condition when the omission runs from a fixed date, and the Board option gives the Board a power to compensate that the notes say it lacks.

quiz.concept: Assisting access on the criminal track
quiz.q: A web producer who left his job after a dispute with his employer posts its server credentials in an online chat room and urges others to use them, and a stranger logs in and alters a news story. The producer never logs in himself. Can he face the offence of doing a contravening act dishonestly or fraudulently?
quiz.ok: Yes, if he aimed at wrongful loss to his old employer, since helping others gain access is itself a contravening act.
no: No, because the offence needs the accused himself to access the system, and he did no more than post the credentials.
Yes, whatever his purpose, because publishing server credentials is criminal in itself without any proof of dishonesty.
No, unless the stranger had terrorist intent, since only the graver offence reaches those who never log in.
quiz.why: In Problem I, Ram's disclosure of the server credentials is assistance under s. 43(g), and because s. 66 punishes any s. 43 act done dishonestly or fraudulently, it applies to him too if the disclosure was aimed at causing his former employer wrongful loss, with possible abetment liability as well. Personal access is not needed, because assisting access is itself one of the ten acts. The terrorist intent option inverts the model method: s. 66F does not arise without terrorist intent, but its absence does not prevent s. 66.

quiz.concept: Inadvertence splits the two tracks
quiz.q: Before leaving a stockbroking firm, Ajay, a programmer, downloads its proprietary trading code without permission. He says he meant to copy only open-source files, and both the adjudicating officer and the criminal court accept this as a genuine mistake. The firm claims compensation, and the police charge him with the criminal form of the contravention. How does his excuse fare?
quiz.ok: It fails against the claim for copying, which needs no mental element, but defeats the charge, which needs dishonesty.
no: It defeats both, because the contravention for taking source code needs an intent to cause damage, an intent he lacked.
It defeats neither, because downloading proprietary code without permission is dishonest whatever he believed.
It defeats only the civil claim, because compensation needs fault, while the crime needs nothing more than the act.
quiz.why: Problem II holds that copying without permission is a s. 43(b) contravention whatever the intent, so inadvertence is no answer to the civil claim, while s. 43(j) and s. 66 need intent to damage or dishonesty, which genuine inadvertence negates. Once his mistake is accepted as genuine, Ajay must still compensate the firm for the copying, but the s. 66 charge fails for want of dishonesty, which is the two tracks working apart. The 'defeats both' option relies on clause (j), which does need intent to cause damage, but overlooks clause (b), which needs none.

quiz.concept: Terms-of-use breaches and criminal liability
quiz.q: A prosecutor argues that breaking a website's terms of use automatically makes a user's access 'without permission', so that any user who downloads in breach of the terms can be charged with the criminal form of the contravention. What is the strongest objection to this argument?
quiz.ok: It would let private contracts define crimes, although the criminal form exists to punish genuine dishonesty or fraud.
no: The Supreme Court has already held that breaching terms of use is never relevant to permission under the Act.
Contract terms can never bear on permission, even for compensation, since only technical barriers define access.
Downloading is copying rather than access, and permission matters only under the access clause of the contravention.
quiz.why: The Aaron Swartz prosecution under the CFAA raised whether breaching contractual terms makes access 'without permission'; no settled Indian authority was located, and the better view reserves criminal liability for genuine dishonesty or fraud, leaving contractual breaches to the civil track. Treating every breach of a website's terms as a crime would let private contracts decide what is criminal, the very criticism made of the CFAA, whereas s. 66 exists to punish a guilty mind. The option saying terms can never matter even for compensation overstates the better view, which leaves such breaches to the civil track rather than outside the Act.

quiz.concept: Tampering needs no lack of consent or dishonesty
quiz.q: With the board's approval, a company's chief technology officer destroys every copy of the source code for its billing system, which he knows a regulation requires the company to keep, to cut storage costs before a system migration. He intends no gain or loss to anyone. Is the source code tampering offence made out?
quiz.ok: Yes, because knowingly destroying code the law requires to be kept is enough, whatever the owner's consent or motive.
no: No, because the owner approved the destruction, and every wrong under the Act requires acting without the owner's permission.
No, because the tampering offence, like the criminal form of the contravention, needs intent to cause wrongful gain or loss.
Only as a civil contravention, because without dishonesty the destruction can found compensation but never punishment.
quiz.why: Section 65 has four ingredients: knowledge or intention; concealment, destruction or alteration; source code used for a computer resource; and a legal requirement to keep that code. It does not ask whether the owner consented or whether the act was dishonest. The chief technology officer knowingly destroyed every copy of code he knew a regulation required the company to keep, so every ingredient is present despite the board's approval and his harmless motive. The 'owner's permission' option borrows the trigger of s. 43, which s. 65 does not share, and no civil contravention arises either, because the owner permitted the act.

quiz.concept: Copying is not tampering with source code
quiz.q: Before joining a rival, a bank programmer knowingly copies, without permission, the source code of the bank's core system, which a regulation requires the bank to keep, and takes the copy with him. The bank's original code is left untouched. Is the source code tampering offence made out?
quiz.ok: No: copying neither conceals, destroys nor alters the code, though it remains a contravention, criminal if dishonest.
no: Yes: taking legally required code to a rival conceals it from the bank, which the law obliges to keep and maintain it.
No: an insider who copies his employer's code commits only a civil contravention, never an offence of any kind.
Yes, if he meant to use it at the rival: the offence is complete once legally required code leaves the bank's control.
quiz.why: Section 65 requires knowing or intentional concealment, destruction or alteration of source code that the law requires to be kept; a copy that leaves the original untouched is none of those acts, even though the legal requirement is present here. The copying is instead a s. 43(b) contravention needing no mental element, and if it was done dishonestly, as taking the code to a rival may show, s. 66 applies too. The 'concealment' option fails because the bank still holds its code unaltered, so nothing has been hidden from it, and the 'insider' option is wrong because s. 66 reaches any person who does a s. 43 act dishonestly or fraudulently.

quiz.concept: Device identifiers as source code
quiz.q: Employees of one mobile operator reprogram the electronic serial numbers of a rival's subsidised, network-locked handsets so that the handsets work on their own network. Charged with tampering with computer source code, they argue that a serial number is a mere identifier, not source code. How strong is their argument, and what must the prosecution still show?
quiz.ok: Their argument fails, as identifiers can be source code, but the codes must also be ones the law requires to be kept.
no: Their argument succeeds, because source code means a listing of programmes, and a serial number is just a number.
Their argument fails, and nothing more is needed, since altering any identifier is tampering whatever the law requires.
Their argument fails, but the prosecution must also prove the handsets were stolen, as this is a stolen-device wrong.
quiz.why: In Syed Asifuddin v State of Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Pradesh High Court, 29 July 2005) the court held, prima facie, that the Electronic Serial Number and the System Identification Code that providers maintain and assign to handsets are computer source code, so altering the ESN attracts s. 65: 'source code' is read broadly to include device identifiers. The notes add that s. 65 applies on that reasoning only if the codes must be maintained by law, because the legal requirement to keep the code is its fourth ingredient and the one most often missed. The option saying nothing more is needed drops that ingredient, and the stolen-device option confuses s. 65 with s. 66B, which concerns receiving or retaining stolen devices.

quiz.concept: Wrongful loss alone is dishonest
quiz.q: Kiran, a student, exploits a flaw to enter his college's server and browses it out of curiosity, intending no gain or loss to anyone. Leela, a former employee, deletes her old employer's client files purely to make it lose business, gaining nothing herself. Neither had permission. Who commits the offence of doing a contravening act dishonestly or fraudulently?
quiz.ok: Only Leela: intending wrongful loss is dishonest without any gain, and Kiran's deliberate entry lacks that intent.
no: Both, because each did a contravening act deliberately, and a deliberate act without permission is a dishonest one.
Neither, because dishonesty needs an intention of wrongful gain to the accused, and neither stood to gain anything.
Only Leela, because deleting files is a graver act than browsing, and graver acts are punished whatever the intent.
quiz.why: Section 66 punishes a s. 43 act done dishonestly, meaning with intent to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss, or fraudulently, meaning with intent to defraud. Leela intended wrongful loss to her old employer, which is enough although she gained nothing; Kiran's entry is a s. 43(a) contravention, but deliberately doing an act is not the same as intending wrongful gain or loss. The 'graver act' option gets Leela right for the wrong reason, because s. 66 is triggered by the mental element, not by the kind of act.

quiz.concept: Holding the device versus using its contents
quiz.q: Dev buys a phone that he knows was stolen. Its banking app still holds the owner's saved password, which Dev uses to transfer money to himself. Which analysis is best?
quiz.ok: Receiving the phone is the stolen-device offence; using the saved password is a separate wrong, identity theft.
no: The stolen-device offence covers everything, because the data and identity held in a stolen phone are part of the device.
Only identity theft applies, because the stolen-device offence is aimed at the thief rather than at someone who buys.
Using the password is the stolen-device offence, while buying the phone is only a civil wrong against its owner.
quiz.why: Section 66B punishes dishonestly receiving or retaining a stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it stolen, and the notes stress that it concerns holding the stolen thing, while misusing the data or identity inside it is covered by other sections. Dev's knowing purchase is the direct case of s. 66B, and his dishonest use of the owner's password is identity theft under s. 66C, with ss. 43 and 66 for logging in to the account without permission. The option folding everything into s. 66B ignores that line between holding the device and misusing what is inside it.

quiz.concept: Comparing ingredients of general and special law
quiz.q: Employees copy their employer's software and data, and by false statements induce it to pay them for maintenance work they never do. Charged under the IT Act and with the general offence of cheating, they rely on the Bombay High Court decision that quashed general charges in a similar software theft case. Applying the later Full Bench ruling, what should happen to the cheating charge?
quiz.ok: It survives, because cheating requires deception, an ingredient that the IT Act provisions on the copying do not require.
no: It is quashed, because once the IT Act covers any part of the conduct, the general criminal law is excluded entirely.
It survives, because the general criminal law always runs alongside the IT Act, however completely the two overlap.
It is quashed, because the IT Act charges are bailable and compoundable, and the accused must get the lighter regime.
quiz.why: In Gagan Harsh Sharma (2018) the Bombay High Court quashed IPC charges because the IT Act covered the conduct, but the Full Bench on the reference in Awadhesh Kumar Parasnath Pathak held that the general law is not excluded where an ingredient of the general offence is missing from the special provision, such as deception in cheating, which s. 43 read with s. 66 does not require. The false statements inducing payment supply that extra ingredient, so the cheating charge can run alongside the IT Act charges. The option saying the general law always runs alongside overstates the position, because Sharat Babu still bars the general offence where both provisions cover the same conduct.

quiz.concept: The unsettled special-law exclusion question
quiz.q: A student writes: 'The Bombay High Court quashed the general charges in the healthcare software case and the Supreme Court dismissed a special leave petition against it, so it is settled across India that the IT Act always excludes the general criminal law for computer misuse.' What is the main flaw?
quiz.ok: A later Full Bench kept the general offence where it has an extra ingredient, and the question is unsettled nationally.
no: Nothing, except that the rule must now be applied against the BNS, since it replaced the IPC after the decision.
The Supreme Court had already held, in the obscenity case, that the general law prevails wherever both laws apply.
A later Full Bench went further and held that the general law always runs alongside the IT Act in such cases.
quiz.why: Gagan Harsh Sharma (Bombay High Court, 2018) quashed the IPC charges because the IT Act covered the conduct, and the special leave petition was dismissed in limine, but a Full Bench of the same court later held that the general law is not excluded where the general offence has an ingredient the special provision lacks, such as deception in cheating. Sharat Babu Digumarti still excludes the general offence where both cover the same conduct, so the position turns on ingredients rather than a blanket rule, and nationally it is unsettled and must now be answered against the BNS. The option saying the Full Bench went further overstates it, since the general law survives only where it has an extra ingredient, and the obscenity option inverts Sharat Babu, which held that IPC s. 292 could not be invoked where s. 67 applied.

quiz.concept: Biometrics as an identification feature
quiz.q: While his flatmate sleeps, Arun presses her thumb on her phone's fingerprint sensor to approve a payment to himself. He never learns or types any password. He argues that identity theft is about passwords and electronic signatures, so it cannot apply. What is the best answer?
quiz.ok: Identity theft also covers any other unique identification feature, and a fingerprint is part of digital identity.
no: His act is cheating by personation rather than identity theft, because he pretended to the bank's system that he was her.
He commits no IT Act offence, because a fingerprint is a physical trait rather than an electronic identification feature.
Identity theft applies only if he kept a copy of the fingerprint, because a credential must be held and not just used.
quiz.why: Section 66C punishes fraudulently or dishonestly making use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature, and the notes explain that digital identity includes biometric details, because a credential does not check who is presenting it. Arun dishonestly used his flatmate's fingerprint to approve a payment to himself, so her credential was used, which is the key ingredient of identity theft.
