The personation option fails because it rules out identity theft although a credential was used, which is exactly the notes' test for s. 66C, and the 'physical trait' option ignores that the section expressly reaches any other unique identification feature.

quiz.concept: Personation must operate through a device
quiz.q: A man visits an elderly woman at home, claims to be from her bank and talks her into handing him cash at the door for a 'card replacement fee'. Which change in the facts would bring the IT Act's offence of cheating by personation into play?
quiz.ok: He makes the same false claim of being from her bank in a phone call, which leads her to pay.
no: He makes the false claim only in person, having earlier texted her to fix a time without mentioning the bank.
He makes the false claim face to face while showing a forged bank identity card printed to look official.
He makes the false claim at her door using the real bank manager's name rather than an invented one.
quiz.why: Section 66D punishes cheating by personation 'by means of a communication device or computer resource', so the pretence itself must operate through such a device; cheating by personation in person falls under the general law, now in the BNS. Making the same false claim in a phone call would bring in s. 66D, as with the impersonating calls the technique map lists under vishing. A text that only fixes a time, a forged printed card or a real manager's name all leave the personation happening face to face, so none of them engages the IT Act offence.

quiz.concept: Personation versus identity theft online
quiz.q: On a dating app, Vikram builds a profile around an invented name and identity, and after weeks of chatting persuades a woman to send him money for a fake medical emergency. He never uses anyone's password or other credential. Which analysis fits best?
quiz.ok: Cheating by personation through a device, since misrepresenting his identity online to induce payment suffices.
no: Identity theft, because creating a false identity online is the theft of an identity, whatever credentials were used.
No IT Act offence, because personation means pretending to be a real person, and his persona was wholly invented.
Only the general offence of cheating, because the IT Act's personation offence needs a hacked or cloned account.
quiz.why: Section 66D punishes cheating by personation by means of a communication device or computer resource, and personation includes pretending to be another, substituting persons or misrepresenting identity, with deception and dishonest inducement; the notes list fake profiles as a typical case. Vikram misrepresented his identity on the app to deceive the woman and induce payment, so s. 66D fits. Identity theft is the tempting label, but s. 66C requires the use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature, and none was used.

quiz.concept: Using a credential versus charging another's account
quiz.q: After records about Hari, an investment banker, are stolen, a fraudster uses the details of Hari's unused credit card to buy a laptop online. The fraudster also manipulates a hotel's billing system so that his own stay is charged to Hari's account. Which analysis fits best?
quiz.ok: The card purchase is identity theft; shifting the hotel bill by tampering is a contravention, made criminal by his dishonesty.
no: Both acts are identity theft alone, since each relied on Hari's details, and the tampering adds nothing further to that.
Both acts are cheating by personation, since in each the fraudster pretended to be Hari in order to get what he wanted.
Neither act is an IT Act offence, since the fraudster never logged in to any account or system of Hari's own.
quiz.why: In the Hari illustration, using his card credentials is identity theft under s. 66C, while charging purchases to his account by manipulating a system is s. 43(h), and s. 66 if dishonest. Buying the laptop with Hari's card details uses his credential, and rigging the hotel's billing system so that the fraudster's stay is charged to Hari is the act s. 43(h) describes: charging services used by one person to another's account by tampering. The 'identity theft alone' option overlooks that separate contravention, and the personation option fails because the fraudster never pretended to the hotel that he was Hari; he tampered with its system.

quiz.concept: Digital arrest is not a defined offence
quiz.q: Fraudsters posing as CBI officers keep a retiree on a video call for days, show her a forged order and make her transfer her savings. A draft charge sheet accuses them of 'the offence of digital arrest'. What is wrong with that charge?
quiz.ok: No such offence exists: the Supreme Court only urged the Union to define one, so this is charged as personation and cheating.
no: It should be cyber terrorism, because impersonating officers of a central agency threatens the authority of the State.
Digital arrest became an offence when the Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance, though only the CBI may now charge it.
Digital arrest is a civil wrong only, so the victim's remedy lies in compensation under the RBI's procedure on mule accounts.
quiz.why: Digital arrest is not a statutory offence: in its suo motu proceedings the Supreme Court on 29 July 2026 only urged the Union to define it as a standalone offence, and the notes say the conduct is prosecuted as personation and cheating. Impersonating officers over a video call to make the victim pay is the core of cheating by personation through a device under s. 66D. The suo motu option confuses taking cognisance and directing a CBI investigation with creating an offence, and the RBI was only directed to frame a procedure on mule accounts.

quiz.concept: Privacy in public: the visibility limb
quiz.q: On a crowded metro, a man slips his phone under a woman's skirt and photographs her undergarment-clad buttocks. He argues that she was in a public carriage, where no one can expect privacy. Does his argument succeed under the privacy violation offence?
quiz.ok: No: the test covers a reasonable expectation that her private area would not be publicly visible, even in public.
no: Yes, because outside trial rooms and restrooms the offence protects only an expectation of undressing in private.
No, but only because the offence protects women, and any image of a woman taken without her consent is covered.
Yes, because the offence protects only places that are private, and a crowded metro carriage is a public place.
quiz.why: Section 66E's Explanation defines 'circumstances violating privacy' as a reasonable expectation of being able to disrobe privately without being captured, or that the private area would not be publicly visible, in a public or private place. A woman in a skirt reasonably expects that her undergarment-clad buttocks, a private area, will not be publicly visible, so capturing that image without consent violates privacy even in a crowded carriage. The option confining the offence to disrobing in trial rooms and restrooms reads only the first limb, and the 'women only' option is wrong twice, since s. 66E is gender neutral and covers only images of private areas.

quiz.concept: Privacy offence charged with voyeurism
quiz.q: The male manager of a clothes shop hides a camera aimed at its trial room and records women customers changing. The police charge sheet lists only the IT Act's privacy violation offence. Reviewing it before trial, what should the prosecutor do?
quiz.ok: Add voyeurism under the general law, which overlaps with the privacy offence and is usually charged with it.
no: Leave it: once the privacy offence applies, the special law shuts out voyeurism under the general criminal law.
Replace it with voyeurism alone, since a trial room in a shop is a public place beyond the privacy offence.
Withdraw it until the footage is shared, since both offences need the images to be published or transmitted.
quiz.why: The classroom events show s. 66E charged together with the general criminal law: the Goa trial room case led to charge sheets under IPC ss. 354, 354C and 509 and s. 66E, and voyeurism (IPC s. 354C, now in the BNS) overlaps with s. 66E, so the two are usually charged together. A man who films women changing in a trial room captures images of their private areas without consent where they expect to disrobe privately (s. 66E), and captures women engaged in a private act (voyeurism), so the charge sheet should add voyeurism. The 'shuts out' option misreads the overlap, since the two offences differ in their ingredients, and a shop's trial room is the notes' own example of a public place where s. 66E applies.

quiz.concept: Voyeurism and privacy violation compared
quiz.q: In one case, a man watches a woman using a lavatory through a gap in the wall, recording nothing. In another, a woman secretly films a male colleague changing in an office washroom, capturing his undergarment-clad buttocks, and sends the clip to friends. How do voyeurism in the general criminal law and the IT Act's privacy violation offence apply?
quiz.ok: The first is voyeurism only; the second is the privacy violation offence only.
no: The first is the privacy violation offence only; the second is voyeurism only.
Both are voyeurism and the privacy violation offence, since each involves a private act.
The first is neither offence, as nothing was recorded; the second is both offences.
quiz.why: Voyeurism (IPC s. 354C, now in the BNS) is committed by a man who watches or captures a woman engaged in a private act, which includes using a lavatory, whereas s. 66E is gender neutral but covers only capturing, publishing or transmitting images of private areas. Watching without recording is therefore voyeurism but not s. 66E, and a woman filming and sending a clip of a man's private area is s. 66E but not voyeurism, which protects women. The option calling the first neither offence and the second both fails on both counts: voyeurism also covers watching, and it does not protect men.

quiz.concept: The privacy offence is image-based, not stalking
quiz.q: After a breakup, Sameer repeatedly messages his former partner Tara and comments on her posts, although she has clearly told him to stop. He has no images of her and has never used her password. Tara's lawyer proposes a charge under the IT Act's privacy violation offence. What is the best advice?
quiz.ok: Charge stalking in the general law instead, since the privacy offence is limited to images of private areas.
no: Charge the privacy offence, since it protects any reasonable expectation of privacy in a person's online life.
Charge identity theft instead, since he contacts her through accounts that are linked to her online identity.
Charge nothing, since stalking needs physical following, and online messages are not following at all.
quiz.why: Section 66E is confined to intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area without consent, so it cannot reach messages that involve no such image. Stalking (IPC s. 354D, now in the BNS) covers a man who repeatedly follows or contacts a woman despite clear disinterest, or monitors her internet, email or electronic communications, which describes Sameer's conduct. The option reading the privacy offence as protecting any online privacy overlooks that it is image based, and identity theft would need one of her credentials to have been used.

quiz.concept: Proving each cyber terrorism limb separately
quiz.q: Prosecutors prove that Tara, intending to strike terror, accessed a ministry server without authorisation and copied restricted files. They cannot show that any harm was caused or likely, or that she had reason to believe the files might be misused. Tara's counsel argues that neither limb of cyber terrorism is made out. Is counsel right?
quiz.ok: Yes: each limb must be proved on its own elements, and here each of them lacks one.
no: No: both limbs share a single punishment clause, so their elements may be combined.
No: terrorist intent and unauthorised access suffice, as harm is presumed once intent is shown.
Yes, but only because cyber terrorism also requires that the server be a declared protected system.
quiz.why: Section 66F creates two separate offences followed by one punishment clause: Limb (A) needs terrorist intent, a listed cyber act and serious harm caused or likely, while Limb (B) needs knowing unauthorised access to restricted information with reason to believe it may be misused. Tara's facts supply part of each, but Limb (A) fails for want of actual or likely harm and Limb (B) for want of reason to believe in misuse. The shared clause in s. 66F(2) fixes the punishment for both offences without merging their elements, which is why a s. 66F problem must be answered limb by limb.

quiz.concept: Exceeding authorised access and likely harm
quiz.q: Kabir, a technician at a metro rail operator, is authorised only to monitor its signalling dashboard. Intending to strike terror in commuters, he uses his own login to send commands that switch off the signals on a busy line, but an alert driver stops her train in time and no one is hurt. His counsel argues that Kabir was an authorised user and that no harm was caused. How should the court treat the argument?
quiz.ok: Reject it: exceeding authorised access is a listed act, and harm that was likely to be caused is enough.
no: Accept it: an authorised user who misuses his own login does not act without authorisation, so no listed act occurs.
Accept it: the terrorism limb is complete only once death, injury or damage has actually been caused.
Reject it, but only because an insider who exceeds his access falls within the restricted-information limb.
quiz.why: Limb (A) of s. 66F(1) needs terrorist intent, one of three cyber acts and harm caused or likely to be caused; the acts include accessing a computer resource 'exceeding authorised access', and 'likely to cause' catches attacks that fail. Kabir's commands go beyond his monitoring role, switching off the signals on a busy line was likely to cause death or injury, and terrorising commuters is intent to strike terror in a section of the people. The authorised-user argument fails because the limb expressly covers exceeding authorised access, and Limb (B) is irrelevant because he obtained no restricted information.

quiz.concept: Denial of access aimed at one community
quiz.q: Aiming to terrorise a religious minority, a group floods the network of a hospital serving that community, so that for two days its doctors cannot open patient records and treatment is delayed. The group never breaks into any system. It argues that it accessed nothing and that its aim was directed at one community, not at India as a whole. Is the terrorism limb of cyber terrorism made out?
quiz.ok: Yes: denying authorised users access is a listed act, and terror aimed at a section of the people is enough.
no: No: without any access or contaminant, flooding a network is only the civil wrong of denying service.
No: the intent must be to threaten the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India as a whole, not of one group.
Yes: any flood that shuts down a hospital's systems is cyber terrorism, whatever the attackers' aim.
quiz.why: Limb (A) of s. 66F(1) lists three alternative acts (denying access to authorised persons, penetrating or accessing without authorisation, and introducing a contaminant), so a flood that locks doctors out of their records is a listed act though nothing was penetrated. The intent may be to threaten the State or 'to strike terror in the people or any section of them', so terrorising one community is enough, and disrupted hospital services are a listed harm; it is that intent, not the choice of target, that makes the attack terrorism, so the 'whatever the aim' option fails. The civil-wrong option is the most tempting, because denial of service is also a s. 43(f) contravention, but that overlap does not stop the same act satisfying s. 66F once terrorist intent and serious harm are present.

quiz.concept: Reason to believe in misuse suffices
quiz.q: Meera, a clerk in a state police records office, knowingly opens restricted files on a pending riot case that she has no authority to view, and passes them to a friend. She has reason to believe he may use them to incite violence, though she says she never wanted that, and nothing has happened yet. Is the restricted-information limb of cyber terrorism made out?
quiz.ok: Yes: knowing unauthorised access plus reason to believe in misuse suffices, with no harm needed.
no: No: the limb requires proof that she wanted or intended the files to be used to incite violence.
No: the limb requires that the files were actually used and that public order was disturbed.
Yes, but only because riot files are State security information, the one kind the limb protects.
quiz.why: Limb (B) of s. 66F(1) punishes knowingly or intentionally accessing a computer resource without or beyond authorisation and thereby obtaining restricted information, 'with reason to believe' it may be used for listed ends, which include public order and incitement to an offence. It needs no terrorist intent and states no harm element, so Meera's knowledge that she lacked authority and her reason to believe in misuse suffice, whatever she wanted and although nothing has happened. The State-security option reaches the right answer for the wrong reason: the limb also covers 'any restricted information', the very breadth that critics attack.

quiz.concept: Conspiracy under the restricted-information limb
quiz.q: Two staff at a state electricity regulator agree to copy restricted files on the grid's security, which they have no authority to open, and to sell them to a foreign group. Neither wants to strike terror in anyone, and both are arrested before either has logged in. Can they be punished under the cyber terrorism provision?
quiz.ok: Yes: the restricted-information limb needs no terrorist intent, and conspiring to commit it is punishable.
no: No: conspiring to commit cyber terrorism is punishable only where the plan is driven by terrorist intent.
No: the restricted-information limb is committed only once restricted information is actually obtained.
Yes, but only because the grid is critical infrastructure, and any plan against it is cyber terrorism.
quiz.why: Limb (B) of s. 66F(1) punishes knowing unauthorised access that obtains restricted information, with reason to believe it may be misused, for example to benefit a foreign group, and needs no terrorist intent. Section 66F(2) punishes whoever 'commits or conspires to commit' cyber terrorism, a clause that covers both limbs, so their agreement is punishable with up to life although neither has logged in. The 'actually obtained' option states what the completed offence needs but forgets conspiracy, a listed mistake; the terrorist-intent option carries Limb (A)'s mental element into Limb (B), and the critical-infrastructure option treats every plan against a vital system as terrorism.

quiz.concept: Critical infrastructure versus declared protected system
quiz.q: A hacker acting purely for money breaks into the control system of a regional power grid. The prosecutor charges unauthorised access to a protected system, relying only on expert evidence that the grid is critical information infrastructure because its failure would cripple the regional economy. What is the flaw in the charge?
quiz.ok: Being critical infrastructure is not enough: the Government must have declared the system a protected one.
no: There is none: a system proved to be critical infrastructure is a protected system by operation of law.
The charge needs terrorist intent, and a hacker acting purely for money does not have it.
The charge lies only for systems that the Government itself owns and runs, which is not shown here.
quiz.why: Under s. 70 the appropriate Government may declare a computer resource affecting critical information infrastructure to be a protected system, and the s. 70 charge lies only if the system has been so declared. Critical information infrastructure describes a resource whose incapacitation would debilitate national security, the economy, public health or safety; proving that the grid fits that description does not make it protected without a declaration, so the expert evidence cannot carry the charge. The 'operation of law' option merges the two ideas, and the terrorist-intent option confuses s. 70 with s. 66F: the notes list s. 70 among the fallbacks for attacks without terrorist intent.

quiz.concept: Weight of a reported trial court conviction
quiz.q: In a moot problem, an engineer used his employer's computer to research a planned attack on a school. Counsel for the prosecution says that the Anees Ansari conviction decides the point, so the court need not examine the elements of cyber terrorism. What is the strongest objection to that use of the case?
quiz.ok: It is a press-reported trial court conviction with no appellate ruling behind it, so it can only illustrate.
no: It was a conviction under the general criminal law alone, so it says nothing about the cyber terrorism offence.
Researching an attack on a computer can never be a listed cyber act, so the conviction was wrong in law.
It was reported only in the press, so it cannot be cited at all, not even to illustrate the offence.
quiz.why: The notes use Anees Ansari, sentenced to life under s. 66F by a Mumbai sessions court (reported in 2022), to show that research and planning on a computer can amount to cyber terrorism, but they treat it with care: it is a press-reported trial court conviction, and no reported appellate judgment on s. 66F was located. A problem must therefore be answered from the text of the section, element by element, with the case used only as an illustration. The option that bars the case altogether overcorrects, since the notes still use it as an illustration, and the 'general criminal law' option is wrong because the life sentence was imposed under s. 66F itself.

quiz.concept: Why the choice of terrorism statute matters
quiz.q: Asha and Bimal are arrested for the same cyber attack. Asha is charged only with cyber terrorism under the IT Act; Bimal is charged with that offence and also under the UAPA. Bimal's lawyer says the extra charge changes nothing before trial, because both already face a non-bailable offence that can carry life. What is the flaw in that view?
quiz.ok: The UAPA adds special sanction rules, extended detention and stricter bail, none of which the IT Act carries.
no: There is none: two charges carrying the same maximum sentence must be treated alike at every stage before trial.
Cyber terrorism under the IT Act can be compounded, so only Asha's case could end in a settlement.
It is Asha's IT Act charge, not Bimal's UAPA charge, that needs a special sanction before it can proceed.
quiz.why: Section 66F is cognizable, non-bailable and never compoundable because it can carry life, but the notes add that choosing the UAPA brings special sanction requirements, extended detention and stricter bail conditions that the IT Act does not carry. The same facts can therefore lead to very different pre-trial treatment depending on the statute charged, so Bimal's position is worse than Asha's even though the maximum sentence is the same. The 'treated alike' option assumes that pre-trial procedure follows the maximum sentence alone, and the sanction option reverses the two regimes.

quiz.concept: Status of the restricted-information limb
quiz.q: A journalist exceeded her authorised access to a government portal and copied restricted documents that she had reason to believe might be used to defame a minister. Charged under the restricted-information limb of cyber terrorism, she argues that the limb is no longer good law. How should her argument be assessed?
quiz.ok: It fails: the limb invites a Shreya Singhal style overbreadth challenge, but it has not been struck down.
no: It succeeds: Shreya Singhal struck down the limb's decency and defamation grounds as vague and overbroad.
It succeeds: the limb was formally omitted from the Act in 2023, following the ruling in Shreya Singhal.
It fails: the limb is beyond any overbreadth challenge, because it requires a specific terrorist intent.
quiz.why: Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down s. 66A for vagueness and overbreadth, and it is s. 66A that was formally omitted from 30 November 2023; Limb (B) of s. 66F(1) was not part of that decision. Limb (B) attaches a possible life sentence to access to 'any restricted information' usable in relation to grounds such as decency and defamation, with no terrorist intent, so read literally it could catch this journalist and it invites a similar critique, but no challenge to it was located. The omission option transfers s. 66A's fate to Limb (B), and the terrorist-intent option describes Limb (A).

quiz.concept: Terrorist intent separates terrorism from extortion
quiz.q: A ransomware group abroad encrypts a city water utility's systems and demands payment, and the water supply fails for two days. The prosecution can prove the intrusion, the ransom demand and the outage, but nothing more. Which additional fact would complete a case of cyber terrorism against the group?
quiz.ok: A declaration by the group that it wants to show that the State cannot protect its people.
no: Evidence that the outage spread across the whole city and continued for two full weeks.
A finding that the utility's systems had earlier been declared a protected system.
Proof that the group's members agreed on and planned the attack together several weeks in advance.
quiz.why: Limb (A) of s. 66F(1) needs terrorist intent as well as a listed act and serious harm. Here the act (ransomware, a contaminant introduced through unauthorised access) and the harm (a failed water supply, an essential service) are already proved, so intent is the missing element, and a declared aim of showing that the State cannot protect its people is intent to strike terror. A longer outage adds harm but not intent, which is why treating every large attack as terrorism is a listed mistake; protected status and an agreement to attack for money do not supply intent either, and without intent the fallback is ss. 43 and 66 (with s. 70 if the systems are protected) and BNS extortion.

quiz.concept: Four categories and the law's response
quiz.q: A website owner publishes online a literary novel exploring a sexual relationship, written mainly as serious literature; a commercially produced video of sexual acts made solely for arousal; and a violent sexual clip that would deprave and corrupt its likely viewers. His lawyer argues that all three stand or fall together, since each is simply sexual content. Is that right?
quiz.ok: No: the novel can be protected by the public good exception, while the video and the clip are punished.
no: Yes: all sexual content published electronically is punished unless the prosecution disproves a public good.
No: only the violent clip is punishable, since material made for arousal is lawful unless it is also obscene.
No: the novel and the video are both erotica, so only the violent clip can be punished under the Act.
quiz.why: The notes sort sexual content into four categories with a rising response: erotica, art or literature not mainly for arousal, is protected by the public good exception; pornography, made solely for arousal, is punished as sexually explicit material when published electronically; and obscene and extreme content is punished. The novel is erotica and can be protected if its publisher proves the exception, while the video and the depraving clip are punished. The 'lawful unless obscene' option misses that sexually explicit material is punished when published electronically without any need to show a tendency to deprave.

quiz.concept: Vulnerable reader versus the Miller test
quiz.q: A novel contains explicit passages that could corrupt an impressionable teenager into whose hands it might fall. Yet an average adult applying contemporary community standards would see the work, taken as a whole, as serious political satire. How would the novel fare under the Hicklin test and under the Miller test?
quiz.ok: Obscene under Hicklin's vulnerable-reader test, but not under Miller's whole-work, average-person test.
no: Obscene under both, since each test asks whether the explicit passages could corrupt some reader.
Obscene under neither, since both tests judge the work by the standard of the average reasonable adult.
Obscene under Miller only, since Miller asks whether the passages appeal to the prurient interest.
quiz.why: Hicklin asked whether the matter tends to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to immoral influences and into whose hands it may fall, so the impressionable teenager decides the case against the novel. Miller judges by the average person applying contemporary community standards to the work as a whole, so a work that such a person sees as serious political satire is not obscene, all the more because Miller also requires the work to lack serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value. The 'neither' option gives Hicklin the average-reader yardstick that the UK Obscene Publications Act 1959 later substituted for it.

quiz.concept: Superseded test cannot settle obscenity today
quiz.q: In 2025 a publisher uploads an e-book of Lady Chatterley's Lover and is charged with electronic obscenity. The prosecution argues that Ranjit Udeshi, which upheld the obscenity offence in a prosecution over this very novel, settles the matter without any fresh inquiry. What is the main flaw in that argument?
quiz.ok: That case applied a modified Hicklin test, since replaced by community standards, so the novel must be judged afresh.
no: That case struck down the general obscenity offence itself, so it cannot support any obscenity charge today.
That case concerned a printed book under the general offence, so it cannot govern the electronic offence.
That case held that literary merit always protects a serious novel, so properly read it actually helps the publisher here.
quiz.why: Ranjit Udeshi upheld IPC s. 292 under Article 19(2) in a prosecution for selling Lady Chatterley's Lover, but it applied a modified Hicklin test under which obscenity without a preponderating social purpose was unprotected. Aveek Sarkar (2014) replaced Hicklin with the community standards test, applied to the work as a whole and in context, so a 2025 prosecution must assess the e-book afresh rather than borrow a result reached under the old test. The printed-book option fails because s. 67 mirrors s. 292(1), so obscenity case law does govern electronic material; what has changed is the test, not its relevance.

quiz.concept: Context decides the community standards test
quiz.q: In Aveek Sarkar, a nude photograph of a tennis player and his fiancée, published to oppose racism, was held not obscene. Which change in the facts would most weaken that conclusion under the test the Court applied?
quiz.ok: The same photograph appearing, with no message at all, on a website designed to arouse its viewers.
no: The same photograph appearing online rather than in print, so that the IT Act offence applied instead.
Evidence that an impressionable teenager who saw the photograph could have been corrupted by it.
Evidence that the article printed beside the photograph used crude and vulgar language about racists.
quiz.why: Aveek Sarkar replaced Hicklin with the community standards test which, as Apoorva Arora (2024) confirms, judges the work as a whole and in context and asks whether it arouses sexual and lustful thoughts, just as Bobby Art had judged the scenes of Bandit Queen in the context of the film's message. The anti-racism message was the context that saved the photograph, so removing it and placing the image on a site designed to arouse goes to the heart of the test. The online option is the most tempting, but s. 67 mirrors s. 292(1), so the same obscenity case law applies; the teenager option revives Hicklin, and vulgar language is not obscenity (Apoorva Arora).

quiz.concept: Profanity and vulgarity are not obscenity
quiz.q: A web series is full of profane, expletive-laden dialogue but shows no sexual act. A High Court upholds an FIR for electronic obscenity and for publishing sexually explicit material, reasoning that the language would corrupt young viewers. What should happen on appeal to the Supreme Court?
quiz.ok: Both charges should be quashed: profanity is not obscenity, and no sexually explicit act is shown.
no: Only the explicit-material charge should be quashed, since language this vulgar is still obscene.
Both charges should stand, since obscenity is judged by its effect on the young viewers most at risk.
Both charges should be quashed, since streamed fiction lies outside the IT Act's content offences altogether.
quiz.why: In Apoorva Arora (2024 INSC 223) the Supreme Court quashed an FIR under ss. 67 and 67A over the College Romance web series: vulgarity and profanity are not by themselves obscene, obscenity concerns material that arouses sexual and lustful thoughts, judged by the Aveek Sarkar community standards test on the work as a whole and in context, and s. 67A needs a sexually explicit act. Profane dialogue without any sexual act therefore fails both offences. The option keeping the obscenity charge is the most tempting, but however vulgar the dialogue, coarse language is not by itself obscene.

quiz.concept: Alternative grounds of electronic obscenity
quiz.q: A subscription website for adults posts images that are plainly lascivious. Charged with electronic obscenity, the site's owner proves that its adult subscribers would not be depraved or corrupted by them, and argues that the charge must therefore fail. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No: the grounds are alternatives, so lascivious material can be obscene even if it would deprave no one.
no: Yes: material is obscene only where it tends to deprave and corrupt the persons likely to see it.
Yes: material shown only to adults who chose to see it falls outside the obscenity offence altogether.
No: the court must instead ask whether the images could corrupt a child into whose hands they might fall.
quiz.why: Section 67 mirrors IPC s. 292(1), which deems material obscene on three alternative grounds: it is lascivious, it appeals to the prurient interest, or, taken as a whole, it tends to deprave and corrupt its likely audience, each judged by community standards. Proof that adult subscribers would not be depraved answers only the deprave-and-corrupt ground, so plainly lascivious images can still be obscene. The 'deprave and corrupt only' option merges the three grounds into one, the adults-only option invents an exemption that the Act does not contain, and the option about a child into whose hands the images might fall revives the Hicklin test that Aveek Sarkar replaced.

quiz.concept: Both ingredients of electronic obscenity required
quiz.q: A man was charged with electronic obscenity merely for 'liking' another user's provocative post, which was followed by an unauthorised procession of several hundred people. Suppose instead that he had written and posted the provocative message himself. Would the charge then succeed?
quiz.ok: No: the message was provocative, not lascivious or prurient, so the content ingredient would still fail.
no: Yes: posting it himself would be publication, the only ingredient that was missing from the original charge.
Yes: a message that provokes an unlawful gathering thereby tends to deprave and corrupt those who read it.
No: the offence requires a sexually explicit act, and a provocative message depicts no such act.
quiz.why: Imran Khan v State of UP (Allahabad HC, 2025) quashed a s. 67 charge on two separate grounds: liking is neither publishing nor transmitting, and s. 67 punishes lascivious or prurient material, not merely provocative content. Writing and posting the message himself would plainly be publication, but that cures only the publication defect, because the content was never obscene. The 'only ingredient missing' option forgets that the case failed on both ingredients, and the 'sexually explicit act' option borrows the test for s. 67A, which s. 67 does not need.

quiz.concept: What triggers the explicit-material offence
quiz.q: Dev posts online a series of lascivious photographs that show no sexual act, and is charged with electronic obscenity. The prosecution would prefer the heavier offence for sexually explicit material. Which change in the facts would make that offence available?
quiz.ok: Proof that the photographs depict a sexually explicit act, whether or not they would deprave anyone.
no: Proof that the photographs would deprave and corrupt the young viewers most likely to see them.
Proof that Dev already has a previous conviction for posting obscene material in electronic form.
Proof that the photographs were shared widely and earned Dev substantial advertising income.
quiz.why: Section 67A punishes publishing or transmitting electronic material containing a sexually explicit act or conduct, more heavily than s. 67, and no tendency to deprave need be shown: once such an act is depicted, the obscenity tests are unnecessary. Only a change in the content itself, to an explicit act, moves Dev from s. 67 to s. 67A. A previous conviction is the tempting option, but it only raises the s. 67 punishment on a subsequent conviction (to five years and ten lakh rupees); it does not turn lascivious photographs into sexually explicit material.

quiz.concept: Public good exception covers explicit material
quiz.q: A medical university posts online a teaching video showing a sexual act for its human sexuality course, and is charged with publishing sexually explicit material. The prosecution says the public good exception is irrelevant because it shelters only material charged under the electronic obscenity offence. How should the court approach the university's defence?
quiz.ok: The exception extends to explicit material, but the university must prove the video serves the public good.
no: The exception is unavailable, because it shelters only material charged under the obscenity offence.
The exception is available, and once it is raised the prosecution must disprove it beyond doubt.
The exception is not needed, as the prosecution must first prove the video obscene by contemporary community standards.
quiz.why: The exception for material proved to be justified as being for the public good, in the interest of science, learning or other objects of general concern, is attached to s. 67A and applies to both ss. 67 and 67A, with an identical proviso to s. 67B. The person relying on it bears the burden of proving it, so the university must show the video's educational justification. The community-standards option is wrong because s. 67A needs only a sexually explicit act: once one is depicted, no tendency to deprave need be shown.

quiz.concept: Downloading, grooming and the adult-child divide
quiz.q: Arun downloads commercially produced explicit videos of adults and keeps them. Bilal downloads explicit images of a sixteen-year-old and keeps them. Chetan spends weeks online steering a fifteen-year-old towards a relationship aimed at sexually explicit acts, though no image yet exists. None of them shares anything. Who has committed an offence under the IT Act's content provisions?
quiz.ok: Bilal and Chetan: the child offence covers downloading and grooming, while the adult offences need publication or transmission.
no: Only Bilal: downloading counts under the child offence, but grooming is no offence until some explicit image of the child exists.
Only Chetan: grooming counts under the child offence, but downloading without any sharing is no offence at all.
All three: downloading explicit material and grooming a child are each offences, whoever the material depicts.
quiz.why: Sections 67 and 67A punish publishing or transmitting material in electronic form, so Arun, who only downloads and keeps adult content, commits neither. Section 67B goes further for children, meaning anyone under eighteen: clause (b) covers seeking, browsing and downloading such material, so Bilal is caught without any publication (Just Rights for Children Alliance, 2024), and clause (c) covers cultivating or enticing a child into an online relationship for sexually explicit acts, which criminalises grooming before any image exists. The 'only Bilal' option misses clause (c), while the 'only Chetan' option repeats the Madras High Court's error, reversed by the Supreme Court, of treating downloading without publication as no offence.

quiz.concept: Storing material in order to report it
quiz.q: While handling a complaint, a school counsellor finds child sexual exploitative and abuse material on a pupil's phone and copies it to her laptop. Which further fact would most clearly take her outside the POCSO offence of storing or possessing such material?
quiz.ok: She handed the material to the police that day and then deleted her own copy from the laptop.
no: She never opened or viewed the files again after copying them across onto her own laptop.
She kept the laptop locked away in her office and protected by a strong password at all times.
She had no intention of selling the material, sharing it for money or profiting from it in any way.
quiz.why: POCSO s. 15, as substituted in 2019, punishes three forms of storage or possession: failing to delete, destroy or report the material with intent to share it; storing it for transmitting, displaying or distributing, except for reporting or court evidence; and storing it for commercial purposes. Handing it to the police at once and deleting her copy answers all three: she reported and deleted it, and her only transmission was for reporting. Secure storage or not viewing the files does not help, since after Just Rights for Children Alliance storage without deletion or reporting can itself indicate the required intention, and the absence of profit removes only the commercial form.

quiz.concept: Inferring intent from keeping the material
quiz.q: A man downloaded CSEAM months ago and it is still on his phone; he has done nothing with it since. Charged with the POCSO offence of storing such material, he argues that nothing shows any intention to share it. How should the court treat his argument?
quiz.ok: Reject it: keeping the material without deleting or reporting it can itself indicate the required intention.
no: Accept it: an intention to share can be shown only by some act beyond storage, such as an offer.
Reject it: his intention is irrelevant, because possessing such material is an absolute offence in itself.
Accept it: an intention can be inferred from storage alone only where it serves a commercial purpose.
quiz.why: In Just Rights for Children Alliance v S. Harish (2024 INSC 716) the Supreme Court set aside the Madras High Court's quashing order, holding that storage or possession without deletion or reporting can itself indicate the intention required by POCSO s. 15; s. 67B(b) separately covers his downloading. Months of keeping the material with no deletion or report therefore support the inference his argument denies. The 'absolute offence' option overstates the holding: intention is still required, and the point is only that it may be inferred from keeping the material.

quiz.concept: Electronic form triggers the special scheme
quiz.q: A shopkeeper sells printed copies of obscene photographs over the counter and also emails the same photographs to customers who order online. How do the IT Act's obscenity offence and the general obscenity offence apply to him?
quiz.ok: The IT Act offence covers the emails and the general offence the prints, since only the emails are electronic.
no: The IT Act offence covers both, as the special scheme excludes the general offence for the very same photographs.
The general offence covers both, as the photographs existed in print before they were ever emailed.
Both offences cover both, as the general offence may always be charged alongside the IT Act offence.
quiz.why: Section 67 asks whether the accused published or transmitted the material in electronic form, so emailing obscene photographs engages it, and under Sharat Babu Digumarti (2017) the general offence cannot be added for that same electronic conduct. Selling printed copies is not in electronic form, so s. 67 does not reach it and the general obscenity offence (formerly IPC s. 292, now its BNS equivalent) governs the prints. The option that puts both kinds of sale under the IT Act overextends Sharat Babu, which displaces the general law only where the offence concerns obscene material in electronic form.

quiz.concept: Special scheme survives the new codes
quiz.q: In 2025 the police charge an uploader with electronic obscenity and, for the same video, with the general obscenity offence now found in the BNS. They argue that Sharat Babu concerned only the repealed IPC, and that the Bombay Full Bench's ingredient test lets both charges run. How should the court respond?
quiz.ok: The general charge fails: Sharat Babu now operates against the BNS, and that offence adds no ingredient.
no: Both charges can stand: the IPC's repeal ended the Sharat Babu rule, so the new general offence now applies as well.
Both charges can stand: the Full Bench test always lets the general offence run alongside the IT Act.
The general charge cannot stand, because the IT Act's offences were absorbed into the BNS in 2024.
quiz.why: Sharat Babu Digumarti (2017) held that where obscene material is in electronic form, s. 67 read with ss. 79 and 81 is a special scheme excluding the general obscenity offence for the same conduct. The IPC's repeal does not end that reasoning, because the comparison is now made against the BNS, and the Bombay Full Bench lets the general offence run alongside the IT Act only where it adds an ingredient; the obscenity offence adds none, since s. 67 mirrors it. The 'absorbed into the BNS' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason: IT Act offences are unchanged by the new codes.

quiz.concept: Cognizable does not mean non-bailable
quiz.q: Sana is arrested and charged with electronic obscenity for posting lascivious images online, her first such offence. The officer points out that the offence is cognizable, but her lawyer argues that she is nonetheless entitled to bail as of right. Is the lawyer right?
quiz.ok: Yes: a first electronic obscenity offence is cognizable, but as a three-year offence it is also bailable.
no: No: under the IT Act every cognizable offence is also non-bailable, whatever its punishment.
Yes, but only because a first electronic obscenity offence is not cognizable under the IT Act at all.
No, if the images depict a woman, since offences against women are excluded from bail as of right under the Act.
quiz.why: Section 77B draws two different lines: offences punishable with three years and above are cognizable, and those punishable with three years are bailable. A first s. 67 offence carries up to three years, so it is both cognizable and bailable; only a repeat s. 67 offence, at five years, becomes non-bailable. The 'offences against women' option transplants the s. 77A bar on compounding into bail, where it has no place, and calling a first s. 67 offence non-bailable is a listed mistake.

quiz.concept: Socio-economic bar on compounding
quiz.q: Rohan, a first offender, dishonestly manipulates a state ration-distribution database, an offence punishable with up to three years, and cuts off subsidised grain to thousands of poor families across the district for three months. The families have since been repaid and want to settle. Can the court compound the offence?
quiz.ok: No: it is within the three-year limit, but an offence affecting socio-economic conditions is barred.
no: Yes: the bar for socio-economic offences applies only to repeat offenders, and Rohan is a first offender.
Yes: beyond the punishment limit, the only bar on compounding is for offences against women or children.
No: the offence is cognizable, and under the IT Act a cognizable offence can never be compounded.
quiz.why: Section 77A lets courts compound offences other than those punishable with life or more than three years, but not where a previous conviction attracts enhanced punishment, or where the offence affects socio-economic conditions or is committed against a woman or a child under eighteen. Rohan's s. 66 offence is within the three-year limit, but cutting off subsidised grain to thousands of poor families for months plainly affects socio-economic conditions, which is a bar of its own. The 'repeat offenders' option merges two separate exceptions: the previous-conviction bar and the socio-economic bar apply independently, so being a first offender does not help him.

quiz.concept: Extraterritorial reach covers civil contraventions
quiz.q: A foreign national working in Singapore, with no presence in India, copies a Pune company's client database from its server in India without permission. Dishonesty cannot be proved, so the company looks only to the civil track for compensation. Does the IT Act reach his conduct?
quiz.ok: Yes: its reach abroad covers civil contraventions as well, by any person, if an Indian computer is involved.
no: No: its reach abroad extends only to criminal offences, and never to civil contraventions such as this.
No: its reach abroad extends only to Indian citizens who commit offences or contraventions outside India.
Not yet: its reach abroad arises only once he is extradited and brought before an Indian court.
quiz.why: Section 75 applies the Act to offences and contraventions committed outside India by any person, if they involve a computer, computer system or network in India. Copying data from a server in India without permission is a s. 43(b) contravention involving an Indian computer, so the Act reaches the Singapore-based foreigner even though no offence is proved. The extradition option confuses reach with enforcement: extradition and international cooperation matter to actually trying a foreign offender, not to whether the Act applies.

quiz.concept: Persons in charge versus other directors
quiz.q: A company commits an IT Act offence, and an independent director who only attends board meetings, with no role in running the business, is charged with it. There is no evidence that he consented to, connived at or neglected anything. He argues that he cannot be convicted on this evidence without having to prove anything himself. Is he right?
quiz.ok: Yes: the deeming covers those in charge of the business; he is liable only if consent, connivance or neglect is proved.
no: No: every director of an offending company is deemed guilty unless he proves lack of knowledge or due diligence.
No: once the company is shown to have committed the offence, every one of its directors shares that liability equally.
Yes, but only because directors are never personally liable for offences committed by their company.
quiz.why: Section 85 creates two routes: persons in charge of and responsible to the company for its business are deemed guilty of its offences unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence, while other directors or officers are liable only where their consent, connivance or neglect is proved. An independent director with no role in running the business falls under the consent, connivance or neglect route, and nothing is proved against him. The 'every director' option extends the deeming, and its reverse burden, beyond the persons in charge to whom s. 85 confines it.

quiz.concept: Active curation forfeits intermediary protection
quiz.q: A video site does not simply host uploads: its staff choose which subscribers receive each clip and edit clips into themed compilations. An obscene clip uploaded by a user ends up in one compilation. A complainant argues that the site cannot rely on the intermediary shield, even though the clip was a third party's. Is the complainant right?
quiz.ok: Yes: the shield covers only intermediaries that do not select receivers or modify content, and it does both.
no: No: the clip was a user's third-party content, and the site itself neither created nor uploaded it.
No, not until it fails to act on a court order or a government notification identifying the clip.
Yes, but only if the site itself initiated the transmission when the user first uploaded the clip.
quiz.why: Section 79 protects an intermediary for third-party content only if it observes due diligence, does not initiate the transmission, select its receivers or modify it, and acts on actual knowledge. By choosing recipients and editing clips into compilations the site selects receivers and modifies content, so it falls outside the shield whatever notice it has received. The court-order option is tempting because Shreya Singhal read 'actual knowledge' as a court order or government notification, but that is a separate condition and cannot rescue a site that fails the others.

quiz.concept: New codes and the ingredient comparison
quiz.q: A charge sheet filed in 2025, for conduct earlier that year, in a court bound by the Bombay High Court, accuses Nikhil of dishonestly altering his employer's payment records, an IT Act offence, and of thereby deceiving the employer into paying him, framed as cheating under the IPC. How should the court deal with the two charges?
quiz.ok: Keep the IT Act charge, recast the cheating charge under the BNS, and let both run, since cheating adds deception.
no: Recast both charges under the BNS, since the new codes absorbed the IT Act's offences when the IPC was repealed.
Keep only the IT Act charge, since a general cheating charge can never be added where the IT Act covers the conduct.
Keep both charges exactly as framed, since the BNS merely renumbered the IPC and an old citation still serves.
quiz.why: Since 1 July 2024 the BNS has replaced the IPC, so the cheating charge must be recast under its BNS equivalent (the notes flag the BNS numbers as unverified), while IT Act offences are unchanged, so the s. 66 charge stands as framed. Whether the general charge can run alongside is decided by comparing ingredients, a comparison now made against the BNS, and in the Bombay High Court the Full Bench lets the general offence survive where it adds an ingredient, deception in cheating being its own example. The 'can never be added' option reflects the earlier Gagan Harsh Sharma approach rather than the Full Bench's ingredient test, which now governs in that court.

quiz.concept: Certificate requirement under the new evidence law
quiz.q: At a 2025 trial, the prosecution produces copies of chat logs taken from the accused's phone, offered as secondary electronic evidence, without any certificate. It argues that the certificate requirement died with the old Evidence Act, and that matching hash values prove the copies unaltered anyway. How should the court treat these arguments?
quiz.ok: Reject both: the new evidence law keeps the certificate, and hash values cannot stand in for it.
no: Accept both: the certificate rule lapsed in 2024, and matching hash values make the copies admissible.
Reject the repeal argument but accept the hash one, since proof of integrity does the certificate's job.
Accept the repeal argument, but let the defence argue at the end of the trial that the copies deserve little weight.
quiz.why: Since 1 July 2024 the BSA has replaced the Evidence Act, and BSA s. 63 (formerly Evidence Act s. 65B) still requires a certificate for secondary electronic evidence. Hash values show that a copy has not been altered, which goes to integrity, but admissibility, authenticity and weight remain distinct questions, so integrity evidence does not dispense with the certificate. The option that lets hash values do the certificate's job merges those questions: proving that the copies are unaltered is not the same as meeting the condition for admitting them.

quiz.concept: Bail and compounding across two charges
quiz.q: Ravi posts to a group chat a video of himself and his former partner, a woman, in a sexual act, which she never agreed to share. He is charged with the image-based privacy offence and with publishing sexually explicit material. His counsel claims bail as of right because the privacy offence is bailable, and asks to compound both charges because she has agreed to settle. How should the court respond?
quiz.ok: Neither request succeeds: the explicit-material charge is non-bailable, and neither charge can be compounded.
no: Both requests succeed: the privacy charge is bailable, and her agreement to settle lets both charges be compounded.
Only compounding succeeds, and only for the privacy charge, because that offence carries three years.
Only bail succeeds, since both charges carry three years, but her being a woman bars compounding.
quiz.why: Section 67A carries up to five years, so under s. 77B it is non-bailable, and Ravi cannot claim bail as of right merely because the accompanying s. 66E charge is bailable. Neither charge can be compounded under s. 77A: s. 67A exceeds three years, and s. 66E, though a three-year offence, is committed here against a woman. The option compounding the privacy charge ignores that bar, which is why compounding s. 66E committed against a woman is a listed mistake.

quiz.concept: Targeting reach: location, not nationality
quiz.q: HealthPal, a Pune symptom checker app with no office or staff in the EU, offers a German version priced in euros. Its users include Germans in Germany, Indian students living in Germany and Indians in India. HealthPal says the GDPR cannot reach it because all its processing happens in Pune, and that if the GDPR does apply, it protects only German nationals. Which response is correct?
quiz.ok: The GDPR applies through targeting and protects everyone using the app in Germany, the Indian students included.
no: The GDPR applies through targeting but protects only the German nationals, not the Indian students, as it follows citizenship.
The GDPR cannot apply, because a controller without an EU establishment is bound only where it processes data there.
The GDPR applies through targeting and then protects every HealthPal user, including the users who are in India.
quiz.why: A controller with no EU establishment is caught by Article 3(2)(a) when it offers goods or services to people in the Union, and the euro-priced German version shows that HealthPal targets people in Germany; where it processes the data does not matter. Article 3(2) protects data subjects who are in the Union, so location, not nationality, decides: the Indian students in Germany are covered, but users in India are not, and their protection comes from the DPDP Act (s. 3(a), from 13 May 2027). The citizenship option is the error the notes warn against, as the example of the Taiwanese bank serving German citizens in Taiwan shows.

quiz.concept: Tied consent: GDPR factor, DPDP definition
quiz.q: In 2028, HealthPal's counsel concedes that tying its free plan to consent to personalised advertising fails the GDPR's rule on conditional services for German users. He argues that the design is still safe for Indian users, because the DPDP Act has no clause on making a service conditional on consent. What is the flaw in his argument?
quiz.ok: It overlooks that the DPDP Act makes consent itself unconditional and limited to the data that are necessary.
no: It overlooks that the DPDP Act adopts the GDPR rule by reference, so the same utmost account test applies.
It overlooks that the DPDP Act lets such a condition stand only after a stand alone notice has described it.
It overlooks that the DPDP Act makes advertising rest on a legitimate interest, which HealthPal cannot show.
quiz.why: The GDPR deals with bundling through Article 7(4) and Recital 43: utmost account is taken of whether a service depends on consent to processing it does not need, and such consent is presumed not to be free. The DPDP Act needs no separate clause because it states the rule more strongly, inside the definition of consent: consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, and limited to necessary data (s. 6(1)), so tying the free plan to advertising consent fails for Indian users too. A notice under s. 5 is required as well but cannot cure a conditional consent, and the Act has no legitimate interests ground at all.

quiz.concept: Contract basis fails twice for health ads
quiz.q: Told that its tied consent fails, HealthPal plans to keep showing German users ads personalised on their symptom data by treating the ads as necessary for its free contract. Its counsel says the point is still open, citing a class slide that shows the Meta complaints under investigation. Which response is best?
quiz.ok: The slide is outdated: the Meta decisions reject that necessity, and contract cannot lift the health data ban.
no: The plan works, because once processing is necessary for a contract the rules on health data cease to apply.
The plan works until the Meta complaints are decided, because the class slide shows the point is still open.
The plan fails, but only because the GDPR forbids every commercial use of health data, whatever the ground.
quiz.why: Class slide 46 is out of date: the Irish DPC's decisions of January 2023 rejected reliance on contractual necessity for behavioural advertising (Appendix F, item 8), so Article 6(1)(b) cannot carry the ads. Even if it could, symptom data are health data, which need an Article 9(2) exception as well as an Article 6 basis; contract is not among the exceptions, so HealthPal needs explicit consent (Article 9(2)(a)). The 'every commercial use' option over-generalises, since explicit consent can lift the prohibition.

quiz.concept: Joint control: functional and stage specific
quiz.q: To earn advertising revenue, HealthPal embeds an advertising network's pixel, which sends German users' in-app activity straight to the network as each screen loads; the network then combines it with other data to build profiles. The network's contract calls HealthPal a mere processor, and HealthPal never sees what the pixel sends. Which statement of HealthPal's position is correct?
quiz.ok: A joint controller despite the contract, but only for collection and transmission, not the network's profiling.
no: A mere processor, as the contract says, so the network alone answers for every stage of the processing.
A joint controller for every stage, profiling included, since embedding the pixel was its own commercial choice.
Not a controller at all, since only the network receives the data and HealthPal never has any access to it.
quiz.why: Controllership is functional, so a contract cannot turn a party that in fact decides purposes and means into a mere processor (Article 4(7)). By embedding the pixel for its own commercial benefit, HealthPal decisively influences the collection and transmission of users' data, so on Fashion ID it is a joint controller for those stages, but not for the network's later profiling, over which it has no influence. Joint control does not require access to the data (Jehovah's Witnesses), and making HealthPal answer for the profiling is a mistake the notes warn against.

quiz.concept: Thirteen is a floor, not the rule
quiz.q: In 2028, HealthPal still lets users aged 13 and above register on their own consent. Its counsel argues that this satisfies both laws, because the GDPR allows a Member State to set the age for a child's own consent as low as 13, and the DPDP Act follows the GDPR on children. What is the flaw in this argument?
quiz.ok: Thirteen is only the lowest age a State may choose, and the DPDP Act needs a parent's verifiable consent below 18.
no: There is none, because thirteen is the age from which both laws let users consent to processing on their own.
Only the GDPR point fails, because Germany may raise its age above sixteen, but the DPDP Act follows the GDPR.
Only the DPDP point fails, because thirteen is the age the GDPR itself sets, though a Member State may raise it.
quiz.why: Article 8 sets 16 as the age for a child's own consent to information society services and lets Member States lower it, but not below 13; 13 is a floor a State may choose, not a rule, so German users below the age Germany has actually set still need a parent's consent. The DPDP Act does not follow the GDPR here: every user under 18 is a child whose processing needs verifiable parental consent and who cannot be tracked or targeted (s. 9). Both 'raise its age' options invert the rule, since Member States may only lower the age.

quiz.concept: Breach notice: risk filter versus every user
quiz.q: In 2028, HealthPal is hacked and the symptom data of its German and Indian users are exposed. Its assessment, which is sound, is that the breach poses a real but not a high risk to users. Whom must it tell about the German users under the GDPR, and about the Indian users under the DPDP Act?
quiz.ok: The supervisory authority, but not the German users; the Board and every affected Indian user.
no: The authority and every German user, and the Board and every Indian user, as health data always carry high risk.
The authority and the Board alone, because users need to be told only where the risk to them is high.
The authority and every German user; the Board alone for the Indian users, unless the risk to them is high.
quiz.why: Under the GDPR the supervisory authority must be notified, where feasible within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk (Article 33), but data subjects must be told only where the risk to them is high (Article 34); a real but not high risk triggers the first duty and not the second. From 13 May 2027 the DPDP Act has no risk filter: every breach is intimated to the Board and to each affected Data Principal, followed by a detailed report within 72 hours (s. 8(6), Rule 7). The 'Board alone' options wrongly import the GDPR's high-risk threshold into the DPDP Act.

quiz.concept: Three regimes before the DPDP duties start
quiz.q: HealthPal is hacked in December 2026, a month after the DPDP Act's second commencement stage, and the symptom data of its German and Indian users leak. Its security was negligent, and some Indian users suffer wrongful loss. Which statement best maps its exposure at that date?
quiz.ok: GDPR duties and fines for German users, and compensation claims by Indian users under the IT Act's sensitive data remedy.
no: GDPR duties for German users, and DPDP breach duties for Indian users, because the second commencement stage has passed.
GDPR duties for German users, but no exposure to Indian users until the DPDP Act's duties begin to apply in May 2027.
DPDP duties and penalties for all its users, because the DPDP Act now governs an Indian company to the exclusion of other laws.
quiz.why: The DPDP Act commences in three stages, on 13 November 2025, 13 November 2026 and 13 May 2027, and fiduciaries' duties, breach intimation included, start only at the last; the second stage brought in only the Consent Manager provisions. The GDPR already binds HealthPal for its German users. Indian users are not left without a remedy, because until 13 May 2027 IT Act s. 43A lets a person who suffers wrongful loss from a body corporate's negligent security of sensitive data, which include health data under the SPDI Rules, claim compensation before the adjudicating officer.

quiz.concept: Male victim: offence stays, compounding opens
quiz.q: Riya sends a female colleague's intimate photographs, taken in private and showing her private areas, to a group chat without her consent. Change one fact: the colleague whose private areas they show is an adult man. How does this change the analysis of that act?
quiz.ok: The privacy offence still applies, but it may now be compounded, as the victim-based bar protects only women and children.
no: The privacy offence no longer applies, though the explicit material offence would still apply if the images were explicit.
The privacy offence still applies, but it now becomes bailable, as the victim-based bar protects only women and children.
Nothing changes, because the privacy offence can never be compounded, whatever the sex of the person it harms.
quiz.why: Section 66E protects 'any person', so transmitting a man's private images without consent, in circumstances violating privacy, is still the privacy offence. What changes is compounding: s. 77A bars it for an offence committed against a woman or a child under eighteen, which is why Riya's original act could not be compounded, but an adult man is neither, so the s. 66E offence, punishable with up to three years, may now be compounded; a s. 67A charge, if the images are sexually explicit, stays non-compoundable whoever the victim is. Bail does not change either way, because s. 66E is bailable for every victim.

quiz.concept: No terrorist intent: fallback charges, same duties
quiz.q: Change the water utility facts: in 2028 a ransomware group abroad encrypts the utility's systems, including its customer records, and demands only a ransom. Nothing shows an intent to strike terror, no data are copied out, and water supply fails for two days. Which statement is right?
quiz.ok: The attackers face the civil contravention, its criminal form and extortion, and the utility must still intimate a breach.
no: The attackers still commit cyber terrorism, since cutting an essential service is serious harm whatever the motive.
The attackers face the civil contravention, its criminal form and extortion, but the utility need report nothing, as no data left its systems.
The attackers face only civil liability, since without terrorist intent their conduct is no crime under the IT Act.
quiz.why: Limb (A) of s. 66F needs a specific terrorist intent, so disrupting an essential service is not enough on its own; without that intent the notes' fallback applies: s. 43, its criminal form in s. 66 (a ransom demand is plainly dishonest), and BNS extortion. The utility's duties do not depend on the attackers' motive: encrypting customer records causes a loss of access that compromises their availability, which is a personal data breach (s. 2(u)), so it must intimate the Board and its customers (s. 8(6), Rule 7). The 'only civil liability' option forgets that dishonesty turns a s. 43 act into a s. 66 offence.

quiz.concept: Build cyber terrorism on the section's text
quiz.q: A student's answer to the water utility problem convicts the group of a terrorist act under the UAPA and the BNS, relies on Anees Ansari as settling that attacks on essential services are cyber terrorism, and never works through the IT Act offence. What is the strongest criticism of the answer?
quiz.ok: It leans on an unverified overlap and a trial court report, not on the elements of the IT Act offence.
no: It relies on the UAPA and the BNS, which the notes' dagger marks as wrong on the definition of terrorism.
It misses that the IT Act offence needs no proof of terrorist intent once essential services are disrupted.
It misses that Anees Ansari confined cyber attacks to the IT Act, which excludes the UAPA and the BNS.
quiz.why: The UAPA s. 15 and BNS s. 113 overlap carries a dagger: it rests on secondary knowledge not checked against the primary text, so it should be mentioned and flagged while the answer is built on the text of s. 66F, element by element (intent, act and harm). Anees Ansari is only a press-reported 2022 sessions court conviction, and no appellate judgment on s. 66F was located, so it illustrates rather than settles. A dagger means 'verify before quoting', not 'wrong', and Limb (A) needs terrorist intent however serious the disruption.

quiz.concept: Same weak point under both constitutional tests
quiz.q: An EU Member State law and an Indian statute each let a health ministry read any health app user's symptom data at any time, for any public health purpose. Judged against each system's constitutional protection, which assessment is right?
quiz.ok: Both are open to challenge for want of necessity and proportionality, despite their legal basis and aim.
no: Only the EU law is open to challenge, since in India a basis in a statute is all that a State measure needs.
Both are open to challenge, but the EU law only under the human rights Convention, as the EU has no data protection right.
Neither is open to challenge, since public health is a legitimate aim that justifies the access in both systems.
quiz.why: In the EU, data protection is a fundamental right in its own name under Charter Article 8, distinct from private life (Charter Article 7 and Article 8 ECHR), and any limit must be provided by law, respect its essence, and be necessary and proportionate (Article 52(1)). In India, Puttaswamy (2017) makes informational privacy part of Article 21, so a State measure needs legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality. Each law has a legal basis and a legitimate aim, but blanket access to every user's health data at any time and for any purpose is where both are vulnerable; the 'India needs only a statute' option is the error that Puttaswamy rules out.

quiz.concept: Tampering offence needs legally required code
quiz.q: Suppose that, before leaving, Riya dishonestly deletes and alters parts of her employer's source code to sabotage a product launch. The code is ordinary product code that the company keeps for its own business reasons. The prosecutor proposes the IT Act's source code tampering offence, arguing that the code is the company's most valuable asset. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.ok: It overlooks that the offence needs code kept under a legal duty, so this is a contravention made criminal by dishonesty.
no: Nothing, because the tampering offence protects any proprietary or confidential code that an employee damages or alters.
It overlooks that tampering with code is a purely civil wrong, so the company can only seek compensation for it.
It overlooks that proprietary code is protected by copyright alone, so the IT Act cannot reach the tampering.
quiz.why: Section 65 punishes tampering only with source code that the law requires to be kept or maintained; Syed Asifuddin (29 July 2005, not 2006 as class slide 18 says) read 'source code' broadly but did not remove that ingredient, and the code's value is irrelevant to it. Without it, Riya's deletions and alterations are contraventions under s. 43(d) and (i), and under s. 43(j) because she altered source code intending damage, and her dishonesty makes them a s. 66 offence. The 'purely civil' option misses that s. 66 is the criminal form of s. 43.

quiz.concept: Recipient identifiability: SRB read with Breyer
quiz.q: HealthPal pseudonymises German users' symptom records, keeps the re-identification key itself, and gives the coded dataset to a university. Relying on a class slide, a student says the coded data are personal data in everyone's hands. Which fact, if true, would make the student right about the university?
quiz.ok: The university can lawfully obtain the key from HealthPal whenever it needs to identify a user.
no: HealthPal itself can re-identify every user at any time, using the key that it keeps in Pune.
The coded records concern users' health, which places them among the special categories of data.
HealthPal stores the key on the same servers as the original, uncoded symptom records.
quiz.why: Class slide 24 is right for the key holder, but EDPS v SRB (2025) holds that pseudonymised data are not personal data in all cases and for every person: for a recipient unable reasonably to re-identify, they may not be. Identifiability is judged from the holder's position, including lawful means of obtaining information held by others (Breyer), so a lawful route to the key would make the coded data personal data for the university too. HealthPal's own ability to re-identify settles only its own position, and neither the sensitivity of the data nor where HealthPal stores the key affects whether the university can identify anyone.

quiz.concept: IT Act unchanged, IPC charges become BNS
quiz.q: A class slide reports a 2023 voyeurism arrest booked under the IPC's voyeurism and personation sections and the IT Act's privacy offence. For identical conduct in 2026, a student copies all three charges unchanged. Which correction best reflects the notes?
quiz.ok: Keep the IT Act charge and cite the BNS equivalents in place of the two IPC sections.
no: Recharge all three under the BNS, which replaced the IT Act's offences along with the IPC in 2024.
Keep all three charges, since the class slides set out the general law on which the course is examined.
Keep the IT Act charge alone, since the special privacy offence now excludes the general law for that act.
quiz.why: The IPC was repealed from 1 July 2024, so for conduct in 2026 the slide's voyeurism and personation sections give way to their BNS equivalents (reportedly BNS ss. 77 and 319, numbers the notes mark as unverified and to be flagged), while IT Act offences such as s. 66E are unchanged. The IT Act does not automatically exclude the general law: s. 66E and voyeurism are usually charged together, and voyeurism has ingredients of its own, such as a woman engaged in a private act. The 'all three under the BNS' option wrongly assumes that the new codes absorbed the IT Act.

quiz.concept: Full Bench ingredient test, both ways
quiz.q: Riya is prosecuted in Mumbai under the IT Act for dishonestly copying the code and deleting the client files. The prosecution seeks to add two BNS charges: one resting on nothing beyond the same dishonest copying and deletion, and one for cheating, alleging that she deceived the IT desk into granting the access she used to copy the code. How should the court treat them?
quiz.ok: Add the cheating charge, as deception is no ingredient of the IT Act offences charged, but not the other.
no: Add both, because the Full Bench now lets general charges run alongside IT Act charges for the same conduct.
Add neither, because Gagan Harsh Sharma bars general charges wherever the IT Act already covers the conduct.
Add both, because Gagan Harsh Sharma concerned only the IPC, which the BNS replaced from 1 July 2024.
quiz.why: Gagan Harsh Sharma quashed IPC charges because the IT Act covered the conduct, but the Bombay High Court Full Bench has since qualified it, and that is the law for a court in Mumbai: compare ingredients, and let a general offence run alongside the IT Act only where it has an ingredient the special provision lacks. Cheating needs deception, which s. 43 read with s. 66 does not, so that charge may be added; a charge resting only on the same dishonest copying and deletion adds nothing, and the special scheme governs. The BNS's replacement of the IPC changes the code the comparison is made against, not the test.

quiz.concept: Struck-down provision versus live offences
quiz.q: In 2026, police register an FIR over a man's 2020 post under the IT Act provision struck down in Shreya Singhal, arguing that it was formally omitted only from 30 November 2023. The post is offensive but contains nothing sexual. What would the police need for a charge that can stand?
quiz.ok: A post that is lascivious or appeals to the prurient interest, which would bring in electronic obscenity.
no: An FIR registered before 30 November 2023, while the struck-down provision was still on the statute book.
A finding that vulgar abuse and expletives alone make a post obscene if they would corrupt young readers.
A charge of publishing sexually explicit material, which needs no proof that the post tends to deprave.
quiz.why: Section 66A was struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015); its formal omission from 30 November 2023 did not keep it alive in between, which is why the notes say it must never be cited as live law, so no FIR date can revive a charge under it. A live offence is needed instead: s. 67 if the post is lascivious or appeals to the prurient interest, judged by community standards. Vulgar abuse is not enough, because Apoorva Arora (2024) holds that vulgarity and profanity are not obscenity, and s. 67A needs a sexually explicit act, which a post with nothing sexual lacks.
